The world’s best racing driver is about to race 100 karts at once

Ars Technica September 16, 2026

Red Bull, Disney+, and ESPN are streaming the race at noon Eastern today.

Later today, Max Verstappen will strap on his helmet and take to the track at the Silverstone circuit in England for a rather unusual race. The four-time Formula 1 world champion is recognized as the leading talent of his generation, but unlike some of the legends that have preceded him, Verstappen’s passion for motorsport extends beyond just the rarified world of F1. With apologies to Midweek Motorsport, but if it has wheels and they keep score, odds are good Verstappen’s down to race it. So at noon Eastern Time (5 pm BST) today, September 16, Verstappen will slip into something a little more basic: a kart.

It’s one of 101 identical karts that have been sourced from Eastern Europe for the event—the other 100 will be driven by a mix of content creators and Red Bull athletes, all of whom fancy their chances at beating one of the world’s greatest drivers at his own game. They get a bit of an advantage, all starting ahead of Verstappen. Once he passes another karter, they’re out of the race, and Verstappen has 30 laps of a purpose-designed layout at Silverstone to get through them all and win.

Other F1 drivers have attempted slightly similar challenges in the past—Alex Albon raced 25 kids last year, and last month Oliver Bearman raced 50 amateurs. But neither is as high-profile as Verstappen, and neither is facing as much competition.

It might have been many years since Verstappen traded his kart for things larger and faster, but that’s no reason to doubt his abilities.

“Max is pretty unique in comparison to the other Grand Prix drivers in that he’s already done the Nürburgring 24 hours in his GT3. He’s out testing those cars often. I saw his quote saying that it’s been a while since he did karting; do we honestly think that he hasn’t gone and done a little test? It’s Max Verstappen! He’s a serial winner, and therefore he’s not turning up here to shine a spotlight on some other individual. He’s going to go for it, and he’s going to try and achieve this target,” said David Coulthard, a Grand Prix winner and one of Red Bull Racing’s first factory drivers.

“Physically, he’ll be in top shape, of course, but it all depends on just how finely tuned the talents are of the other competitors,” Coulthard told Ars. “Some of the Red Bull athletes I know from my time involved with the company, most of the other sports really love Formula 1. So finding guys and girls that are prepared to jump in a kart and have a go is not difficult. …Formula 1 is the peak, and then karting is where all of those guys have honed their skills. And even the late great Senna, asked about his happiest memories in racing, returned to competing against a British guy called Terry Fullerton and karting when he came over from Brazil to race in Italy. It’s like a first love. There’s a real connection between the highest level of the sport and let’s say the lowest level of the sport.”

Yesterday, those other competitors got some practice time on a shortened version of the layout they’ll use today. And they had some help on hand in the form of another Red Bull racing driver, Arvid Lindblad, who has made his F1 debut this season in the Racing Bulls junior team. Half the field got a taste of today’s race when 50 of them tried to beat Lindblad to the checkered flag. Starting from 51st, he managed to overtake all but one.

“The drivers were trying hard, and that was really cool to see,” said Lindblad. “They weren’t scared or intimidated or anything, with even some of them who aren’t very used to karting. The general level, it wasn’t easy for me. Some of the good guys are fast, and they’re only going to get better.”

Anyone who has ever gone racing in a rental kart knows that the equipment can be highly variable. Not here.

“All of the carts are going to be ballasted to make a complete level playing field weight-wise,” said Simon Corney, senior executive producer with Whisper, which is producing the event. “So everyone has identical equipment, and this was one of the stipulations that Max had as well. He didn’t want any advantage, he didn’t want them to have any advantage. For him, whilst the race is going to be fun and we’ve got a few tricks up our sleeve in terms of broadcast to make it racing, in terms of the actual racing itself, Max and Red Bull wanted it to feel to be a legitimate racing challenge because he wants to win by right.”

If the other karters work together, Verstappen’s day could be quite difficult. “If they all went line astern or side by side, then he’s going to have to get creative. But the one fun thing that I’ve been made aware of is that he’ll be able to talk to all other competitors. So in terms of making this a bigger insight into the minds of the drivers, then I’m curious to know just what spare capacity he has to actually either psych the guys out in front of them or how,” Coulthard said.

Max vs. 100 will air live on Disney+ and ESPN at noon ET today.

Lawmakers target Flock cameras with a threat to highway funding

Ars Technica September 16, 2026

A bipartisan bill would restrict Flock cameras to a handful of public safety uses.

A bipartisan pair of US lawmakers tell WIRED they plan to introduce legislation today that would strip federal funding from states that fail to restrict the use of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers. The devices, which help police track the location of vehicles tied to crimes, have become the subject of nationwide backlash in recent months over more nefarious uses by officers.

The No FLOCK Act—for Federal License-Plate Observation and Camera Keeping—directs the US secretary of transportation to withhold 10 percent of annual financial support due to states for highways, roads, and bridges if it fails to ban Flock and similar devices for all but five use cases. Congressmen Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat representing Chicago suburbs, and Michael Cloud, a Republican whose Texas district includes Corpus Christi, are cosponsoring the bill.

The legislation says that Flock cameras could be used only for “enforcing toll systems, identifying stolen vehicles, missing or endangered persons, vehicles registered to persons with a warrant for a felony offense, or investigating a vehicle involved in a felony offense.” Notably absent are uses like conducting traffic studies, investigating minor drug crimes, and enforcing parking and speeding rules.

“Our investigation into Flock exposed serious gaps in oversight, and this bipartisan bill would put clear limits in place to prevent abuse while preserving legitimate public safety uses,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.

But the bill stops short of banning Flock systems altogether, which has been the number one demand from supporters of a global protest movement against the Atlanta-based company and its competitors. It also doesn’t stop Flock users from broadly sharing license plate tracking data with other government agencies, including immigration authorities.

Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the proposed bill.

If the legislation passes this year, states that fail to comply with it would begin losing out on tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars in annual transportation funding starting in October 2028.

The Department of Transportation calculates the amount of so-called surface transportation funds it gives to states based on factors such as how many roadways they have and how busy they are. Congress has repeatedly threatened taking away the funding to pressure states into taking action on public safety. The tactic helped establish a national minimum drinking age, standard rules for what constitutes driving under the influence, and regulations for billboards alongside highways.

Another bipartisan bill introduced in Congress recently called for banning the use of federal funding to purchase Flock cameras. Flock’s lobbying spending in Washington, DC, has been steady over the past 18 months, and it recently hired a fifth firm to help with the efforts, according to federal records.

A number of issues related to emerging technologies, including rogue AI systems, data center construction, and law enforcement abuse of Flock cameras, have become major topics in the upcoming US midterm elections, which are now less than two months away. But it’s unclear whether any legislation designed to address voters’ concerns will advance through Congress anytime soon, let alone gain the approval of President Donald Trump.

The president expressed support for Flock cameras on Sunday, telling reporters that they help law enforcement authorities. Lawmakers largely agree, but they are frustrated by cases in which police officers have been caught using Flock footage for personal reasons, such as stalking their one-time romantic partners. One report found at least 100 instances of alleged abuse over the past eight years.

“Taxpayers shouldn’t be forced to fund the shredding of their own civil liberties or the growth of a surveillance state,” Cloud said in a statement. “Flock cameras are enabling mass surveillance of Americans, infringing on the Fourth Amendment.”

About 25 states and US territories have laws about automated license plate readers, including mandating transparency about the systems and requiring unnecessary data to be promptly deleted, but few of the measures limit types of uses, according to the New York University School of Law’s Policing Project.

The bill is “a first step toward reining in unchecked surveillance,” Cloud said, adding, “we can protect public safety without sacrificing the privacy of Americans.”

This story originally appeared on wired. com.

How chimps teach their kids tool tricks

Ars Technica September 16, 2026

Adults first demonstrate tool use, then hand over the implements to their infants, who copy the behavior.

Chimpanzees are known to use rudimentary tools when foraging for food. According to a new paper in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, this learned behavior is passed down from adults to offspring through social learning. Specifically, adult chimps deliberately model the behavior, then turn their tools over to the youngsters so they can mimic the same motions.

“Receiving food and tools from experienced individuals, which we call food or tool transfer, may help chimpanzees learn to use technology to extract foods that are difficult to access,” said co-author Andreu Sánchez-Megías, a graduate student at the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute Spain in Senegal. “Tool transfers thus appear to be a form of teaching, together with observation and supervised practice. It appears that mothers are the main models and teachers for young chimpanzees in this manner.”

As we have previously reported, tool use was once thought to be one of the defining features of humans, although Charles Darwin observed chimpanzees using stones to crack nuts in 1871. In 1960, the late primatologist Jane Goodall observed a chimp named David Greybeard bend a twig, strip off the leaves, and use it to spoon termites out of a nest and into his mouth. When he learned of the behavior, Goodall’s mentor, Louis Leakey, famously observed, “Now we must redefine ‘tool,’ redefine ‘man,’ or accept chimpanzees as humans.” Since then, chimps have been observed making sponges out of leaves to soak up liquids, shaping sticks to collect algae, and sharpening rudimentary spears for hunting.

Other examples of tool use have been observed in various species, although the behavior seems to have evolved more frequently among monkeys and apes. Dolphins can toss objects as a form of play, which some scientists consider to be a type of tool use, particularly when it involves another member of the same species. Potential purposes include communication, social bonding, or aggression. (Octopuses have also been observed engaging in similar throwing behavior.)

In the wild, observed tool use by birds has been limited to the corvids (crows and jays), which show various other complex behaviors—they’ll remember your face and recognize the passing of their dead. In 2012, a captive cockatoo named Figaro was observed spontaneously using multiple steps to process a tool, behavior has never been seen in this species in the wild. And earlier this year, a pet Swiss brown cow in Austria named Veronika caused a sensation because she likes to pick up random sticks and use them to scratch herself. It’s a form of multipurpose tool use and suggests that the cognitive capabilities of cows have been underestimated by scientists.

This latest study focuses specifically on tool transfer behavior in chimpanzees. Chimpanzees are known to be social learners, and according to the authors, prior research has shown that chimpanzees’ mirror neurons fire in response to both actions directed to objects (transitive) and not directed to objects (intransitive), much like humans. So chimps were ideal subjects to study the role of social learning in tool transfer.

Between 2017 and 2025, the authors collected observational data from the chimpanzee population at the Dindefelo Community Nature Reserve just southeast of Senegal, in the Kedougou region. They ended up with nearly 15 hours of video footage from camera traps set up at 14 different locations. Subsequent analysis of the footage revealed 33 instances of tool transfer behavior and three attempts (where a tool was either offered and rejected, or another chimp attempted to take a tool and failed). They also captured four instances of baobab fruit transfers; the chimps use stone or hard pieces of wood to crack open the fruit, an example of proto-tool use.

Of the tool transfers, 58 percent were in the context of ant dipping (using a twig to scoop up ants), while 30 percent and 12 percent, respectively, occurred during algae fishing and termite fishing. The original tool holders were usually adults (58 percent) and predominantly female, with most of the recipients (42 percent) being infants. About 30 percent of the tool transfers were a mother handing the tool to her offspring, and in all but one case, the recipient initiated the voluntary transfer. There were a couple of cases where a chimp simply stole the tool or fruit, prompting a retaliatory strike from the original holder or said holder grabbing back the tool.

The authors highlighted two case studies of tool transfer in particular: one involving ant-dipping (see video above), the other involving baobab fruit transfer (see video below). In the first, recorded in February 2018, a small group of chimps was clustered around an ant nest as the adults engaged in ant-dipping. An adult female named Soukki dipped a twig into the ant nest and left it there as she brought over her infant, Saïsaï. Saïsaï then pulled out the twig and ate the collected ants. A subsequent recording showed Saïsaï fully mimicking her mother’s ant-dipping behavior.

In the second case study, recorded in December 2021, a mother chimp named Féré brought three baobab fruits to a rocky outcrop with several other chimps, including her male infant, Fotti. Fotti initially tried and failed to break open a baobab fruit by sweeping it along the rocky surface several times. Then a male juvenile showed up, grabbed the fruit, and pounded it against the rocky outcrop a few times, then guided Fotti’s hand to help him mimic the motion. Fotti can be seen watching the juvenile closely and then repeating the pounding motions, eventually succeeding in breaking open the fruit (although he dropped it off the outcrop’s edge afterward).

“Teaching is one of the strategies that chimpanzees use to transfer information and skills between individuals,” said Sánchez-Megías. “It requires an active role from the teacher, who must modify their behavior to facilitate the transmission of information to the learner, and this is why teaching is thought to have evolved to transfer information that is too complex to be acquired through simpler mechanisms, such as individual or observational learning.”

Frontiers in Psychology, 2026. DOI: 10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1868894 (About DOIs).

The Roman telescope has enough gas for 22 years, double NASA’s expectations

Ars Technica September 15, 2026

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is the first NASA observatory designed for in-space refueling.

NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is gliding toward its distant observation post on a pinpoint trajectory so precise that engineers estimate the spacecraft’s fuel load will last twice as long as their initial expectations, the space agency confirmed Monday.

The $4.3 billion observatory’s designers originally planned to load enough propellant into Roman’s four fuel tanks for a minimum lifetime of five years, plus a potential five-year mission extension. That was a conservative estimate. NASA officials knew an on-target launch and perfect execution of the observatory’s first post-launch course correction maneuver would leave Roman with a hearty fuel reserve.

“As a result of exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team, brilliant execution by the operations team, and a precise launch from SpaceX, Roman has fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations,” Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, said in a press release.

The James Webb Space Telescope received a similar lifetime boost after a picture-perfect launch on a European Ariane 5 rocket in 2021.

The Roman telescope launched August 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, kicking off a mission to widen our view of the Universe. Roman’s telescope and scientific instruments will provide astronomers with images of the sky at the same resolution as NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, but with 100 times the field of view. It would take Hubble a century to observe what Roman will see in a month.

Astronomers hope Roman’s broad vision will reveal insights into the largest structures in the Universe. Roman’s Wide Field Instrument, fitted with 18 near-infrared detectors, will produce images equivalent to those of a 300-megapixel camera. Its wide viewing area will allow Roman to map galactic clusters, along with the filaments of matter and dark matter that string through the cosmos. Mapping so much of the sky could help astronomers study the nature of dark energy, scientists’ name for the elusive force driving the acceleration of the Universe.

The Falcon Heavy released Roman on a trajectory that will take it a million miles from Earth, where the spacecraft will loop into a “quasi-halo” orbit around the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, a point of balance between the gravitational pull of Earth and the Sun. It will take Roman about three months to reach L2.

The launch was so accurate that the first big burn with Roman’s control thrusters, executed one day into the mission, consumed just 40 pounds (18 kilograms) of hydrazine fuel, down from the preflight allocation of 441 pounds (200 kilograms), NASA said.

“I do thank SpaceX for putting us down the middle. It’s going to help us in terms of long-duration performance, how long we can stay at L2, as well as our positioning capability,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA’s associate administrator, during a talk Tuesday at the American Astronautical Society’s Glenn Space Technology Symposium.

Roman launched nine months ahead of the schedule set by NASA during the mission’s confirmation review in 2020. It also launched lighter than planned. Both are rather unusual in the annals of NASA science missions.

The observatory’s actual weight at completion was 17,760 pounds (8,056 kilograms), approximately two tons less than its maximum allowable weight. This allowed ground crews at Kennedy Space Center to load 290 gallons of hydrazine into Roman’s fuel tanks, more than engineers anticipated early in the mission’s design phase. The hydrazine feeds 24 thrusters scattered around the outside of the observatory.

At launch, the fully fueled Roman observatory weighed 20,224 pounds (9,173.5 kilograms), still a half-ton below its weight limit, a NASA spokesperson told Ars. In addition to the extra fuel, Roman’s lower mass meant its thrusters did not have to fire as long for the course correction maneuver the day after launch.

“A spacecraft’s mass changes throughout the design and build process, so we base the propellant budget on a set maximum value so we won’t come up short,” said Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard. “We track the propellant needed based on actual mass throughout integration and testing as well, to make sure we have wiggle room. Since Roman’s was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed to for the 10-year requirement.”

A second course correction planned for later this month will give Roman the last tiny boost to get into position for another maneuver in early December to slip into its final orbit at L2. “According to current projections, both maneuvers will use less fuel than planned, potentially saving even more for future science,” NASA said.

Roman’s thrusters will perform additional station-keeping burns roughly every 28 days. The observatory will also use its propulsion system to periodically unload momentum from its six reaction wheels, which normally control Roman’s pointing.

The mission’s exceptional fuel savings lower the likelihood that NASA will need to send a refueling mission to Roman any time soon. The observatory’s life-limiting resource will likely be propellant, and NASA set a requirement early on in Roman’s development that the spacecraft be refuelable.

NASA has serviced a space telescope before. Astronauts on five Space Shuttle flights visited Hubble to carry out a range of tasks, including repairs of the telescope’s aberrant vision, maintenance work, and the installation of more powerful science instruments. Hubble does not have a propulsion system, so visiting Space Shuttles also boosted the observatory’s orbit around Earth.

Officials prepared Roman to receive a potential uncrewed servicing mission. NASA attached a grapple fixture on the bottom of Roman similar to those used by the robotic arms on the International Space Station and the Space Shuttle. Roman also has navigation aids—a retroreflector and external reference points—to help guide a servicing mission on final approach.

“While Roman is nowhere near as serviceable as the Hubble Space Telescope was, we do have everything that’s necessary to enable the rendezvous and capture and docking with a hypothetical servicer; that’s the point of the grapple fixture,” said Jackie Townsend, Roman’s project manager at NASA Goddard. “Then, in 2020, when we were baselined, we were told that we would focus on refueling. So the blanketing around the fueling port has been designed especially so that it’s easier for a robot to get in there if we needed to refuel.”

The blanketing around the fueling port also has a magnetic closure to simplify opening and re-closing by a robotic servicer, Townsend told Ars.

There are no servicing spacecraft currently available that could travel out to Roman’s position a million miles from Earth. Several US companies are developing refueling satellites for use in low-Earth orbit and geosynchronous orbit, primarily for the US Space Force. Two Chinese spacecraft docked last year to conduct the first satellite-to-satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit.

Everything else onboard Roman has been working well for more than two weeks since launch, according to Kshatriya, NASA’s highest-ranking civil servant. The telescope opened its aperture cover on September 1, allowing starlight to fall on its primary mirror for the first time.

“All the preliminary checks are good,” Kshatriya said. “In fact, we got some data on the Wide Field Instrument just a couple days ago. All the mirrors, all the CCDs are chilling down in the right way. We do false current tests to make sure that we’re getting the right connectivity, etc. All that’s green across the board on all 18 (detectors), which is awesome.”

Roman’s other instrument, a coronagraph designed for direct imaging of exoplanets, also performed well during preliminary checkouts.

“When we get first light, it’s going to be a big party,” Kshatriya said.

“Filmmaker” suing PassThePopcorn may be banned user out for revenge

Ars Technica September 15, 2026

Allegedly fake filmmaker targeted trackers like PassThePopcorn, BroadcasTheNet, and HDBits.

Some of the most widely used private torrent trackers for pirating movies suspect that a banned user may have posed as a filmmaker protecting copyrights in a failed attempt to seek revenge.

TorrentFreak has been tracking this story closely, reporting last September that an alleged independent filmmaker named Matthew Schneider sued six private trackers for infringing copyrights on some films that he supposedly made. Trackers targeted include PassThePopcorn, BroadcasTheNet, and HDBits. For months, the filmmaker sought to get Cloudflare to unmask operators of the trackers through a copyright fight, which went on until trackers alerted the court last month that Schneider appeared to be an impostor.

In a sworn declaration, the actual filmmaker behind the movies cited in the complaint wrote that he had no association to the plaintiff in the case. “I am not involved in, nor have I ever appeared in, this case,” Schneider wrote.

To keep the copyright fight alive, the plaintiff swore, “I’m a different Matthew Schneider.” He then claimed to have coincidentally made three films with the same exact titles as the other filmmaker’s movies, Split: A Film Anthology, Do Us Part, and Orlando Gloom, Always the Same.

For the judge, Andrea R. Wood, this unusual turn in what could have been a major case was unexpected. TorrentFreak noted that this was the first copyright case to target “multiple prominent private torrent trackers,” and the judge warned that the plaintiff could face sanctions if the private trackers’ allegations were true and he filed a frivolous claim with intent to deceive the court.

As pressure mounted on the plaintiff to clarify his complaint, he abruptly decided to voluntarily dismiss the claims, TorrentFreak reported Tuesday. But that last-minute move might not save him from being sanctioned.

At a hearing that TorrentFreak attended, one of the attorneys representing one of the tracker operators, Erin Russell, confirmed that at least one defendant would be seeking sanctions.

Although the plaintiff maintained at the hearing that his legal name is Matthew Schneider, the defense raised an alternate theory the trackers have about his true identity.

Linked to the email address that the plaintiff used in his self-represented court filings, an account was found that showed he was “not a stranger to private torrents” and was likely banned for selling or trading invites, TorrentFreak reported. Most likely, the plaintiff is a disgruntled user of private trackers who “bears ill will” over their likely blacklisting, Russell suggested, without showing evidence.

For the private trackers, sanctioning the plaintiff will depend on proving more than just that he’s not who he says he is, though. The court will need to know his actual identity to form a judgment and know who to sanction, which Russell said at the hearing will be a practical challenge for private trackers frustrated by these developments.

At the next hearing on October 2, the plaintiff will seemingly have one last chance to defend his claims as genuine. Not only will he be required to appear on camera, showing defendants who they’re really up against for the first time, but the judge is also supposed to review one of the films that he allegedly made that shares a title with one of the other Schneider’s movies.

It’s “an odd situation,” Judge Wood told defense counsel at the hearing, where the plaintiff promised to end delays and send over a copy of his movie, as well as enter a sworn affidavit in response to the sanctions motion.

18-year-old dies of measles in PA from severe neurological complication

Ars Technica September 15, 2026

Teen developed acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a known measles complication.

A fourth person in Pennsylvania has died of measles, the state health department confirmed Tuesday. The latest death was in an unvaccinated 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County.

In the announcement, the state health department also confirmed a county coroner’s report over the weekend of the death of an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County. The state had previously reported two deaths in Lancaster County; both were infants—a newborn boy and a 6-week-old girl, both too young to be vaccinated.

According to the Mifflin County coroner, Andrea L. Alcalde, the 18-year-old’s cause of death was determined to be acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), which is a rare but known severe complication of measles. The condition is characterized by a rapidly progressing autoimmune disorder in which aberrant inflammation from an infection strips away the protective coverings of nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. Before measles vaccines were widely used, ADEM was commonly associated with measles, though other viral infections can also spur its development.

In a new release posted to the coroner’s Facebook page Tuesday, Alcalde said the death determination was made after a review of medical records and all available information. Alcalde said no other information would be released about the deceased.

The state health department released a statement confirming the measles death of the 18-year-old, as well as the death of the 40-year-old. The two deaths will be added to the state’s outbreak data dashboard Wednesday as part of the regular update, the department noted.

So far, the state has reported 693 measles cases in 38 counties this year. There have been 99 cases reported in the last seven days. In all, 133 people have been hospitalized.

“My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen said in a statement, referring to the two latest deaths. “We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the MMR [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccine—which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades.”

The deaths are unlikely to be quickly included in national data collected by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which is under the tight control of anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Amid Pennsylvania’s deadly outbreak, Kennedy has disputed deaths, spread misinformation about the MMR vaccine, and reportedly ordered the CDC director to exclude reports of the two babies’ deaths.

The CDC has also changed how it counts measles deaths in national reporting. The agency previously relied on determinations and reporting from state and local health officials. Now, it says, it will only report death records received by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which is a system designed not to monitor ongoing outbreaks but to track death trends over long periods. The US Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, did not respond to questions from Ars Technica about the new rule.

Pennsylvania’s state health department noted in its announcement today that its determinations of measles-associated deaths were made after thorough investigations. The state uses a measles-associated death definition modeled after criteria for illness-associated death determinations set by the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE).

Even with changes to the CDC’s measles data reporting and suspicions that many cases are going undetected, the CDC is still reporting nearly 3,300 measles cases this year. That’s higher than last year’s record tally of 2,289 cases, which led to three deaths. It’s also the highest total seen since 1991, when there were 9,643 cases. The US declared measles eliminated in 2000 after blocking domestic transmission over a 12-month period via high vaccination rates. With vaccination rates slipping well below the target of 95 percent, measles is roaring back, and the US is on track to lose its elimination status.

SpaceX declares Starship ready for orbit, sets launch date next week

Ars Technica September 15, 2026

Reaching orbit would mark a significant milestone.

Pending regulatory approval, SpaceX said today it intends to launch its 14th Starship mission as early as September 22. This flight is notable, as it will be the first time that SpaceX attempts to launch the experimental vehicle into orbit.

The company set a target liftoff time of 7:15 am local in Texas (12:15 UTC), with a 75-minute launch window. Sunrise in Brownsville, Texas, is 7:17 am CT, so the launch could make for some striking imagery.

The super heavy lift rocket will be carrying 26 of the larger V3 Starlink satellites into an orbit 275 km above the Earth. In an update on its website, SpaceX said the Starship upper stage will seek to complete six orbits around the Earth before completing its mission after about 10 hours.

Reaching orbit would mark a significant milestone in the company’s Starship development campaign, which conducted its first test flight on April 20, 2023, and has since made progress in fits and starts. With the upcoming mission, SpaceX continues to make modifications to the Starship vehicle as it seeks to improve the third iteration of the Super Heavy booster and Starship upper stage. After recent successes, the company appears to be closer to developing a fully reusable, super heavy lift rocket.

During the most recent Starship test flight on July 24, the vehicle’s first stage performed nominally during ascent. However, after a successful boostback burn, the vehicle experienced problems during the return through Earth’s atmosphere.

“In the terminal phase of the burn, the three center engines showed signs of ice clogging, which triggered an early end to the maneuver,” SpaceX said in its update on Tuesday. “The booster went on to attempt a landing burn, with 8 of the 13 planned engines reigniting before the booster made a hard splashdown in the Gulf. The Super Heavy on this upcoming flight has hardware modifications to improve filtering to the engines and software changes to enhance relight reliability.”

Accordingly, this first stage will not attempt to return to the launch site. Rather, it will attempt to make a controlled landing in the Gulf of Mexico. If successful, this could set up a first-stage catch on the subsequent flight of Starship.

During the upcoming test flight, the upper stage will attempt to reach orbit for the first time and deploy operational payloads. These Starlink satellites, significantly more capable than V2 mini Starlink satellites launched on a Falcon 9 mission, will then use onboard propulsion to raise their orbits.

Despite a largely successful ocean landing of the Starship upper stage during the July test flight, this mission will not attempt a return of the upper stage to the launch site in Texas. Instead, SpaceX plans to gather more data about heat shield performance. The company said it had made several upgrades since the mission two months ago, based on data gleaned from the vehicle both in flight and once recovered in the Indian Ocean, largely intact.

“[The upgrades] include additional retention mechanisms added to tiles in areas deemed to be at highest risk of falling off during ascent, addressing recently discovered areas that offer flow paths behind tiles for plasma, and flying multiple areas with a curved tile design that has shown the ability to reduce heating in the gaps between tiles,” the company said.

Additionally, two tiles recovered from Ship 40 are planned to be reflown on Ship 41, marking the first tile reuse for Starship.

Xtracycle’s Swoop ASM e-bike brings an automatic transmission to cargo bikes

Ars Technica Long form August 26, 2026

A steel frame cargo bike with a unique twist: You can let it choose your gear.

The Velotric Discover M e-bike we reviewed earlier this year had a feature I found somewhat annoying: It would sporadically block much of the display with an alert telling me I should be in a different gear. While the implementation bugged me, the concept made a certain degree of sense; most e-bikes now know your cadence, how much torque you’re generating, and how that power is being translated into speed. That’s everything you need to know to determine an optimal gear.

Somewhere in the back of my mind, I thought, “If you’re so smart, why don’t you just shift for me?”

I was completely unaware that Shimano had already developed a system that did exactly that. And for the past few weeks, I’ve been using it on a $4,500 cargo bike from Xtracycle called the Swoop ASM that let me see what it’s like to hand control of my gears to an electronic brain.

The short answer is that the electronics on the Swoop really are smart enough to figure out when it should be shifting. But the system is less adept at the actual shifting process, making for rides that are less smooth than they could be when it’s active. But you can shut that feature off, and the Swoop will shine as a fantastic cargo bike.

Xtracycle got its start providing cargo trailers for mountain bikes and then branched into dedicated cargo bikes. The Swoop ASM is a long-tail cargo bike with what’s called a mullet setup: a larger tire up front and a smaller one in back. The small wheel is designed to help keep the weight held by the large rear rack a bit closer to the road. It also has a front suspension to help cushion the ride.

Notably, the bike is built with steel tubes. Most manufacturers’ lineups use a mix of either carbon fiber and aluminum because those two materials can be made into the exact same shape, simplifying manufacturing. But other materials still have their fans, as they can offer distinct combinations of weight, stiffness, and vibration dissipation.

I haven’t owned a steel tube bike since the 1990s, but the Swoop was a good reminder of why it still has its fans. It’s relatively lightweight (just under 70 lbs/31 kg) for its size, its ride is very comfortable, and it was surprisingly responsive when I stood in the pedals to accelerate away from stops. Despite its highly specialized geometry, the Swoop felt like a fundamentally good bicycle.

There are limits to how well a single frame size can adapt to different body sizes, but Xtracycle does its best to widen the comfort window. It includes a double-telescoping seat post to maximize the seat-pedal distance flexibility. There’s also a quick release on the front handlebar clamp, making it easy to tweak the angle where the grips meet your hands. I found settings that were relatively comfortable but still a bit short of ideal for my 6-plus-foot (188 cm) frame—even with the seat post at its recommended maximum, I could touch the toes of both of my feet down while seated.

Beyond that, plenty of nice touches make this a solid cargo bike. These include protective covers for the rear wheel and chain to keep clothing and limbs from accidentally getting entangled. A robust U-shaped kickstand keeps the bike stable even if you park it when fully loaded, and there’s a front cargo rack that can hold some baggage.

The rear rack can be outfitted with a large range of accessories; mine came with the default setup meant for carrying passengers. This means footrests extending out at the level of the rear hub and two handgrip bars running parallel to the bench seating. But remove a soft cover, and the metal beneath reveals a series of slots that allow a wide variety of attachments to be fitted into place.

You can also use one of Xtracycle’s bag attachments in this setup; I was provided one that ran the full length of the rear attachment and held a fair amount of cargo. Adding a second would have handled all of my typical shopping needs. (While having only one bag might seem awkward, the bike performed very well with everything I was carrying loaded on one side.)

The only problem is that this hardware makes the rear wheel extremely difficult to reach. I struggled to lock the back tire to anything, and I considered myself fortunate to not have to figure out how to deal with a flat.

All those basics make the Swoop a solid entry into the cargo bike market. What sets it apart is its use of a Shimano Cues Di2, one of the component maker’s low-end electronic shifting systems. Its mere existence surprised me, since I thought Shimano was reserving electronic shifting for higher-end component lines. But the company not only took it lower in the range; it added a couple of surprise features to its electronic shifting.

First, the basics: the drivetrain uses a single chainring on the cranks and a 10-speed rear cassette. The rear derailleur requires only a power source and control signals—no cable required. Once properly aligned with the cassette gears, it executes a perfect shift every time it’s told to. This shift includes a brief period when the derailleur over-travels to ensure the chain engages the next ring along, then drops back into the optimal location for continued cycling.

Everything in the system—the derailleur, the controllers, and the motor—takes power from a single removable battery. If the battery’s charge is good, you’re set to ride.

The mid-motor offers three levels of assist, adjusted through a controller on the left side that also includes the power button and a simple display. Shifting is controlled by the one on the right, which lacks a display. Separating the two allows each to be fairly minimalist, making it easy to find the control you need by feel.

On its own, the system worked beautifully. Shifting was fuss-free, and each change was blissfully silent. The assist worked well, and its three levels seemed to cover any needs short of going up steep hills with lots of cargo. This is not a bike that lets you skimp on pedaling in hot conditions; there’s no throttle, and even the highest setting of assist still requires you to exert some force on the pedals. But the motor definitely cuts down on the effort you have to make.

The battery, while looking fairly compact, easily handled dozens of miles without needing a recharge, which means several days of typical errands. While the battery lacks a carrying handle, it’s easy to take it out to charge it, as it pivots sideways out of the frame. When in place, it acts as a protector that keeps anything on the left side of the bike from sliding through the frame and getting tangled in the chain.

This is the first Shimano e-bike system I’ve tested, and it was just as good as you’d expect from a company that has come to dominate cycling drivetrains. Shimano Cues may be its lower-end system, but there’s no apparent skimping on the quality. And that’s before the bonus surprises Shimano has included.

Somewhere in one of the controllers, Shimano’s software gathers all the relevant information about your ride: how fast you’re going, how much force your feet are exerting on the cranks, what gear you’re in, and how fast your legs are churning (and possibly more?). And it uses that data to do a couple of interesting things.

One is what it calls Free Shift. Normally, a bike can’t shift to a different gear unless you’re turning the pedals to move the chain, which can potentially create problems. For example, you could move the derailleur down a gear but not complete the shift before stopping, meaning that the shift would be made when you start pedaling again, and the chain is under a lot of tension as you crank away from a full stop. Or you could move the derailleur several gears over without the chain following.

But the whole point of having a motor is to move the chain. So if you shift without pedaling and the bike isn’t stationary, the Cues system will use the motor to move the chain just enough to complete the shift. It does so without speeding up the bike at all.

Practically, this means that as you coast to a stop, you can simply hit the downshift button a few times, and the system will go into a low gear to make it easy to start up again without requiring you to turn the cranks. It’s … weird. Decades of cycling experience have programmed me to instinctually move my legs when I shift. Those instincts are suddenly superfluous.

It gets even weirder if you enable the automatic transmission. Shimano has included two settings, one for general riding and one for hauling cargo or passengers. When the system recognizes that you can get more out of your pedaling in a different gear, it will simply move you into that gear. That includes doing all the downshifting as you’re coasting to a stop and rolling back up through the gears again as you accelerate away from it.

Let me make that clear: You can coast to a stop without turning the cranks or touching the shifter, and you’ll still be in a different gear when you start up again.

The system is remarkably good at matching when I feel a shift is needed—Shimano’s programmers have done a fine job. Because of that, it’s pretty easy to induce a shift by altering your pedaling, as well. You can tell when it’s close, and just a bit more force will cause the system to send you up a gear. It’s kind of pointless to do so, since the buttons that shift up and down still work when it’s in auto mode, but I found myself doing it regardless.

The downside is that these shifts are not situations where instinctual actions are superfluous. To execute a smooth shift, you have to ease tension off the drivetrain by pedaling with less force, allowing the chain to slide over onto a neighboring gear with a bit less stress. Failing to do so can make for a clunky, inefficient shift and wear down components over time.

My problem with the automatic transmission mode was that I could tell when a shift was likely to come, but I couldn’t predict its precise moment. So it typically came while I was pedaling away happily, with full tension on the chain, making for a loud and awkward shift. This was especially unpleasant when accelerating away from a stop, when the bike would make three or four clunky shifts in rapid succession, each emitting a noise that told me I’d just done something I’d spent years learning to avoid. Living in a neighborhood with lots of four-way stops meant I sometimes experienced that every single block.

Shimano is not stupid, and these systems use parts that are specifically hardened to handle the added strain and wear. But it still felt bad every time I heard and felt that clunk.

The Swoop is not an inexpensive bike; at $4,500, it sits somewhere between the Trek Fetch+ 2 and the Urban Arrow Family I’ve reviewed previously. While it lacks the latter’s capacious cargo tub, the longtail form factor provides a much more bicycle-like riding experience. I’d rate its ride as superior to the Trek because of its frame and front suspension made for a more pleasant ride.

I also prefer Shimano’s drive system to the Bosch used by the other two bikes. It just felt better integrated with my pedaling, plus a bit quieter and less intrusive. The electronic shifting is a bonus—it’s not needed, but it definitely makes for a nice experience, and one where Shimano’s integration means you don’t have to worry about the status of the two additional batteries needed by many electronic systems. I don’t think I’d use the automatic shifting, but I could see where a less experienced cyclist might feel they benefit from it.

So while it’s on the pricier side, the cost seems to be in line with the features it offers. If those features are important to you, the Swoop is definitely worth consideration.

In the end, though, I’m not a huge fan of electronic shifting. I hate worrying about battery levels just to ride my bike, and I like the feel of a well-aligned mechanical shifter clicking into place. But even I have to admit that Shimano’s software does a fantastic job of shifting at the right times, and I think the system could really work well for anybody who hasn’t learned to associate a clunky-sounding shift with bad things.

Google Pixel 11 series review: Is the magic fading?

Ars Technica Long form August 19, 2026

Google’s new Pixels make some compromises but still manage to be good phones.

Google’s approach to making smartphones has changed a lot over the years. It started with Nexus phones aimed at the tinkerer and enthusiast niche back when there were countless companies making smartphones. Today, there are far fewer, and Google’s hyper-polished Pixel lineup is seeing less competition and higher sales. So maybe Google thinks it can just keep doing what works. The new Pixel 11 series is Google’s most refined yet, featuring sleek designs, smart software, and incredible screens. They’re also rather boring.

Google made precious few hardware changes in its 2026 phones, shaving off a fraction of a millimeter here and dropping a gram there. The design language has been the same now for three generations, all while prices continue to inch upward. And this year, Google’s hardware has actually regressed in a few key areas. Despite that, the Pixel 11 phones aren’t bad—they’re some of the best 2026 has to offer. But it feels like Google is forgetting that it’s not just competing against Apple and Samsung. It also has to compete against the Pixels of yesteryear.

Just like last year’s Pixel 10 series, Google’s 2026 lineup includes three flat phones and one foldable. The flat Pixels are the same size, and even side-by-side, it’s hard to tell them apart from their predecessors. We’ve got almost identical aluminum and glass sandwich designs, which do admittedly look very nice. They still have Pixelsnap, too.

The Pixel 11s feel extremely solid, and Google has finally managed to make the buttons less wobbly. The base model Pixel also has a flatter camera bar, which makes it a little more pocket-friendly. The three flat phones are all still eSIM-only in the US—the international versions and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold retain their SIM card slots.

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL keep the taller camera bar on the back, but it’s nice that the cameras are centered on the back, unlike Samsung phones. You can set a Pixel down on a table, and it’s stable enough to poke at. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold still has that off-center camera module, which makes it less stable.

The back of the phone is also home to the Pixel 11’s new HiLight module. This ring of LEDs is inside the camera flash of the Pro phones to act a bit like an old-fashioned notification LED. However, it’s mostly tied to Gemini to indicate when the AI is listening or responding. It also lights up to tell you when one of your favorite contacts calls. And that’s it.

HiLight only works when the phone is face down—if the accelerometer detects any other orientation, it won’t light up. So it really only makes sense if you’re using “OK Google” hotword detection and leaving your phone face down a lot. Annoyingly, you can’t even have the LEDs light up for text messages from your starred contacts.

It’s really a baffling addition to Google’s phones. It would be questionable even if it had all the functionality of a classic notification LED, but it barely does anything as it currently stands. Honestly, give me the thermometer back. That at least had a theoretical use, even if it didn’t come up very often. HiLight has been so hobbled that it might as well not exist. Google says more features will be added later, but why the slow drip? We had notification LEDs figured out 20 years ago.

The displays on the Pixel 11 OLED screens are all fantastic, and Google says they’re twice as scratch-resistant now. While the base model stayed the same, all the other screens got a little brighter this year. These phones are perfectly legible in bright outdoor light, even the Pixel 11 that remained at 3,000 nits. The other phones have a peak brightness of around 3,600 nits. They are a bit more reflective than Samsung’s latest flagship phones, which have an anti-reflective quality, but the Pixels still look great. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s internal screen is a bit too reflective due to its plastic top layer, though. So far, Samsung is the only company that has worked to address that issue in foldables.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold saw the biggest chassis change compared to last year’s model, but even here, the difference is minor. It’s a few tenths of a millimeter thinner, but that’s not enough to notice unless you have both phones to compare. It certainly doesn’t look or feel as supernaturally thin as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or even last year’s Z Fold 7. Oddly, the two halves of the phone are also slightly different (the side with the cover display is thicker). You can feel the difference when holding the phone, and while it doesn’t affect usability, it’s a little strange from a tactile perspective. The screen also still has a fairly deep crease compared to the Z Fold 8, which has almost none now.

Google is, however, doing foldable durability right. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is IP68 rated for water and dust protection, and the back panel is a new glass fiber composite that Google claims is “nearly impossible to crack.” Still, the Pixel foldable is much heftier than the latest foldables from Samsung or Motorola.

Google’s new Pixel phones ship with Android 17, not that you would know from listening to Google. It doesn’t talk about Android much anymore, let alone Android version numbers. Regardless, Google has the best version of Android on its phones. While you do get the full suite of Google apps that you may not use, there’s no superfluous filler, sponsored placements, or duplicative apps. If you use Google’s products, the Pixel 11 series is ready to go out of the box.

Google’s apps, widgets, system UI, and home screen have a unified aesthetic that even Apple would envy. However, Google has oversimplified some things in recent updates, like surfacing suggested widgets instead of showing you the full list by default and using a larger, less dense home screen grid. Still, the Pixel build of Android has great vibes.

It also has a ton of AI. There are hints of Gemini in numerous apps, but that’s also true when you access these products in a browser. The on-device AI features can be mostly ignored if you just don’t tap any of the buttons with the AI sparkles on them, but that’s getting harder.

For example, Gboard now has AI-assisted voice transcription built in for Pixel phones. When you tap the mic input button (which now has the telltale AI sparkle), you get a feature called Rambler. Rather than directly transcribing your words with all the mistakes intact, it essentially summarizes what you say to remove “ums” and streamline what you meant to say if you have to correct yourself. This works in the way that AI summarization tends to work, making you sound polished, stilted, and sometimes weirdly positive.

Gemini is also a key part of the experience even more so now that Google has announced Assistant will begin shutting down in the coming weeks. Like Samsung’s latest phones, the Pixel 11 series includes expanded AI automation in more than 40 apps, like Airbnb, Best Buy, DoorDash, eBay, Delta, and more. It’s basically a robot that helps you buy things.

The story here is the same as it was on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Gemini is capable of navigating these apps with some difficulty. It usually gets where it needs to go, adding items to your cart or pre-booking a reservation. However, it takes much longer than it would if you did it yourself, and its decisions are sometimes suspect. You have to carefully evaluate what Gemini does in these apps, which makes the feature much less useful.

Google continues to offer seven years of OS updates, along with monthly security patches and quarterly Pixel Drop feature updates. This is on par with Samsung and a bit longer than almost everyone else. Google’s updates also arrive in a timely fashion, whereas even Samsung may take several months to roll out new versions of Android.

Google is not interested in talking about smartphone performance in the traditional way. It readily admits the Tensor chips are not optimized for winning benchmarks, but it claims the new Tensor G6 offers 25 percent faster web browsing and up to 20 percent better power efficiency. This seven-core Arm chip sports the same middling GPU as last year’s G5, along with a new MediaTek modem.

As expected, the Pixel 11 series doesn’t show well in benchmarks, trailing the flagship phones from other smartphone makers. But those are all just abstract numbers that might describe how the phone performs in some situations.

In daily use, the Pixel 11 phones feel great. Animations are fluid, touch response is instant, and apps open quickly. Google’s phones can feel faster than even the Galaxy S26, which is sometimes inconsistent despite being the fastest on paper. Google’s chip is also more thermally stable than high-end Qualcomm chips, losing under 25 percent of its performance during extended use.

Gaming is more of a problem for Google, though. The company is still using the same PowerVR GPU in the new Tensor chip, which is markedly slower than what you get in high-end chips from Qualcomm or Apple. Consequently, if you’re playing graphically intensive games like Genshin Impact or the mobile port of Red Dead Redemption, you will get lower frame rates with the Pixel. For the simpler, free-to-play games most people play, the Pixel is plenty powerful.

It is notable that Google has backtracked on RAM in the Pixel 11. Previously, Google cited the need for running bigger on-device AI models as a reason to upgrade base SKU Pixel phones to 16GB of RAM. However, the 2026 Google phones start at 12GB, and you have to upgrade to get 16GB. That means you’re looking at a minimum of $1,219 for the Pixel 11 Pro with 512GB of storage and 16GB of RAM.

Heavier apps and games may close more quickly on the 12GB versions of the Pixel 11, but the difference has been minimal in my testing. However, should you have to make that kind of compromise with a phone that costs $100 more than its predecessor? Probably not. That said, Google’s phones are generally better at keeping apps in memory than, say, Samsung, which only has 12GB of RAM in its $2,100 foldable.

Battery life is also complicated with the Pixel 11 series. All the batteries are slightly smaller across the board this year. The flat phones are less than 100 mAh smaller, but the Pixel 11 Pro Fold dropped more than 200 mAh compared to last year’s foldable. Yet Google is claiming similar battery life this year, somewhere between 24 and 30 hours, depending on the model.

In my time with the Pixel phones, they haven’t seemed to run dry faster. So that’s good… sort of. Ideally, we should be seeing battery life expanding beyond this “about one day” window we’ve been stuck in forever. Very few phones have managed to do that, and Google doesn’t seem interested in making the kind of changes (See: OnePlus’ last hurrah) that would support substantially longer battery life.

There is some good news in the battery department. The Pixel 11 Pro XL has finally gotten a charging boost, now topping out at 45 W instead of 30 W. The base model, 11 Pro, and Fold are still at the lower wattage, but now all of them at least have 25 W wireless charging with a compatible Qi 2.2 pad.

Google’s camera hardware has gotten a few minor tweaks this year. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL have all the same setup—a 50 MP primary, 48 MP 5x telephoto, and a 48 MP ultrawide. However, the main and telephoto sensors are new components that promise better optical quality. The Pixel 11 and 11 Pro Fold have a new 48MP primary sensor. The foldable has the same 10.8 MP 5x telephoto and 13 MP ultrawide from last year, and the flat phone has a new 13 MP ultrawide and the same 10.8 MP telephoto as the Fold.

Most of the changes are in the software controlling those cameras. In general, these changes are clever and could be nice to have for certain situations, but they’re not game changers.

There’s a new feature called Magic Capture that lets you outsource the shutter button to the on-device AI. Once you activate this mode, the phone starts recording a video. When it determines the moment is right, it can snap full-quality still photos as well. This works well in theory, but it’s not infallible. Generally, if the scene isn’t too busy and your subject is around the middle of the frame, the AI will reliably snap a photo. This works a lot of the time—I’ve gotten some genuinely cool shots with Magic Capture, but it also sometimes misses the moment. If a photo is important, I’m going to do the legwork of tapping the shutter myself.

11 Pro and 11 Pro XL photos:

Google also says the Pro phones have a new Instant Night Sight feature, but calling it “instant” may be overselling it a little. You’ll still get a timer telling you to hold the phone still, but the captures are noticeably faster. That could be the difference between a blurry photo and something usable. So while it’s not as fast as a regular photo (and certainly not instant), it’s still a nice upgrade.

However you’re taking photos with the Pixels, the results will be impressively sharp. With quick captures and powerful processing, even moving subjects are clear. Even the most expensive phones from Samsung and Apple struggle here. Google’s dynamic range is also better than you’ll see on other devices, resolving details in light and shadow very well.

Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold photos:

However, Pixel photos have a specific look, and it might not be ideal for every situation. With the Pixel 11, Google has debuted Camera Looks to address the situation, but it’s a little confusing. There are new default styles, like natural and shadows, that are retained each time you open the camera. Then there are the more dramatic filter-like looks you access by swiping in the viewfinder. This includes options like velvet, digi, and editorial. You can imagine this like something akin to film simulations on Fujifilm cameras. You can also edit any of the looks to your liking, changing sliders for highlights, tint, grain, and more.

Camera Looks:

While they’re a bit clunky to access, Camera Looks give you a ton of new shooting options on Pixel phones. They’re perfect if you’ve gotten tired of the super-sharp processed look of smartphone photos.

The Pixel 11 phones are good devices. The regression on RAM is a bummer, but the 12GB phones still feel very fast and keep apps in memory well enough for all but the most picky buyers. Likewise, the slightly smaller batteries are less than ideal, but the battery life doesn’t seem to have taken a dive.

Additions like Camera Looks and stronger displays are nice, but they’re probably not worth an upgrade for current Pixel users. And HiLight doesn’t even figure in. If you have a Pixel 10, Pixel 9, or even something older, you don’t need to run out and buy a Pixel 11. These phones are still more than serviceable, and they have years of support left. With such minor updates in 2026, Google is essentially competing against its older phones.

If you’re due for an upgrade, either because your current phone is in bad shape or you’re thinking about switching to Pixel, you’ll probably like what the Pixel 11 has to offer. However, you’d probably like the Pixel 10 just as much. You’ll probably be able to find last year’s model at a discount, and it still has six years of software support left. Again, Google is a victim of its own success here.

And what about Google’s foldable? That’s a tougher sell. Even in the US, Google has stiff competition. Both Samsung and Motorola offer foldables that are thinner, faster, and have longer battery life. These phones all cost about the same and get similar levels of support, but Google’s software is a bit better overall. Still, I’d probably choose a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with its more compact frame over the Pixel 11 Pro Fold right now, even if it’s a little more expensive.
