Thomas Tuchel led England to third place at the 2026 World Cup

Sixty-five days after England's semi-final defeat by Argentina, Thomas Tuchel will name his first squad since the World Cup on Friday.

While the tournament ultimately ended with a spectacular 6-4 win over France in the bronze-medal match, the Three Lions left the United States with a long list of what ifs.

Now, with four games in the space of 11 days coming up during the extended international break, fans will get a glimpse of what Tuchel's next England side might look like.

Could players like Trent Alexander-Arnold be recalled? Will others like Alex Scott make their debut? And how might we expect them to play?

BBC Sport senior football correspondent Sami Mokbel, journalist Jess Anderson and BBC Radio 5 Live's John Murray go through the big questions facing Tuchel.

Sami Mokbel: Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Hall are among the players to have been named in England manager Thomas Tuchel's provisional squad for the forthcoming Nations League internationals, though it remains to be seen whether they make the final cut.

Liverpool winger Ngumoha was part of a contingent of young players that flew with the England senior squad for their pre-World Cup training camp in Palm Beach.

He was unexpectedly handed his debut in the warm-up game against New Zealand, impressing in a second-half cameo.

But the 18-year-old is yet to be picked in a full senior England squad - although he is in with a chance of being selected by Tuchel for the forthcoming games against Spain, the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Hall's World Cup omission raised eyebrows given England entered the tournament without a natural left-back.

Before naming his full squad on Friday, Tuchel is required to submit a preliminary squad of players from which he will name his final party.

It is understood Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott, Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly and Everton pair Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Jarrad Branthwaite are also among the names selected in Tuchel's extended list.

Attacking duo Cole Palmer and Phil Foden are on there too, after being two of the biggest omissions from Tuchel's squad for the World Cup.

That decision was deemed a mistake from certain circles, given they are two of English football's most creative players.

Meanwhile, Tuchel is expected to omit Jordan Henderson, Dean Henderson and John Stones because of injury.

Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico

FA to canvass England players in World Cup review

Jess Anderson: One of the most talked-about issues surrounding England is who they turn to in the absence of captain and star striker Harry Kane. At the World Cup, Tuchel simply did not turn to anyone. Kane started all seven of England's matches up to the semi-final and was substituted only twice - both times late on with the game already won.

Kane was rested for the bronze-medal match, with Ivan Toney the preferred option, although the Al-Ahli striker did not score in the 6-4 win over France. Toney will not be an option this international break as he has since been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear in court later this month.

Ollie Watkins' shock summer move to Saudi Arabia puts his England future into question, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin is the man in form with four goals in four games for Leeds United.

This could be the moment for Tuchel to start to further integrate Liam Delap, who is improving at new club Nottingham Forest and has yet to make a senior England appearance. He scored his first goal for Forest in last weekend's win at Aston Villa.

What would you change about England's squad?

John Murray: In the immediate aftermath of the semi-final in Atlanta, Tuchel and the players spoke of being too passive. At the squad announcement it will be interesting to hear what conclusions Tuchel has reached on why that was the case, and how they came to surrender the initiative to Argentina from 1-0 up with just over half an hour to play.

Head of the queue for a recall is Cole Palmer, who seems to have recaptured the form he was missing last season, which resulted in his omission from the World Cup squad.

What England fans will want to see against Spain at Wembley, is Palmer and his like taking the initiative and imposing themselves on their opponents in a way that was so lacking in the latter stages against Argentina in July.

John Murray: Happy or not, that's what they've got - but this has to be better than another group of qualifiers such as the one they had for the World Cup, against teams way below them in the world rankings.

In those matches last autumn England played some of the best football they have so far produced under Tuchel.

But, while that helped establish patterns of play and build confidence, you never really know until you face the best. That clearly will be the case from the outset in the Nations League, with this opening match against the new world champions.

These matches will also provide preparation for the next Euros in 2028 when, assuming they qualify, England will be playing opponents like this at Wembley. And, lest you forget, this tournament does provide an opportunity to win a trophy which would be the best possible way for Tuchel and his team to step on from their third place at the World Cup.

Sami Mokbel: This will be a key theme to watch over the next three weeks. The spirit was high in the England camp during the World Cup - as evidenced by their brilliant victory against Mexico in the last 16 with 10 men.

But the devastating semi-final defeat by Argentina, and questions over England's approach as a 1-0 lead became a 2-1 loss late on, led to some form of an inquest in the England camp into what was to blame.

Away from the height of those emotions in July, the Football Association is completing a review into England's World Cup campaign. The FA has been keen to stress that this assessment is a standard process, rather than an indication of wider concern or alarm about England's third-place finish.

Indeed, key figures at the FA view the tournament in which England achieved their best finish since 1966 as a success, and the organisation has already backed Tuchel before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign.

Tuchel and members of his backroom team gave their contributions to the review at St George's Park in late August. England players' opinions are also being gathered before a report is presented to senior bosses at the FA.

The ongoing review will also look into the impact of the team's permanent Kansas City base during the tournament. After every game, they returned to Kansas City - and the effects of the travelling will be analysed.

The content of the review won't be made public, but the next three weeks will give an indication of whether the camp is still as together as that night at the Azteca.

Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.

A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.

Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex".

Police said they had followed more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, taken more than 300 statements and carried out detailed searches at more than 10 addresses and on numerous vessels.

Det Ch Insp Toby Elcock, from the Major Crime Team, said: "While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne's family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty.

"Throughout this investigation, Joanne's family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time.

"As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable."

He stressed that the police would still like to hear from anyone with information about Sheen's disappearance.

London Fire Brigade was called on 5 August to a blaze that damaged about two hectares of shrubland in an area known as Bedfont Pits.

The human remains were discovered a week later, and a post-mortem examination suggested they had come from a woman aged between 25 and 45.

A Metropolitan Police spokesman confirmed the remains were found by a member of the public at the site close to Bedfont Lakes Country Park.

Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate a £20,000 reward for information that supports the investigation.

Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020 - two months after she was last seen.

Several people were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no charges were brought and the investigation remained unsolved.

At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him in the following 24 hours, before a child's body was discovered on Wednesday afternoon at a nearby pond. Earlier, police said his body had been formally identified.

"Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much," said father Rhys Woods.

"This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us, we were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him. That's what we kept telling ourselves the whole time."

People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.

Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation.

"You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."

He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it".

"The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives."

He finished the post by addressing his son.

"It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."

Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.

Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches".

"It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond.

"I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time."

King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands

BBC News Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:33:12 GMT

King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.

Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.

The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".

He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".

"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.

Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.

He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".

The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.

But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.

"The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.

Sarah Friar, OpenAI's chief financial officer, said AI had the potential to solve some of society's "hardest problems" - but agreed its growing capabilities raised questions about safety and "how we ensure it always serves people".

"We need to address those questions together," she said.

"No one company or government can do that alone and I'm grateful to His Majesty for convening this discussion at such an important moment."

Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.

The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.

In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.

After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.

He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.

The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.

Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.

Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.

Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".

Additional reporting by Philippa Wain

Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high

BBC News Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:05:38 GMT

The Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.

The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.

But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.

The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.

The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money. Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.

The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August.

On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year. It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".

Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.

Other major central banks have increased rates to counteract higher prices.

On Wednesday, the US Federal Reserve announced its first hike in three years while the European Central Bank has raised rates twice since June.

Of the nine members on the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), six voted to hold rates at 3.75% while three - including the Bank's chief economist Huw Pill - wanted to raise them to 4%.

While financial markets have priced in the possibility of several rate rises next year, Bailey said the global backdrop remained "hugely unpredictable at the moment".

He said that for interest rates to come down there would need to be "an end of conflict in the Middle East... and energy prices coming really back to where they were before this conflict began".

There were some positive notes from the Bank of England.

It said the UK economy had been "more resilient" than it had expected and raised its prediction for economic growth from 0.1% to 0.4% for the period between July and September.

It also said that because the effect of higher energy costs had not yet spilled over into other areas of the economy, food price inflation was now predicted to be 4% by the end of the year, less than the Bank's previous forecast of 6-7%.

Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages.

The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.

The move will have a significant effect on borrowers like Andy Pargeter from Flintshire and his wife. They are coming off a five-year fixed rate mortgage of 1.19% in November. Earlier in the year they had hoped that interest rates might be falling at this point. However with rates held steady they now expect to pay around £300 more a month.

"We're in a fortunate position where we're able to accommodate that [increase]," he told BBC News. But he expects it will have "a knock-on effect in terms of how much we potentially save every month".

"It's definitely been something… I have constantly been thinking about."

Alongside the interest rate decision, the Bank also said it would halt its so-called "quantitative tightening" (QT) programme.

It will pause its annual sale of government bonds – which are a kind of IOU that can be traded on the financial markets – and will instead sell off smaller chunks over eight years.

The Bank bought £895bn of mainly government bonds during periods of economic turbulence such as the global financial crisis and the Covid pandemic to help keep the economy on an even keel. This was known as "quantitative easing".

Since 2022, it has been offloading the bonds, including through sales. This has contributed to higher interest rates – or yields – on bonds, making it more expensive for the government to borrow money.

The Bank said discussions to put in place a plan to reduce the current £488bn stockpile of bonds had started a year ago, implying the decision was not related to the recent rise in long term borrowing costs.

The news that the Bank of England is overhauling its QT programme prompted an immediate reaction.

The yield on 30-year UK government bonds fell from 5.86% on Thursday morning to 5.75% following the Bank's announcement. Yields on 10-year bonds dropped from 5.31% to 5.22%.

Verified video shows wreckage of Saudi fighter jet shot down over Yemen

BBC News Thu, 17 Sep 2026 13:47:36 GMT

Footage verified by the BBC shows the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen.

The US-made aircraft was "downed using a locally manufactured surface-to-air missile" as it "conducted hostile operations" over the Marib region, according to a Houthi statement on Wednesday.

Experts have told BBC Verify the incident is a "propaganda coup" that shows the Houthis' military capability has advanced and they are prepared to further escalate its conflict with Saudi Arabia.

Using satellite imagery to match features in the landscape seen in the footage, BBC Verify was able to pinpoint the crash site to an isolated location in the hills west of the Yemeni city of Marib.

The long-running conflict between a Saudi-led military coalition and the Houthis has escalated in the last week after the armed group launched an offensive against pro-government forces.

This led to the Houthis seizing key territory near the south-west coast, close to vital international shipping channels in the Bab al-Mandab strait.

In one of several video clips released by the Houthis, men with assault rifles can be seen at the crash site inspecting the wreckage. The fighters celebrate as they lift the jet's almost-intact tail fin which features the Saudi flag and a four-digit serial number.

The fate of of the crew is not known.

The Houthis also released a thermal video clip - which cannot be fully verified due to a lack of visual details - that appears to show a fighter jet in mid-flight being struck by a missile.

BBC Verify has contacted the Saudi Ministry of Defence for comment.

Baraa Shiban, Yemen analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, told BBC Verify the incident showed it was "very clear the Houthis have been taking advantage of advice and technological support" from Iran.

"They continue to develop their military arsenal and capabilities to make it more and more painful on Saudi Arabia," he said.

Downing the F-15 is also a "propaganda coup", said Yemen expert Adam Baron from the Washington-based New America think tank, as Saudi air support is considered to be "key to any significant pushback" against recent Houthi gains.

"An eye-for-an-eye has been a huge element of the group's public messaging. This is partially to show that air support will come at a price," he added.

BBC Verify used the position of the sun and satellite imagery to locate the distinctive landscape seen in the footage - including cliff faces and hills - to an isolated mountainous area about 25 miles (40km) west of Marib.

Satellite imagery published on Wednesday also shows a new dark shadow at the same location, which appears consistent with scorch or burn marks at a crash site.

The aircraft in the wreckage has been independently identified by Nick Brown, a weapons expert from military intelligence company Janes, as an F-15 Strike Eagle. He based his analysis on distinctive elements seen in the footage including the tail fin arrangement, radar antenna and missile warning system sensors.

The four-digit tail number visible on the wreckage also appears to be consistent with that of an F-15 Strike Eagle operated by the 55th Squadron of the Royal Saudi Air Force based at King Khalid Air Base near the city of Khamis Mushait in south-west Saudi Arabia.

This base, about 245 miles (392 km) from the crash site, was targeted last week by what the Houthis described as a "barrage of missiles and drones". Satellite imagery analysed by BBC Verify appears to show damage to at least three aircraft hangars or shelters.

The base is one of a series of high-profile Saudi targets struck by the Houthis in recent days including an oil refinery in the city of Jizan.

Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday it had destroyed a Houthi drone close to the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, which the Houthis have denied targeting.

The group said on Thursday that Saudi Arabia had launched 40 air strikes against Yemen over the past 24 hours.

Additional reporting by Shayan Sardarizadeh and Alex Murray

Portsmouth's lifeboat station remains temporarily out of service following anti-migrant protests.

The RNLI also said it helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant demonstrators who went into the sea.

Following the protest, the charity's chief executive said staff had faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse. The lifeboat station was taken out of service on 10 September, meanwhile, abuse aimed at volunteers also forced the lifeboat museum in Poole to shut for several days.

Peter Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI – our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel.

"The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe."

He added: "Stand by them, not against them and their families. I am extremely proud of and grateful for their vital lifesaving work."

Balaclava boys on electric bikes: How to tackle the problem?

BBC News Thu, 17 Sep 2026 05:04:52 GMT

From the Pentland Hills near Edinburgh to the streets of the country's biggest cities, a common menace is causing irritation, alarm and in some cases even death.

The sight of young men, their identities hidden by black balaclavas, tearing around on electric bikes or scooters is becoming a familiar one.

The picture above was taken by a man who posted on social media about "morons on electric bikes" scaring a nearby horse as they rode illegally on public footpaths.

Aside from being showered with gravel churned up by the "gobby" miscreants, no-one came to harm that day, but others have not been so lucky.

Earlier this year, a court was shown distressing dashcam footage of the moment a masked 18-year-old on an electric motorbike ploughed into a woman on a pedestrian crossing in Sunderland.

Gloria Stephenson, 86, died at the scene. The rider - Billy Stokoe, who had taken cannabis and was using his mobile at the time of the crash - was jailed for more than six years for causing death by dangerous driving.

Few would dispute that illegal e-bikes and scooters are a growing problem, but what can be done about it? Here are some of the options.

The term e-bike is often used loosely to cover a range of different vehicles.

Strictly speaking it refers to an electrically assisted pedal cycle (an EAPC) where an electric motor kicks in to take the strain off the rider while pedalling.

By law, the motor cuts out at 15.5mph (25km/h) and its continuous power is capped at 250 watts.

But these safeguards are easily bypassed by "tuning kits" or software hacks that make them capable of running much faster, sometimes in excess of 40mph.

A quick search of online marketplaces reveals all sorts of modifications on offer, often shipped from eastern Europe, including motorbike-style twist grip throttles which allow the rider to accelerate without pedalling.

Then there are electric dirt bikes from manufacturers such as Sur-Ron which look like mountain bikes but are capable of about 50mph - and 70mph or more if modified.

Unlike legal e-bikes they require a licence and insurance to be used in public spaces or on roads.

E-scooters are also popular - despite it currently being illegal to ride them on public roads or pavements except in certain rental zones.

What they all have in common is that they are expensive, ranging from a few hundred to several thousands of pounds, and modifications can cost hundreds of pounds more on top.

Seizing and destroying them represents a significant penalty.

A new law and rules introduced this summer gave police in England and Wales greater powers to seize illegal vehicles without the need for a formal warning if they are being used in an anti-social manner.

In Scotland, ministers say they are in favour of increasing police seizure powers, although they point out bikes can already be seized under certain circumstances.

Catching the offenders is a problem for the police - it's a crime where its very nature means the suspects have a fast and highly manoeuvrable method of escape.

A patrol car can easily be evaded by heading down a narrow alleyway or through bollards. David Kennedy from the Scottish Police Federation says more dangerous tactics are also employed.

"These individuals on these bikes will come up one-way streets the wrong way so there's no way a police officer in a car or even on a motorbike would be safe to follow them," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

Some forces across the UK have responded to the challenge by setting up specialised units backed up by drones.

In parts of inner city London, Metropolitan Police officers have been equipped with a fleet of 25 Sur-Ron dirt bikes - partly funded with proceeds of crime money.

As part of a crackdown targeting mobile phone thefts - which in London often involve such bikes - they claim it has helped cut offences by 13,000 in a year.

A number of forces have successfully used drones to track illegal e-bike riders rather than engaging in risky pursuits.

Officers monitor suspects from above, then their colleagues are directed to move in on foot to make seizures and arrests.

In Devon and Cornwall officers have also sprayed illegal riders and their bikes with SmartWater - a forensic marking product that contains a unique chemical code which becomes visible using ultraviolet light.

One of the most sinister aspects of e-bike misuse is that riders often wear black balaclavas or "ballys".

Whether it is a practical attempt to hide their identity or part of a youth sub-culture, there is no doubt that many people find the sight of masked youths intimidating.

The debate about the appropriateness of wearing balaclavas in public places goes wider than e-bikes, encompassing anti-social behaviour, crime and some anti-immigration protests.

New restrictions introduced just this week under Operation Reclaim in Nottingham give police and council officers the power to order people to remove face coverings, backed up by £70 fixed penalty notices.

Exemptions apply for religious, medical and certain other legitimate reasons.

David Kennedy from the Scottish Police Federation says there is definitely "more to do" on face coverings although he cautions that localised enforcement might simply see youths moving elsewhere.

"If you are on an e-bike and you are wearing a face covering, the concern I have got is you are not wearing a helmet," he adds.

"I don't see many people travelling about the city centre on e-bikes wearing helmets."

Many parents are unaware that knowingly allowing their child to use an illegal e-bike or an e-scooter in a public place could land them with a fine or points on their driving licence.

Under the current law, e-scooters can only be used legally on private land.

The only exceptions are a number of rental trial zones, all of them located in England, yet some parents regard e-scooters as legitimate toys.

Riders of legal electrically assisted pedal bikes must be at least 14, and any illegal modification means the bikes qualify as a motor vehicle/moped, requiring registration, a driving licence, tax and insurance.

If an under-18-year-old is stopped by the police, their parents could potentially be accused of "causing or permitting" a driving offence with a possible £300 fine and six penalty points.

And even a child too young to drive can have points added to a "ghost licence" which can transfer to their provisional when they are old enough to apply for one.

Some argue the problem needs to be addressed earlier, before a young person gets hold of an e-bike or e-scooter, by targeting the point of sale.

This could range from clearer warnings about the rules, to a mandatory buyer information and registration scheme which would make it easier for police to trace vehicles used in crime or anti-social behaviour.

Last year an all-party Westminster inquiry called for action to close a legal loophole that allows illegal vehicles to be sold under the guise of off-road use.

The MPs also suggested that online marketplaces be held accountable for unsafe products such as the modification kits that are sold on their platforms.

Moral outrage at the behaviour of young people is nothing new and predates the invention of e-bikes by a considerable margin. Historians have found texts bemoaning declining standards dating back 4,000 years to ancient Mesopotamia.

Some might argue the e-bike scourge is just the latest manifestation of an age-old problem and that rather than demonising the "bally boys" a better approach is to try to understand the boredom and frustrations that underpin the trend.

In Aberdeen, alongside police enforcement action, one go karting centre is offering free sessions where e-scooter and e-bike riders can use them in a legal and safer environment.

But given the scale of e-bike misuse, can such schemes make an impact?

The backdrop is a long-term decline in services for young people and financial pressures on local authorities and charities that provide them.

A report from the YMCA last year found council-funded youth services in England and Wales have lost more than £1bn since 2010 with hundreds of youth clubs shutting and youth worker posts disappearing.

Youth Scotland, citing research by Unison, paints a similar picture.

Whether the answer is drones, dedicated police units or creating more positive ways in which young people can fill their day, the common denominator is fresh thinking and - arguably the biggest challenge - extra resources.

Rosenberg: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter

BBC News Thu, 17 Sep 2026 05:00:36 GMT

The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).

That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.

This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.

Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.

But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say.

"We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.

That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?

Far from it.

For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.

As for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.

I said no surprises. But there have been some.

"Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.

The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns.

"The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."

In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:

"The Communist Party, onwards we go!

"We're with the people, don't you know?"

More X Factor than exit poll.

Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:

"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"

It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.

"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament.

"In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."

I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing.

But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.

And if a party doesn't support the war?

One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.

Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election.

"The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me.

"This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place.

"It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."

For now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat.

"Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."

Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.

The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.

Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.

In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.

The war is front and centre of people's minds here.

"We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen."

"I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."

Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing.

"What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."

Expectations are low that this election will change much.

"Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied.

"Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

This will helps us understand and study the history of the moon and other airless, cratered objects in the solar system, but it could also aid in future exploration. “If we’re trying to send rovers or astronauts or build things on the moon, we want to understand the properties of the surface,” says Powell. “It comes at a cost though – higher metabolic rates mean higher food requirements and potentially more active hunting to acquire it,” he says.

Most ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica isn’t due to melting at the surface. Instead, these ice sheets are shrinking mainly because glaciers are flowing faster into the ocean, raising the risk of feedback loops that could accelerate sea level rise.

While rising air temperatures thaw ice at the surface, glaciers also lose ice at the coast. Relatively warm ocean water melts the underside of the glacier and icebergs calve off its tongue, drifting equatorward to eventually melt. The quicker a glacier flows, the more ice it will lose to the sea.

The longest satellite record ever compiled shows ice loss has sped up by a factor of four since the 1980s due to global warming. It found that 84 per cent of this acceleration was caused by glacier flow and only 16 per cent by surface melt, a much higher proportion than expected.

Advertisement

“Now we can say with confidence that it has been because glaciers are flowing faster,” says Inès Otosaka at Northumbria University, UK, one of the authors of the study. “It was quite surprising to me and to some colleagues that actually 84 per cent of the mass loss is really driven by glaciers flowing faster to the ocean, rather than being half and half or 60-40 surface melting.”

Free newsletter

Scientists have known that ice loss was accelerating mainly because of an increase in the speed of glacier flow, although exactly what proportion of ice loss was due to this factor has been uncertain. The Antarctic ice sheet is cold enough that there is essentially no surface melt. But in Greenland, air temperatures do go above freezing, causing surface melt. The proportion of surface melt versus ocean loss can vary from year to year.

Glaciers flow downhill due to gravity, but water within the sediments underneath them, or water that has trickled down from surface melt, can lubricate the glacier base and speed up this flow. Ice loss at the front of the glacier can also decrease resistance. In Antarctica, the breakup of ice shelves that extend in front of the glaciers and often buttress them against outcroppings of land has caused glaciers to accelerate.

“A higher share of ocean-driven ice loss is concerning because ocean-ice feedbacks can produce faster, nonlinear responses,” says Michael Meredith at the British Antarctic Survey.

Many glaciers such as the Thwaites “doomsday glacier” in Antarctica lie over bedrock that slopes downward from the coast to the interior. As they melt, more ocean water can pour into this bowl, causing runaway melt in a feedback known as marine ice sheet instability (MISI).

Scientists also fear that as the thin snouts of glaciers retreat, the ice faces at the front of them could get too tall, collapsing and driving further retreat in what is known as marine ice cliff instability (MICI).

Ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica has raised sea levels 3 centimetres since the 1970s, putting up to 9 million more people at the risk of coastal flooding and erosion. Sea level could rise by up to 2 metres this century alone.

These estimates attempt to account for feedbacks, but if more ice loss is due to glaciers flowing into the ocean, it increases the risk that they aren’t doing so fully.

“The real concern is that poorly-understood instabilities such as MISI and MICI could push future Antarctic losses above the currently-expected range, which is why they remain a major uncertainty,” says Meredith.

Together, they reveal the structure of the sun’s chromosphere, which is the layer just above its visible surface, but below its corona.

That proximity to the sun caused remarkable activity on the comet, creating two long plumes, one made of dust and the other of electrically charged plasma.

With a more earthly setting, the winner of the Skyscapes category is Botswana Star Trail, taken by Stefano Pellegrini. It captures the movement of stars above a grove of baobab trees over the course of 340 camera exposures, each lasting 30 seconds.

Ukraine developed USVs after scuttling its only major warship early in 2022 to prevent its capture. In October 2022, Ukraine carried out a successful attack with seven sea drones, damaging a Russian frigate and a minesweeper at the Sevastopol naval base in Crimea.

From 2024, the Russians copied Ukraine, building small, fast USVs with explosive warheads to attack ports, bridges and shipping. The Russian Orcan in this month’s action was likely to have been heading towards the Ukrainian port city of Odesa as part of a campaign targeting cargo ships.

With plug-in solar panels, you simply buy a kit, place it in a sunny spot and plug it into a wall socket. There’s no installation cost, no certification and no planning permission. The devices are popular in many European countries and the UK government legalised them on 27 August to boost renewable energy generation and cut down on household bills.

Prior to this legalisation, Mark Coles, the head of technical regulations at the UK Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET), told New Scientist about several potential issues. One surrounded residual current devices (RCDs), the safety devices found in fuse boxes that sense when current is leaking to ground – a sign of electrocution or a short circuit – and almost instantaneously cut power. Most RCDs used in the UK aren’t suitable for current flowing in both directions and so could malfunction if used with plug-in solar panels.

Advertisement

Another of the IET’s concerns is what happens if there are multiple kits in use in an area and a power cut occurs. In theory, the plug-in kits should also shut down in order to prevent “islanding”, when one home’s power stays live. But if they are still generating power, then they could deceive each other into thinking the grid is live and keep running. The problem then is that power can jump past the fuse box and electrocute maintenance workers in the area fixing the outage.

The IET made these concerns clear to the UK government both before and during the consultation by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) that ended on 30 June. But Coles says the issues weren’t addressed and now present a risk.

“It was a done deal before it went out, I’m sure,” says Coles. “It’s been rushed. There needed to be time to develop a proper standard for these things, because we feel under certain circumstances that there’s an increased risk to life.”

Plug-in solar is coming – how dangerous is it and is it worth it?

Coles says the risks emerge only when there’s a perfect storm of problems, but that this will inevitably lead to an injury or a death over time if plug-in solar panels are widely adopted.

Extensive scientific studies have been carried out to determine how quickly damage is done within the human body from electric shock. Based on that research, UK RCDs are required to trip and cut off current within 40 milliseconds. But there are no similar standards for plug-in solar panels, which Coles suggests could – if things go wrong, and in very limited circumstances – take longer to shut down.

“You could be exposed to the electric current for longer than you should have been,” says Coles. “You’re in the danger zone.”

The IET’s advice is to get an electrical inspection prior to committing to plug-in solar in order to minimise risk.

Free newsletter

A DESNZ spokesperson told New Scientist that “we have funded an independent contractor to fully test the electrical safety of plug-in solar devices on UK electrical house wiring practice, which found these products to be safe”.

The department added that it had looked at testing with older household electrical safety devices and found no evidence that their ability to provide protection was affected when used with the type of plug-in solar systems sold in Europe.

Coles agrees that tests were carried out, but says that they focused on plug-in solar kits sourced outside the UK, because none was legal here at the time, and with brand new RCDs. That has two problems: legal RCDs in the real world can be much older, and of older design, and there was no clear definition or regulation for plug-in panels that were tested, meaning that ones now for sale may act differently.

“They spent this money on getting these units tested, but these units were non-standard units,” says Coles. “So it’s not like I’m testing something that’s been made to a product standard and I’m seeing how it conforms to this product standard. So I don’t see the point of spending the money. From our point of view, it’s being rushed.”

El Niño drought: Wairarapa farmers warned of dry conditions and feed shortages

New Zealand Herald September 17, 2026

Wairarapa could be in for a two-to-six-month dry spell with low or no rainfall. Photo / Emily Ireland

Wairarapa farmers still picking up the pieces from severe weather events this year are being advised to prepare for one of the driest summers on record.

A Greater Wellington Regional Council report details two scenarios underpinning its response to an El Niño climate pattern set to affect the Ruamāhanga and Wairarapa coast catchments this summer.

The “most likely scenario” was a two-month dry spell with low or no rain, resulting in urban areas experiencing water restrictions and Wairarapa farms facing dry conditions that reduce pasture growth and require supplementary feed.

The “most credible worst-case scenario” was a six-month dry spell with low or no rainfall, triggering restrictions and emergency water distribution.

The regional council report said this could collapse Wairarapa agriculture, causing economic and social stress, raising wildfire risk, and triggering full activation of regional emergency management.

It said current guidance suggested the event may be “intense but relatively short-lived”, weakening during the second half of summer and potentially ending by winter 2027.

Council director for knowledge and insights Dave Hipkins said the current forecast indicated “it’s going to be one of the strongest events on record” and the highest drought risk was expected this summer.

El Niño, and its opposite, La Niña, are naturally occurring climate patterns.

El Niño occurs when the surface water in the equatorial Pacific Ocean gets unusually warm, disrupting global and local weather.

Typically, it occurs every few years and lasts for several months.

Past events in 1972-1973, 1982-1983, and 1997-1998 caused severe droughts in eastern parts of the country.

Greater Wellington Wairarapa councillor John Hart said he was concerned some farmers, particularly in the Wairarapa coast catchment, could be heading into “what could be a serious drought with a deficit of on-farm water infrastructure, if farm dams that were damaged by this year’s extreme weather events haven’t had a chance to be repaired yet”.

“I’ve asked Greater Wellington staff to look at surveying farmers to see if they need assistance, but if they have compliance concerns about getting work done, I’d urge them to get in touch.

“The welfare of farmers and their livestock is our priority concern right now.”

Hart said the farmers he had spoken to were not panicking yet, “but they are starting to make plans to adapt if the drought eventuates”.

The Greater Wellington Regional Council report said current soil moisture and water resources across the region remained generally healthy following a wet autumn and early winter.

The council will continue to engage proactively with water users and landowners, ensure regulatory readiness, and prepare operational activities within parks and catchments for elevated fire and drought conditions.

Auckland gym assault: Victim thanks bystanders who came to aid after suffering serious injuries

New Zealand Herald September 17, 2026

The mother of two spoke to the Herald about her recovery and the minutes after the alleged violent incident.

The victim of an alleged Auckland gym assault says she is grateful for those, including a mystery nurse, who rushed to her aid before paramedics arrived.

The 23-year-old mother, who did not want to be named, spoke to the Herald about her recovery, the bystanders who supported her and the minutes after the alleged assault during a workout at a Mt Wellington gym earlier this month.

She recounted what she could remember, including her plans to run and call police for help before she was allegedly dragged and locked in a gym bathroom by her attacker.

She remembered trying to unlock the door and opening a little gap.

“I like screamed for help and then he shut it.

“I don’t remember anything else after that.”

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

She was eventually found unconscious and covered in blood.

“I don’t know how long I was there, like lying there until they found me.”

A few of the 25-30 people at the gym helped, including one woman who stayed beside her until an ambulance arrived.

She said an unknown woman, whom she understood was an emergency department nurse who lived nearby, was called in to help by her father, who was at the gym.

“She stayed with me the whole time and was helping me. I couldn’t actually see her. I don’t know what she looks like because my eyes were like closed.

“I could not open my eyes. It was just blood everywhere.”

She said she never got the woman’s name and couldn’t remember much, but she was “a really good lady” who helped her wipe her face.

A man also helped by alerting her sister to what had happened.

“I wasn’t able to talk and say it at the time, but I truly am so grateful.”

She said other people at the gym took off their jackets and jumpers and put them around her because she was shivering.

The young woman said she had just been discharged from hospital after surgery on her hand and fractured nose.

Alongside significant bruising, she said her knees were injured, and her front teeth were knocked out.

“My whole face, it’s like a whole list of broken.”

She was grateful to be recovering for her children, one of whom was autistic.

“... My daughter has special needs. I’m just glad I’m healing now, and she’s going to be okay.

“I know my son would have been okay, but with my daughter, she’s like literally glued to me ... She had the worst time while I was in hospital, but now she’s really happy.”

She feared she might experience post-traumatic stress when she thought about returning to a gym.

Her message to other women concerned about violence was to “just leave” at the first red flag.

Specialist family violence service Shine told the Herald that one in two New Zealand women experienced physical or sexualised violence from an intimate partner or ex-partner in their lifetime.

No matter how it was done, family violence was never okay, it said.

“All people who experience violence deserve help and support to be safe, and all people who use violence should be held accountable.”

Anyone experiencing family violence was encouraged to contact Shine’s free helpline for confidential support.

A 20-year-old man has been charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and theft.

He is due to reappear in the Auckland District Court on October 13.

Sick overstayer’s deportation costs Immigration NZ $85,000

New Zealand Herald September 17, 2026

New immigration figures show 1400 deportations took place in the year to July. Photo / 123rf

By Gill Bonnett of RNZ

A woman was deported at an estimated cost of $85,000 to New Zealand taxpayers, after she and her own government refused to pay for it.

New immigration figures show 1400 deportations took place in the year to July, of which a third were enforced and paid for by Immigration New Zealand.

They are on the rise, but less than half the number taking place before the pandemic.

In one case flagged under ministers’ no surprises policy last year, a Korean woman was being deported after overstaying since 2012.

She was told to leave a year later but did not, and only came to authorities’ attention again in 2024 when police were trying to identify a woman in hospital who had suffered two strokes.

“The client remains in hospital and has since undergone two brain operations and requires significant ongoing rehabilitative care,” officials told Immigration Minister Erica Stanford.

“The client is expected to be cleared to fly in the coming weeks; however, she requires two medical escorts as part of a medical transportation plan for her deportation.”

Immigration Compliance met with the Korean Consulate and the Auckland health management to discuss her deportation in March last year.

“The Korean Consulate confirmed that the Korean Government will not pay for the repatriation costs of the client as she is unregistered in Korea due to her period of absence from the country. They did agree to issue an emergency travel document once flights are arranged.

“A quote for medical repatriation using the accredited New Zealand Air Ambulance Service was provided to Immigration Compliance at a total cost of $85,000.”

The deportation with medical transportation, which needed deputy chief executive sign-off, was approved and she was deported in May last year.

Figures from 2024 show just over half of deportees are overstayers, 30% are for other visa breaches and the rest – about one in six – had committed crimes.

New figures released on Tuesday showed an estimated 19,000 overstayers in the country, 6559 of whom had arrived in the past three years.

Te Puke dog trainer hopes to return to using Donovan Park after ban outcry

New Zealand Herald September 17, 2026

Te Puke dog trainer Mandy Woods and Rottweiler Ziya at Donovan Park. Photo / Kelly O'Hara

A Te Puke dog trainer who has hosted lessons at a local park for years has been told she needs a formal concession.

Mandy Wood says she is relieved to have a way to return to Donovan Park, after previously being told she could not use it and might face fines if she tried.

She said the Western Bay of Plenty District Council initially told her this was because of concerns about sharing space with a disc golf course, and operating a commercial business in the park.

The council says a formal concession is required under the Reserves Act, and it would help her arrange this.

Wood said she had been “absolutely shocked” initially, as the park had been her classroom and workplace for almost eight years.

Alongside paid classes, she has hosted free training sessions through Hungry Dogs of Te Puke.

She said she worked with the dogs on-lead and stayed well clear of the disc golf area.

“There has never been an incident involving our groups during these years.

“We’ve actually worked well together. We made a compromise and it was okay for me to be in one designated area away from the line of throw.”

She said the council told her in July she would be fined if she held sessions in any part of the reserve.

She stopped her Te Puke-based sessions and shifted to Gordon Spratt Reserve in Pāpāmoa.

She shared her story on social media and her client, Jake Johnson, started a petition seeking to allow her to continue using Donovan Park, which received more than 570 signatures.

The Tauranga Disc Golf Association (TDGA) created the nine-hole course in Donovan Park in September last year.

Association treasurer Ryan Alderton said the group had shared the park with Wood for “quite some time now”, peacefully and without affecting each other.

“We are more than happy to continue sharing the space with Mandy if she is successful in gaining permission from the council to keep on training dogs at Donovan Park.”

Alderton said the group had not complained to the council about Wood training dogs at the park.

He believe they came independently from a member of a family who were not club members.

He said it was great for Te Puke to have someone like Wood who could train dogs that needed extra attention.

The group hoped she would be able to return to training in Donovan Park alongside people playing disc golf.

Wood said she was relieved to find out she could resume using the park for training sessions if she met several conditions.

She must apply for a concession to operate her commercial business on council land.

She also needs to secure public liability insurance to protect against third-party liabilities as part of the formalisation process.

Once the licence was approved, the council would publicise that Wood’s business was legitimate and establish clear guidelines for timetables and usage so dog trainers and disc golfers can fairly share the space.

Western Bay of Plenty District Council reserves and facilities manager Peter Watson said under the Reserves Act, commercial activities on reserve land required a formal concession.

“We have spoken with Mandy about what is required and are committed to working with her to establish an appropriate arrangement.”

He said this would help protect her business interests, ensure the council met its obligations under the act, and confirm appropriate public liability insurance was in place.

“Formalising the activity through a concession will also provide certainty around operating times, enabling other reserve users, including disc golf participants, to better plan their use of the park.”

Watson said this would help minimise conflicts between user groups and support the fair and effective sharing of the reserve.

Retirement village repayments: Leaked plan cuts maximum wait to nine months

New Zealand Herald September 17, 2026

Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka addressed proposed changes late last year. Photo / Sylvie Whinray

A leaked document reveals the Government’s changes to its planned reform of retirement village repayments for residents, now proposing a maximum repayment period of nine months instead of 12.

The Herald has obtained a leaked copy of what appears to be a press release in the name of Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka, who is leading the reform.

Potaka’s office declined to comment on the leak, referencing an expected announcement later this morning.

The document stated the Government had agreed to introduce the Retirement Villages Amendment Bill next term to legislate a nine-month repayment period, which was three months shorter than what was initially suggested by Potaka and Seniors Minister Casey Costello in December.

The legislation would also require retirement village operators to pay 10% of a former resident’s “net termination proceeds”, replacing a provision that would have required interest to be paid after six months if a unit remained unlicensed.

The changes update what Potaka and Costello proposed following a review of the Retirement Villages Act, which was an item in the National-New Zealand First coalition agreement.

The two ministers in December said a bill was expected to be introduced mid-2026 but it hasn’t eventuated.

The Herald has reported on several cases of retirement village residents waiting many months for repayments. One case reported last month concerned a 97-year-old retirement resident who faced having to borrow money because he had to wait 15 months for repayment from his village, which he’d had to leave for a private hospital.

Last month, Labour announced its own election policy addressing the issue, proposing a three-month maximum repayment period and a 10% upfront payment, capped at $50,000, made within five working days.

In the leaked press release, Potaka said the Government had “listened carefully to older Kiwis and their whānau” in changing its proposed reform.

“In December, I said these reforms needed to be practical, balanced and built to last. I stand by that.

“But listening did not stop when the first decisions were announced. Older Kiwis told us the balance needed to shift further towards residents.”

Potaka estimated the 10% payment would likely be around $60,000 for a resident buying an “average priced retirement village villa in 2028/2029”. It would not apply to villages with fewer than 50 units, while other exceptions were made where residents controlled the sale and price, the resident received at least half of the capital gain or the village was in receivership.

He argued nine months struck a “fair and responsible balance” between residents getting repaid sooner and “protecting the affordability and viability of retirement village living”.

In a nod to Labour’s policy, Potaka said he had “looked closely at the three-month option” but claimed it would hike costs for future residents.

He cited official modelling, which has been publicly questioned by the Opposition and resident advocates, that suggested a three-month repayment period could increase costs of entering a village by about $118,000 “if all costs were passed on to residents” and require the sector to “hold or access between $3.2 billion and $4.1 billion”.

“I will not make a promise that sounds good but risks higher costs, reduced services or fewer choices for older Kiwis,” Potaka said.

Other aspects of the Government’s proposed reforms included protections for residents such as stopping weekly fees and fixed deductions after an occupation right agreement ended. A more efficient dispute resolution system would also be introduced.

Village operators would still be required to take reasonable steps to enter into a new agreement for a former resident’s unit in a timely manner and at the “best price reasonably obtainable”. They would also be required to provide regular updates and obtain a valuation if a unit hadn’t been relicensed after six months.

Potaka said the new repayment requirements would apply to agreements signed one year after the legislation was passed, meaning it was unlikely the changes would come into force until well into the second half of next term, presuming a full six-month select committee process was undertaken.

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.

Auckland city centre intensification: Government targets height limits in growth proposal

New Zealand Herald September 17, 2026

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop (left) and Prime Minister Christopher are attending a Committee for Auckland event today where they will talk about changing the city's planning rules. Photo / Mark Mitchell

The Government has unveiled sweeping proposals to allow buildings of unlimited height in the heart of Auckland.

An investigation into the city’s planning rules has recommended removing restrictions on building heights, tower dimensions and separation, setbacks, and floor-area ratios in the city centre.

The Government is seeking feedback on the proposed changes, which it says could unlock significantly more housing, jobs and economic activity.

RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon are set to speak further about the plans at a Committee for Auckland event this morning.

Bishop said the recent opening of the City Rail Link had been transformative.

“The next step is making sure our planning rules support Auckland to take full advantage of that investment, by allowing more people and businesses to locate close to world-class transport infrastructure,” Bishop said.

“Auckland’s city centre is already an economic powerhouse. It accounts for around 8% of New Zealand’s GDP and nearly 6% of the country’s jobs.

“There is enormous potential for it to grow further. Earlier this year, we launched an investigation into whether Auckland’s city centre planning rules were holding that growth back, and that work is now complete.”

The Government said economic modelling indicated that if the commercially feasible development is delivered and occupied, the recommended changes could support about 17,000 additional dwellings, 31,600 residents and 37,200 jobs in the city centre.

The modelling estimated the changes could increase annual national GDP by about $1.87 billion at full uptake, with a present value of about $42.6b over 40 years.

Auckland Minister Simon Watts said the report also recommended removing non-contributing sites from the Karangahape Rd Historic Heritage Area.

“These are sites within the heritage area that do not themselves make a significant contribution to its recognised heritage values, often because they have already been substantially altered or redeveloped,” Watts said.

“This would create greater opportunities for redevelopment on sites with limited heritage value, while continuing to protect the buildings and places that give Karangahape Rd its distinctive character.”

Examples of non-contributing sites included the Mobil petrol station at 565 Karangahape Rd and the “gravel pit” development site at 538 Karangahape Rd.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown said the proposals were a practical way to make the most of infrastructure Aucklanders had already paid for.

“I’ve consistently said Auckland needs to intensify in the right places. That means enabling more homes and businesses close to rapid transit, jobs and existing infrastructure.

“We have invested billions of dollars in the City Rail Link and in the roads, pipes and other infrastructure that supports the central city. Our planning rules should help us get the best possible return from that investment.”

Brown said the job now wasn’t just to enable capacity, but to ensure things were built so Auckland could make the most of the City Rail Link.

Public consultation on the proposed changes runs until 11.59pm on Friday, October 16.

The city-centre proposals are separate from Plan Change 120, Auckland Council’s wider housing intensification plan, which is open for submissions.

The final plan would allow apartment towers of 10 and 15 storeys to be built near most inner-city train stations along the Western, Eastern and Southern rail lines.

Six-storey developments would be permitted along the busiest bus routes.

The Committee for Auckland released its latest State of the City report last month, finding Auckland was fast becoming an innovation centre and taking baby steps towards becoming a tech hub.

Katie Bradford is a Senior Correspondent at the Herald. She has been a broadcast journalist for over 20 years and was based in the press gallery for 10 years. She specialises in politics, business and Auckland issues.

TVNZ investigative journalist and broadcaster Indira Stewart has revealed she is undergoing chemotherapy after being diagnosed with grade three breast cancer.

“Did this photo shoot a couple of days before starting chemo. Diagnosed with Grade 3 breast cancer, tumour was aggressive, started chemo two weeks later.

“Looking at these photos now is like looking at an old friend … I haven’t left home a lot this year but when I have, I’ve hidden my cancer pretty well with false lashes, drawn-on eyebrows and cold capping (a technology that preserved about half my hair volume)."

She said the post would come as a surprise to some.

“I haven’t even had a chance to tell many people. There are friends and family who will find out through this post and I know they will understand …"

Stewart said in the post that treatment had led to early menopause and a mastectomy at 41. “But I got a new boob and I LOVE IT.”

“I’m still doing chemo, along with other treatment. The journey feels long but I feel lucky and grateful. This is a reminder to get checked fam, get your mammogram if you’re eligible and don’t put it off.”

Her post has been met with an outpouring of support from friends, family, colleagues and supporters.
