Canterbury reclaims top spot in ASB Regional Economic Scoreboard after strong growth

New Zealand Herald September 17, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Canterbury has reclaimed the top position in ASB’s latest Regional Economic Scoreboard, a ranking driven by strong consumer spending, population growth, a resilient labour market and a firm housing sector.

The ASB Regional Economic Scoreboard, released today, uses the latest quarterly regional statistics and ranks the economic performance of New Zealand’s 16 Regional Council areas.

The Canterbury region returned to first place in the second quarter (Q2) of 2026 after taking second place for Q1, while Taranaki recorded one of the strongest turnarounds in the country.

Meanwhile, Auckland slipped to sixth place as weakness in the housing market continued to weigh on the region’s performance.

ASB’s acting chief economist Kim Mundy said Canterbury “has the full package right now”.

“Households are spending, businesses are investing, the labour market remains resilient and strong dairy returns are providing an additional boost to the economy,” Mundy said.

Canterbury’s labour market held up in Q2, with employment up 2.6% year-on-year and one of the lowest national rates of unemployment at 3.6%.

The region’s housing market remained strong, with house prices rising 3.3% annually.

High dairy prices boosted export returns, while continued population growth and major events bolstered by One New Zealand Stadium supported economic activity during the quarter.

Core retail sales in Canterbury grew 8.8% year-on-year, the strongest result in the country.

“What’s interesting about the retail data is that we can see there’s been a 4% year-on-year decline in tourism spending in the region, suggesting the strong retail sales in Q2 was driven by locals rather than visitors,” Mundy said.

Canterbury’s place on the scoreboard comes just a week after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said Christchurch shows what New Zealand needs to look like.

Speaking at NZME’s Project Canterbury business breakfast at One NZ Stadium, Luxon explained why he sees Christchurch as a shining example of New Zealand’s future.

However, Canterbury isn’t the only region that has climbed the ranks, with Taranaki delivering the biggest surprise, climbing to second place in the rankings after sitting near the bottom last quarter.

Mundy said Taranaki recorded one of the “country’s strongest rebounds”.

Employment growth in Taranaki was among the strongest nationally, construction activity surged 47.1% year-on-year and new vehicle registrations increased 21.6%.

“Taranaki recorded one of the country’s strongest rebounds, benefiting from strong dairy and meat sector performance, supported by the Fonterra capital return payout and favourable export conditions,” Mundy said.

“These strengths likely offset some weakness in the oil and gas sector.”

There were also plenty of bright spots for Southland, with strong house price growth, a surge in new car registrations and solid retail sales growth underpinning their result of third place.

“While housing markets remained subdued across much of New Zealand, Southland’s housing market continued to show remarkable resilience, with annual growth in both house prices and house sales remaining the strongest in the country,” Mundy said.

Strong dairy and meat exports, with Fonterra’s capital return payout, continued to support the regional economy.

Retail sales rose around 7% over the past year, while new car registrations increased sharply.

“The region’s Achilles heel has been its softening labour market, with employment falling 2.9% annually,” Mundy said.

“However, agriculture remains a significant contributor to the local economy and is currently performing strongly, helping offset some of the weakness in the jobs market.”

The City of Sails slipped down the rankings to sixth place, underperforming the national average across most indicators in ASB’s Q2 Regional Economic Scoreboard.

Despite new car registrations rising strongly, reflecting demand for electric vehicles, and building consents showing healthy growth, other regions recorded even stronger gains in these areas.

“Auckland’s housing market remained a key drag on performance, with both house prices and sales down significantly on a year ago,” Mundy said.

“Buyers continued to hold the upper hand as listings remained high and demand subdued.

Mundy said while some sectors were bolstering Auckland, other factors created “ongoing uncertainty” for the region.

“Population growth and tourism are providing some support to the region, but Auckland’s economy continues to contend with cost-of-living pressures, interest rates trending higher, a soft labour market and ongoing uncertainty,” Mundy said.

“While these challenges may weigh on activity in the near term, the region remains well positioned to benefit as economic conditions gradually improve.”

Despite a slowing economy, New Zealand’s export sector remained resilient in Q2.

Export volumes rose 6.4% over the quarter and 10% on a year ago, while export prices increased 3.5%.

Dairy, meat and wool all posted solid gains, helping offset the surge in import prices from the Middle East conflict.

“Exports look set to remain a key source of support for the economy, underpinned by firm commodity prices and a weak New Zealand dollar,” Mundy said.

“For now, New Zealand’s two-speed economy appears likely to persist.”

Mundy said the subdued economic backdrop is expected to continue, with Middle East tensions adding to uncertainty.

“We expect further 25-basis-point hikes from the RBNZ [Reserve Bank] in October and December, taking the OCR [Official Cash Rate] to 3.25%,” she said.

“Higher interest rates are likely to weigh on consumer spending and delay a broader housing market recovery.

“While the outlook remains data-dependent, inflation is expected to stay close to 4% through the rest of 2026 and labour market conditions are likely to remain soft.”

The ASB Regional Economic Scoreboard ratings are updated every three months and are based on 11 measures, including employment, construction, the retail trade and house prices.

Australian rugby league superstar Reece Walsh has signed a major deal with the NFL’s Seattle Seahawks.

Briggs, Australia’s most beloved rapper, goes hardcore

Sydney Morning Herald September 18, 2026

The Yorta Yorta rapper makes his hardcore punk debut with his new band Big Noter.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

As a solo artist and one half of ARIA-winning duo A. B. Original (with Trials), Yorta Yorta artist Adam Briggs has long been one of Australia’s most acclaimed and popular rappers. But he has a simple response for anyone who might be confounded by his sudden, and unexpected, pivot to hardcore punk.

“Those imaginary lines of ‘you can’t do this’ and ‘you shouldn’t do that because you do this’? First of all, I’ll do what the f--- I want,” he says with a laugh from his home in Melbourne.

“Second, I do things I’m passionate about and that I have my heart in. I just wanted to do something different. I wanted to make a different kind of record and just explore.

“If you look at my career and the things I’ve done, I’ve always done different shit. I’ve done rap, comedy, written kids’ books, written episodes of TV. I’ve acted in films, I’ve acted in TV. I’ve always done something different, so this shouldn’t be such a surprise.”

The perfectly titled Songs in the Key of Wrestling is Briggs’ debut hardcore album with his new band Big Noter (the band also features Steve Smith on drums, with Leigh Davies on guitars and Craig Strain on bass). If the sonic delivery is different, the tenacity is signature Briggs.

Over thunderous riffage, opener My Genocide preaches collective liberation; It’s All Good Til It’s Not questions moral complacency; and Identity celebrates pride in self-determination. Album closer What’s the Matter with Adam? is a rhetorical dig at our mental health crisis.

“There are all these sick people, so at some point the system has failed,” says Briggs. “Even for me, I’m looked at as some kind of well-off dude, but for me to be able to get in to see a psych, it’s taken nearly 18 months. Some people don’t have the capacity and the facilities to wait that long.”

What prompted him to seek mental health treatment? “Just trying to be a better person, man, that’s all. I’m not an emergency case, I don’t hear voices and stuff,” he says with a laugh.

“I’m a fortunate person and I get to express myself in a lot of interesting ways, and I’m forever grateful for that, but I don’t measure my personal success as the benchmark for where we’re at as a society and as a community. If my mates are struggling, so am I.

“People will talk about going to see their personal trainer and whatever, but there’s a stigma around seeking therapy or seeking mental health treatment. The sooner we equate physical health and mental health as one and the same, the better off we’re all going to be.”

It’s immediately clear on Songs in the Key of Wrestling that no matter the genre, righteous fury remains the driving force behind Briggs’ creative expression. His work is a literal manifestation of John Lydon’s famous claim that “anger is an energy”.

“For sure, but I have to balance it with humour,” Briggs says, pointing to songs like What Ya Swingin’ At and Big Noter (recorded with Idles singer Joe Talbot) that revel in brash braggadocio.

“It’s meant to be over-the-top, like an action movie, the kind of stuff we grew up on. Because the thing is, when I’m angry, bro, I can’t focus. I’ve got to be Zen when I write, I’ve got to be calm to focus, and that’s when the anger comes through. But even when they’re angry, these songs are fun. Because there’s a release to it. Finally, you get to breathe.”

Hip-hop and hardcore have always lived side by side for Briggs. As a ’90s kid growing up in Shepparton in country Victoria, Rage and Recovery were his gateways to heavy music. “Scratch the Surface by Sick of It All, that was a huge one for me,” Briggs recalls. “And then I found Terror’s One with the Underdogs EP when that dropped. That was very much my kind of shit.”

Born in the streets and community halls and fuelled by alienation, hip-hop and hardcore have always shared more similarities than differences. It’s Public Enemy sporting Minor Threat tees. Ice-T fronting Body Count. Even Beastie Boys were a hardcore band before they bought an 808 drum machine.

“And Sick of It All are a band from Queens, you know what I mean?” adds Briggs. “I hung out with them for a bit, and Lou [Koller, the Sick of It All singer, who died in July] – rest in peace, legend – was telling me stories about seeing Kool G Rap outside his high school. They were up on all their rap shit because they’re all from the same ’hood.”

Even today’s biggest hip-hop stars, like Travis Scott and rage-rappers Playboi Carti and Ken Carson embrace the overlap. Look at their gigs and they resemble hardcore shows: there’s a circle pit going, kids are stage-diving and slam-dancing, complete release.

“The boundaries are imaginary, bro. They don’t exist,” says Briggs of the genre switch. “It’s what I felt doing this Big Noter record. It’s the same message, it’s just how I’ve chosen to deliver it. Not much really had to change. It’s the same moral code and the same values, which to me is the most important part of anything I do.”

In a nod to the overlap, he recruited some famous friends to appear on the album. On What’s the Matter with Adam?, Tom Morello of iconic rap-rockers Rage Against the Machine contributes a typically blistering guitar solo that sounds like turntablism-meets-Space Invaders.

On the interlude A Message from Chuck, Briggs gets his friend Chuck D of Public Enemy to deliver a few words shouting out Yorta Yorta Nation and calling out January 26. “I wanted to pay homage to rap because I didn’t want to create this idea that I was leaving hip-hop,” Briggs says.

“When I wrote a kids’ book I wasn’t leaving hip-hop. When I was writing for Disenchantment with Matt Groening I wasn’t leaving hip-hop. But suddenly I shift genres and I’ve left something behind? Nah, that’s not it.

“Having Chuck on the record is just an acknowledgment of the community he’s been a part of as well,” Briggs adds, noting Public Enemy’s famous link-up with heavy music stalwarts Anthrax on 1991’s Bring the Noise. “He sent it back with multiple takes and I was like, sick.”

It did, however, create one lasting bit of light-hearted concern. “I was saying to a mate, like, in this world of AI, I bet a lot of people will think I just got this AI Chuck D to shout out Shepparton and Yorta Yorta Nation,” he says, laughing.

“But f--- it because I know what’s what. A lot of the things I do on my albums and in my career are solely for me, so I don’t even trip.”

Big Noter’s Songs in the Key of Wrestling is out now. The band will perform at The Tote in Melbourne on September 19.

Larissa Lambert, Australia’s empress of R&B, is ready for her close-up

Sydney Morning Herald September 18, 2026

Amid viral success and mental health struggles, Australian music’s best-kept secret unveils her long-awaited debut album.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

If R&B has been perennially overlooked in Australia, Larissa Lambert has been its best-kept secret. The 30-year-old has a voice so warm and vibrant it could melt your butter, fry your pancakes, boil your coffee – the full breakfast. It’s the kind of thing a religious person might call “a gift from God”. When did she know she had it?

“This is so cliche but, honestly, I knew since I could f---ing talk,” Lambert says with all the bluntness that’s made her a social media favourite. “I have memories of my family and people at school sitting around me being like, ‘do it again!’, and I’d sing a line and they’d be like, ‘whoa!’ So I knew, like, ‘I’m good at this’. There was no doubt about it. I had no plan B. I was like, ‘I’m gonna be a singer’.”

More than a decade into her career, with viral successes and plaudits from superstars like SZA and Justin Bieber to her name, she’s finally releasing her long-awaited debut album, Yearning. Filled with her effortless vocals, production flourishes that flitter between Y2K nostalgia and club trends, and writing that coolly probes her desires and insecurities, the album is a cohesive triumph. It begs the question: why did it take so long?

“I just never felt like I was ready,” says Lambert. “I was always like, ‘people are expecting so much from me’, so it needed to feel authentic. It needed to be me.”

Wearing black leather pants, her pierced septum gleaming, Lambert looks every bit the star as we speak in a room the size of a confessional in Virgin Music’s offices in inner-Sydney’s Chippendale. We’re barely 10 minutes into the interview when she begins to outline the harrowing challenges that, at least partly, skewered the timeline to her debut.

Three years ago, Lambert suffered psychosis following withdrawals from an addiction to prescription Valium. “My brain basically just went f---ing haywire. It took me a whole year to get back to normal,” she says. “During a psychosis, your whole world is flipped. I just felt hopeless. It’s f---ing scary.

“It’s like a panic attack on steroids. Everyone’s different with how they experience psychosis; some people can be aware they’re in it and some people can completely black out. I understood what was going on but you’re in an intense state of paranoia, you have intrusive thoughts, your moods are up and down. Writing was the only thing that was keeping me sane.”

She’d been through drug psychosis before, years prior when she was 22. “That was from an edible, actually, because even marijuana is a big trigger for psychosis. If your family has a history of mental health issues you should never touch it,” she says.

She’s more protective of herself now. “No substances, I’m 100 per cent sober,” she says. “I used to have a very addictive personality and I couldn’t say no, couldn’t turn down the party phase. Growing up, it was always like that.

“The music industry, artists, creatives – we’re so addicted to escapism, especially if you come from not the best upbringing. You tend to emotionally regulate through substances. In my case, that’s what it was. I never knew how to deal with my emotions, so I would smoke to get out of them or take some sleepers to mellow out.

“It’s so toxic, man, and it catches up to you. It caught up to me. So I’m 100 per cent sober, straighty-180 now. Maybe a little sip of wine here and there, but otherwise … I can’t, it’s not worth it.”

Lambert had been working at a pizza shop in her home town, Rio Bravo in Ballarat – “incredible pizza, one of my favourite jobs I ever had” – when she scored her first break. At 16, a scout from The X Factor, then airing on the Seven Network, phoned, inviting her to an artist development camp after seeing videos she’d posted on Facebook of herself singing on her bedroom floor. “I thought it was a scam,” Lambert recalls. “He was like, ‘we’ve got this camp, it’s $500’. I was like, you’re f---ing joking.”

After verifying the call was legit, she used funds she’d been saving to buy a laptop to accept the offer. Her boss at the pizza shop paid for her flights to Sydney. “He was a blessing,” says Lambert. At the camp, she was successfully recruited into the girl group Paris Inc.

“It was fun. It felt like training,” Lambert recalls of her time on The X Factor. “I needed it for my confidence. I used to be really, like, inwards. Being in the girl group helped me come out of my shell.”

In 2019, after Paris Inc split, Lambert received interest from the States; a girl who was working with R&B star Jeremih – famed for his DJ Mustard-produced smash Don’t Tell ’Em, still a barbershop staple – found her on Instagram and pitched her to the singer. “He took me under his wing,” says Lambert. “He mentored me about how the States works, the culture, the people, certain flows and how to add more pockets to my songs. I’m so grateful for him. He wanted to sign me at the time but I ended up turning it down because I wanted to stay independent.”

Even now, Lambert remains an independent artist. She must’ve had major labels chasing her for ages? “Oh yeah, I’ve had an offer from pretty much every single label, but it’s always just been a standard label deal,” she says.

What does that mean? “It means they’ll give you a label deal out of the 1980s where there’s nothing – literally, less than minus – in your favour,” she says, laughing. Her current arrangement with Virgin Music is a distribution deal, where she owns her masters and licenses them to the label for a set period.

“Virgin were the only label that respected me, understood the vision and listened,” Lambert explains. “With a lot of the major labels, you’re just another TikTok viral sensation they’re gonna sign, and if you pop off, you pop off. I feel like labels have lost the art of developing an artist.”

When labels approached her in the past, being a young artist, how did she know the deals weren’t in her best interests? “My intuition, I guess. It just never felt right.”

She pauses and recalibrates. “Actually, you know what it was? It’s because I went viral before I ever signed anything, so I started seeing my cheques!” she says with a laugh. “And knowing that a label would take 80 per cent of my earnings just to say they have me but not do anything for me? I was like, that is stupid, you’re not taking my money!”

Back in 2021, a cover she sang of SWV’s Weak went “stupid viral” on TikTok. “Someone from the Philippines, and Indonesia as well, they started a dance trend to it. All these different trends took off. It was like a tree branch. It just kept going.”

Lambert once said the viral cover made her “a lot of money”, enough to keep her career going. How so? “Well, I dropped the full cover on Spotify and then, you know, you make money from the master percentage. But then all the publishing obviously goes to SWV. So they made a good chunk off me, too!”

She’d lucked into the exact kind of virality record labels employ entire departments to manufacture. “Yeah, and you can’t,” says Lambert. “You can definitely make a song viral if you put millions of dollars into it but is it gonna stick, though? Authentic viral is so special but no one knows the f---ing recipe. If I did, I’d go viral every time.”

The experience gave her a unique insight into industry machinations, which was significant when record labels came calling. “They literally take 80 per cent of your earnings – it’s crazy! Like, how are you supposed to live? Off a tiny advance that’s supposed to last you three years? It doesn’t make sense. In my opinion, if you’re an artist and you sign to a label, you shouldn’t be working a nine-to-five. You should be able to put all your time and focus on your music and have an advance that will last you,” she says.

“But, like, it’s a risk on both sides because labels are also risking a lot of money on certain artists, so I get it. But that’s why I chose to stay independent with a distro deal, and I vouch for that for any up-and-coming artists as well. It’s good because it forces you to learn every angle, so you’re never getting taken advantage of.”

On social media, Lambert’s gift has earned praise from SZA, Bieber and Ty Dolla $ign, a case of game recognising game. Do such co-signs translate into anything tangible? “Like, does it bring people to me?” Lambert asks. “Oh, of course. Especially when they’ve shared my stuff, they put on so many new listeners. But just having the recognition from them is crazy. The fact that my idols are seeing me and appreciating me? It’s a huge pat on the back to let me know I’m doing something right.”

It makes it even more intriguing that she didn’t release her debut album sooner. Any other young artist would’ve been convinced to capitalise on the moment while there’s heat.

“I know, I look back and I wonder if I could have, but I don’t think it would have worked,” says Lambert. The key to unlocking her album, she says, was linking up with executive producer Khaled Rohaim. Rohaim – a Grammy-nominated Sydney producer who has worked with stars including Rihanna, Doja Cat and The Kid Laroi – had long had Lambert in his sights.

“He was trying to get me to leave the girl group when I was 17 and I was like, ‘who is this guy?’,” Lambert says, laughing. “I had no idea what he’d done but he actually has some of the most insane credits. Eventually I ended up doing a session with him three years ago, and we’ve been inseparable ever since.”

The album’s emotional through line lies in its title. “Yearning” is a term that has had a cultural blow-up this year, a buzzword that’s defined a generation’s pushback against the casual nonchalance of online dating. It’s also long been the central emotion in R&B, from Jodeci’s Feenin’ to Kehlani’s Folded.

“It’s about letting go of ego, bringing back authenticity and longing and openness,” says Lambert of her album’s message. “We’re in such a culture of being independent and being within yourself, and it’s toxic because we’re not meant to be like that. It makes people go insane and get depressed.”

She sees the album as an antidote to an era of dark, brooding R&B. “I feel like R&B went through a period where ‘dark love’ was trending, and I just kind of miss the cringe love song.”

Lambert has said Yearning “was created during a period of genuine clarity and inner alignment”. She’s reached a point in her life where she’s at peace and ready to tell stories she wasn’t comfortable with before.

“I was always worried about, oh, what if I tell people I’ve gone through psychosis and they’re like, ‘oh, little druggy!’ I think that’s why it’s taken me so long to have my debut album,” says Lambert.

“I just got so in my head. I started making songs for other people rather than the reason why I started making music in the first place, which was artistry and expression. But you’ve just got to get to a place of not giving a f---, and that’s when it all flows out.”

Larissa Lambert’s debut album Yearning is out now.

Kluivert and Rayan rock Real Sociedad as Bournemouth win on European bow

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 21:14:08 GMT

The first goal that AFC Bournemouth ever scored in Europe could be heard out on the Bay of Biscay. A tradition from Real Sociedad’s old Atotxa ground, once lost but now recovered at Anoeta, dictates that a single flare is set off every time the visitors score while two are lit when the home team do; that way those out to sea know the score. And so it was that at 21.41 on a Thursday night in September 2026, Justin Kluivert found the net and a man named Juan Iturralde ran out into the street to let everyone know what had happened.

Back in Dorset and high in Anoeta, where 2,000 Bournemouth fans sang their way through this most special of occasions, they knew. They had waited their whole lives for this and it was a nice way to mark the history they made, their arrival announced to Europe with fireworks and a 2-1 victory in San Sebastián, the city where it all began for Andoni Iraola, the manager who brought them here.

Iturralde ran into the night three times – he went once more when Rayan made it 2-0 after 20 minutes and again when Sergio Gómez made it 2-1 on 57 – and might have gone more too. After a superb first half, Bournemouth had to hang on, sometimes desperately, in the second. For a while it had seemed a lead would slip away from their grasp for the fifth time in six games this season, but Djordje Petrovic came to their rescue with two astonishing saves from Orri Óskarsson in the final, dramatic minutes. They had done it, everyone at the final whistle. It had been some battle and they had given everything.

That resistance hadn’t appeared necessary an hour or so earlier. Bournemouth had waited 127 years for a first European game and considerably less for their first goal. They had been playing 10 minutes and 43 seconds and when it came they celebrated it twice. A lovely shift of the body from Evanilson started it, the Brazilian receiving and releasing Adrien Truffert. The cross was perfectly placed, bent behind the defensive line for Kluivert to score.

High in the north-east corner Bournemouth’s fans went up but down in the south-west corner the flag did too, it didn’t take the video assistant referee long to prove that was wrong, and allowing them to do it all again while Iturralde set off into the street. Truffert was on the run again soon after, Alex Scott’s glorious long, looped, curling ball dropping into just the right place for Rayan to head the second.

There was an ease about the way Scott had completed the pass – an almost gentle turn of the ankle, the ball delivered as if by hand – and about the way he played. Amid the speed and intensity he glided. Around him, teammates flew everywhere, Marcus Tavernier especially, and Real Sociedad could not keep up. Three times they threatened from dead balls too: Evanilson headed the first off the post, António Silva headed the second wide and Óskarsson just about headed away a third. Songs from the corner sung to a backdrop of frustrated whistles from the rest of Anoeta.

From the home fans there was relief when half-time arrived without the lead being extended. There was also a reaction, a dash from Ander Barrenetxea signalling their intent and an increase in volume. Petrovic made a superb save from Beñat Turrientes on 56 minutes and almost immediately Real Sociedad pulled one back. Gómez’s curling cross bent all the way through, past the outstretched legs and into the far corner.

This was a different game and a different place now, Real Sociedad’s version of Bad Moon Rising interrupted by an “huuy!” when Gonçalo Guedes’s effort was pushed past the post by Petrovic. Already this season Bournemouth had lost leads against Manchester City, Everton, Newcastle and Brentford, most of them late, and a familiar feeling only increased as Gómez’s fantastic ball sent Guedes through on the left, only for the Portuguese winger to try to cut inside rather than shoot. From the loose ball, Mikel Oyarzabal’s subtle, clipped shot floated onto the top of the bet.

after newsletter promotion

Gómez was not their only problem. Luka Sucic shot wide on 81 minutes and then Gómez slipped Óskarsson in for what should have been the equaliser. Petrovic though saved that and, somehow, stopped the Iceland striker from five yards in the final minute.

Ultimately, the fireworks were finally over on Bournemouth’s famous night as a European journey that was once unimaginable was heard across the sea.

Tom Banton’s six-hitting wins T20 for England after Dawson derails Sri Lanka

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 21:05:14 GMT

Banton and Brook lead England home in style

Big hitting leaves Sri Lanka looking out of their depth

England extended their extraordinary hex over Sri Lanka to a 14th game, with the tourists looking as out of their depth as the balls that were repeatedly deposited into the River Taff as their opponents cantered to their target of 146 to win by six wickets, with 47 balls remaining.

More than a dozen years have passed since Sri Lanka, crowned world champions in the format a month earlier, beat England by nine runs at the Oval. They have lost every meeting since and with this one also the series, and while much about this game contrasted with Tuesday’s first encounter in Southampton – starting with England winning the toss and choosing to chase – the outcome did not: another emphatic home win, sealed in the end in slapdash style: no-ball, wide, single, wide, single, muted celebration.

It was the six-hitting that most obviously illustrated the disparity in batting quality and power between the sides. Only two Sri Lankans managed to clear the boundary, and none more than once. Tom Banton doubled their collective tally on his own on his way to his fifth and fastest half-century in T20s; Harry Brook managed three sixes, and he faced only eight balls.

The evening had started promisingly for Sri Lanka, put in to bat with the ball racing at the slightest invitation across an outfield slick from a brief pre-match shower, but they soon went from scoring at pace to unravelling with similar rapidity. Lahiru Udara, bumped up a spot to open, got the evening off to a strong start alongside Pathum Nissanka, and after five overs they stood at 55 without loss. They scored 90 for nine off the remaining 15.

Liam Dawson initially derailed them. Udara, having scored 21 off 20, drove high to mid-on, where any fielder but the 6ft 5in Jamie Overton would have clawed at thin air but this one nonchalantly plucked it out of the sky. Kamil Mishara, bumped down a spot to No3, came in and miscued his first ball back to the bowler. Sri Lanka attempted to rebuild but instead they crumbled.

If Dawson’s introduction was productive, his final over was expensive. With five to go the tourists found themselves on 115 for five, whereupon Charith Asalanka, the captain, and Wanindu Hasaranga plundered 18 to spoil the spinner’s figures. That established a platform for a late-innings surge; they scored just 12 more, for the loss of four wickets, from their last four overs. Sonny Baker bowled two of those, his last a wicket maiden, to continue his fine form from the series opener in Southampton, and their total of 145 felt seriously underpowered.

For a while England tracked them closely: they too had scored 55 after five overs, though by then Nye Donald, now of Derbyshire but born in Swansea and originally of Glamorgan, had mishit successive Eshan Malinga deliveries into the sky, the first landing safe and the second not so much, caught by Hasaranga at mid-on. And like Sri Lanka they were two down in the sixth, Jos Buttler’s wild slash giving Mishara the chance to run 20 yards to his right from behind the stumps before taking the catch. Until that point Buttler had looked in fabulous touch, and if he will not have been satisfied with his contribution of 30 off 16, becoming the first man to pass 15,000 runs in T20 cricket might have helped him come to terms with it.

after newsletter promotion

After an epic unbeaten century at Southampton, Brook’s innings here was more of a cameo, but still thrilling for as long as it lasted. Three times in a single Hasaranga over he hit monstrous shots over midwicket off the back foot but he was punished for attempting a fourth, though it took a superb sprinting, diving catch by Malinga to do so. It was the first time Brook had been dismissed in this format since early July, four innings in which he had scored a mere 284. He is not quite invincible in this format but at home his team are coming close: beaten just once under his captaincy, and that in a rain-affected five-over shootout here last September. They have never gone unbeaten in a summer featuring more than two T20s; Saturday’s final fixture at Old Trafford will be their eighth of 2026, five of those against India’s world champions, and they don’t look like stumbling any time soon.

Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 21:04:24 GMT

HMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhood

The founder of Addison Lee owes £20.5m in tax after a tribunal dismissed a claim that he should be treated as a nom-dom despite living in the UK since childhood.

John Griffin had argued he should be treated as a nom-dom due to his connection to Ireland, saying: “I was and am besotted with Ireland, infatuated with Ireland. I believe that I have always been and am Irish.”

HM Revenue and Customs challenged the domicile status on Griffin’s self-assessment tax returns from 2013 to 2020, which would have allowed the 84-year-old to not pay UK tax rates on foreign earnings kept outside the country.

This week, a London tribunal ruled in the tax authority’s favour.

Griffin was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine, according to tribunal documents.

HMRC argued that England should be considered Griffin’s home, with the businessman raising a family in Hertfordshire and building his London-based taxi empire, having founded Addison Lee in 1975.

Tribunal judge Michaela Snelders and tribunal member Gill Hunter said: “We are satisfied that by 5 April 2013, Sir John had settled in England in every meaningful sense.”

“England was where he had established his home, raised his family, built his business, accumulated his wealth and organised his personal, social and professional life.

“Although he retained a powerful emotional attachment to Ireland and a genuine hope that he might one day spend more time there, those sentiments never crystallised into a sufficiently definite intention to make Ireland his permanent home.”

The tax chamber tribunal was told Griffin spent eight nights in Ireland in 2015, one of the years he claimed to be domiciled there, which the chamber ruled was “inconsistent with someone seriously preparing for permanent relocation”.

As part of his appeal against HMRC’s stance, Griffin had argued that his domicile should be the same as his father, Jack, who had come to England from Ireland in search of work in 1935. Under UK law, a child’s domicile is the same as their father’s if the parents were married at the time of their birth.

Legal counsel for HMRC, however, said Griffin’s domicile status under UK law would have changed when his father’s domicile of choice became England. They argued it had done so some time before Griffin reached adulthood at the age of 21 in 1963. The tribunal agreed with HMRC’s stance.

The ruling caps off a long-running inquiry into Griffin’s tax affairs and reflects the period after he sold Addison Lee to private equity firm the Carlyle Group in 2013. The business was reported to be worth £300m at the time.

Having Irish domicile would have potentially allowed Griffin to avoid being taxed on earnings made outside the UK, a legal benefit of being classified as a nom-dom. The tribunal’s ruling makes his worldwide income from the period subject to UK tax rules, with HMRC calculating that he owes an additional £20.5m covering the seven-year period.

Nom-dom status was scrapped by the Labour UK government in April 2025, after a promise a year earlier by Rishi Sunak’s Conservative administration to do the same.

Griffin, knighted in 2024 for services to business and charity, did not give evidence in person to the tribunal after HMRC accepted he was not medically fit to do so due to “cognitive decline”.

New cat species identified for first time in more than a century in Bolivia

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 20:43:38 GMT

New species of wild feline was discovered in Bolivia’s Yungas forest that is smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.

The cat, called tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger ⁠cats found across much of South ⁠America. It was found in Bolivia’s ​lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18in (46cm) long and weighs about 3lbs (1.4kg), making it smaller than the average domestic ⁠cat.

Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.

“Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors ⁠of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.

Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat ​samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it ‌could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said.

Tiger ‌cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.

Tiger ‌cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.

Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.”

One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives in the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.

Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?”

The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South ‌American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.

“We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said.

Genetic analysis suggested ​that the tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4m years ago.

“The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.

The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca empire that included the area it inhabits.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list tracking the status of species currently treats ⁠tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining populations.

The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess ​the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the tilcayo ​could be considered endangered when assessed on their own.

The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one of the ​region’s most threatened ecosystems.

The mountain forests ‌face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural ​expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. ​Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz added.

“Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 20:33:37 GMT

Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his life

Days before Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the “Putney pusher”, killed himself, he told his family that the police investigation was “murdering him”.

He had “no fight left” in him, he told his sisters, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker, and could not see an end to the Metropolitan police investigation, or the online abuse.

Brandram’s lawyers warned the Met last week that his mental health had deteriorated and he was receiving treatment in a psychiatric hospital after renewed press reporting that he had been released under investigation.

“He said a couple of days ago that this investigation was murdering him. Day by day, he was slowly being murdered,” Hicks, 40, said through tears.

“He saw no end to this investigation,” added Voelcker, 45. “My sister and I were keeping a close eye on him because he was telling us he couldn’t go on. He said it more than once in the week before, that he couldn’t keep going. All we could do was just reassure him. We had faith in the system, we had faith in the police, and they neglected him. They failed in their duty of care to him, to the wider family, and we do not want to see another family going through this.”

The pair insisted that Brandram, 44, was not the “Putney pusher” and that he died thinking no one would believe in his innocence.

He was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm on 15 June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge in south-west London.

The case attracted considerable media attention but appeared to elude detectives, who wound down their investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects.

But there was renewed interest in the case after Brandram’s arrest, which his family described as heavy-handed and disproportionate. A number of officers in body armour reportedly swooped on his home address, his sisters said, while a reporter who had been tipped off about the arrest filmed the ordeal.

Although Brandram’s name was not published in the media because he had not been charged, his family said that biographical information in reports made him easily identifiable. He was described as a wealthy banker who lived in a £1.4m west London home and an army veteran with links to royalty. Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was a great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria.

While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs.

His sisters said there was no forensic evidence linking Brandram to the Putney incident and that he had a prominent military tattoo and a withered calf which, they said, distinguished him from the man in footage of the attack on 5 May 2017.

That morning, Brandram had walked from his home in Notting Hill Gate to his office in Bond Street and sent his sisters an email from his work account, which they said he could only access from his workplace. They said that evidence was passed on to the police.

They added that Brandram had volunteered to take part in an identification parade and provided his DNA for comparison with a sample recovered at the time of the incident. Hicks said detectives told Brandram just days ago that they still did not know when the DNA analysis would be completed.

“Our brother willingly provided DNA in an attempt to obviously help clear his name and to complete the investigation, and for weeks now we’ve been asking the police just to complete the DNA test,” Voelcker said.

“We’ve always maintained that he’s innocent. He always maintained he was innocent. We just needed the police to complete their inquiry, and it just felt particularly egregious that they were just hanging this DNA test over him.”

Hicks said as details of the case kept being reported in the press, her brother became preoccupied by online abuse on forums such as Reddit.

“His reputation within a couple of days was in tatters. People saying he’s the alleged pusher, and you can imagine the vitriol that was coming out online,” Voelcker said.

“You can imagine what people might say about somebody they think tried to push a woman in front of a bus. There was a lot of people had a lot of views about our brother, about his background, about where he worked.”

“And the problem was he was reading it all every day,” Hicks said. “The vitriol is still there and that’s what’s so heartbreaking for us, is that when he took his own life he died thinking that effectively everyone hated him and thought he’d done something awful and that no one would see that he was innocent and he knew that his family were behind him but it wasn’t enough.”

The sisters said Brandram had stayed with them in recent days after his mental health deteriorated following the publication of an update about the case that said he had been released under investigation.

“He was really talking about ending his life and ending things. And he was very low and said he felt like he had no fight left in him. He couldn’t see the end,” Voelcker said.

Brandram was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for six days before being discharged on Sunday.

His family insisted the Met police were warned about his mental health.

Voelcker tried to boost his mood on Tuesday by telling him it was a beautiful day and that he had many friends and his family supporting him. He was found dead at his home in Chiswick, west London, later that day.

The family said their priority was to clear their brother’s name and “to ensure another family does not have to go through what we have as a result of the police delays and leaks to the media”.

Hicks said: “Nick was really very loving, enthusiastic. He had an infectious character to be around, very funny. He was an extrovert, so he loved people. He was a much-loved father and uncle.”

Voelcker added: “He spent a long time in the army before going into the city. And his reputation was important. He was a proud man. I think that’s the thing and even the fact that he needed to seek help from a psychiatric hospital was a big deal for him.”

Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families.

“The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing.

“Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence.”

He added that the force had made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September.

Floyd Samba lit up this tie up with a debut that will have the 17-year-old grinning for a while after a superb goal in each half ensured Manchester City advanced to face Brighton in the last 16 in their defence of the Carabao Cup.

Samba has an older brother by a year, Tyrone, who is also in the academy. Their father, Christopher, is a former Blackburn and QPR defender.

With a game featuring speed, awareness and a poacher’s eye, he hopes to make a case for regular first-team game time. Given the elite-level forward competition this will be tough, but tonight was a fine calling card.

Samba said: “A debut like that is mind blowing. I couldn’t believe it – that’s just the beginning, I’ve got a big career ahead of me.”

For Enzo Maresca, a sixth successive win maintains a 100% record for his nascent project (barring the Community Shield) and points to how the manager is shrugging off doubts about succeeding Pep Guardiola.

Of Samba, he said: “Satisfying for the two goals, the entire performance he was good. He didn’t play [before] as a 9, we tried in the last two or three days. He is very good at finishing so it was a very good game for him. He is not a 9 for sure but he was good.”

City host Sunderland here on Sunday. Defeat Régis Le Bris’ side and Maresca will enjoy his three-week international break. You would not bet against them doing so – City are improving with each outing, as they did against Norwich.

Many opponents are blown away at the Etihad, so for the 14th-placed Championship side to initially tap the ball about was impressive.

Maresca’s formation was fluid and reaped a first dividend when Nico O’Reilly’s cross was fumbled by the visiting goalkeeper, Daniel Grimshaw. The ball dropped to Allan and he delivered it back across for Samba to cutely head home.

City doubled their lead when Samba laid the ball off to Ayyoub Bouaddi, the midfielder hit the ball to Rayan Cherki and, as Grimshaw advanced, he beat the keeper to his right.

Watching from the touchline, Philippe Clement hoped his side were not about to crumble as the first half neared its end. He was relieved when Samba, running in, was thwarted by a Grimshaw dive at his feet.

Yet his men ended the period chasing City: an exhausting task that showed the control the host exerted. In a sparsely attended tie, this was precisely what Maresca wished – it meant that his main man, Cherki could be rested, as Ryan McAidoo replaced him for the second half.

Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 19:29:44 GMT

Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035

Britain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet a Nato target of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday.

Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime minister Andy Burnham.

In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.”

The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually.

Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met with Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry.

Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey.

Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts.

Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews.

But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade. Decisions on future spending are likely to be left to the next government spending review due next year, prompting the Nato leader to engage in public lobbying on his trip to Britain.

Rutte said he was certain the Burnham government remained behind the ultimate goal and the need to increase defence spending gradually. “I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there,” he told the BBC.

“There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year,” Rutte added.

A day earlier, Rutte gave a speech to at Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire, in which he warned that the 32 country military alliance faced “the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with wars in Ukraine, the Middle East coming at time of rising state competition.

Nato needed “more UK and more Europe”, he added, to take up the slack as the US reduces its military commitment to the alliance. Trump has long argued that the UK and Europe should match US levels of defence spending and take the lead in defending the continent from Russia aggression.

By getting Diana’s sons to walk, “that would surely guarantee against insults flying”, he wrote.

The memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, due to be published next week, has already made headlines, with Spencer alleging that during a heated phone call before Diana’s funeral, the king remarked: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”

Buckingham Palace issued a robust rebuttal on Wednesday evening, saying in a statement: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”

In new extracts, published on Thursday on the website of the Daily Mail, which is serialising the book, Spencer suggests that some inside Buckingham Palace were “relieved – indeed pleased” at Diana’s death in a Paris car crash. It was his suspicion that Charles’s first reaction must have been to think how he could now marry Camilla Parker Bowles.

According to Spencer, Diana had confided in a friend that days before their wedding, Charles had told her “she needed to know he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her”, and she was certain he was “entering their marriage with his heart elsewhere”.

Diana tried to break off the engagement after finding a bracelet Charles had bought for Camilla, who is now the queen, he writes. But their father was “appalled”, telling her “it was impossible to pull out of such an enormous commitment at that point”.

Spencer says in the book that he also believes Charles may have contributed to the princess’s eating disorder, saying Diana’s waist shrank from 29in to 23.5in between the engagement and wedding after she was “devastated” at her fiance squeezing her waist and saying: ‘Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we.”

He was also convinced Diana had ADHD and, like himself, suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria. He writes: “It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. The excerpt goes on to say that Diana told him she was going to get divorced and that “my husband is in love with his valet”.

Spencer, 62, has said he wrote the memoir to correct “untruths” told about his elder sister.

The row over the book overshadowed a busy day for the royal family, with the Duke of Sussex also entered the mix with an engagement of his own.

Harry, who it is understood was aware of his uncle’s book in advance but not its contents, arrived at the inaugural Invictus Spirit awards in London on Thursday evening in his first appearance since returning to the UK from the US last month.

The Prince and Princess of Wales were on their first official trip to the Isle of Bute off the west coast of Scotland. The couple, who hold the titles of Duke and Duchess of Rothesay in Scotland, visited the namesake town of Rothesay, dropped in at a shinty club and stopped at a pub while meeting community leaders and volunteers.

Charles, meanwhile, was appearing in public for the first time since Spencer’s allegations were aired, at an AI summit he had convened at Dumfries House, in Ayrshire. Addressing global tech leaders, he warned of the “existential dangers” of AI systems falling into the wrong hands.

As those who have created these technologies had warned, AI risked “developing darker capacities – perhaps even to take life”, he said. The king spoke of the need for reassurance that “our humanity remains sacred” and “that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls”.

The Australian athlete who caused a storm by winning a Hyrox event in China despite soiling herself during the race has apologised to the “people of China” and rival athletes in a statement online.

Posting on Instagram, Joanna Wietrzyk offered a “sincere apology” to the “people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing”.

Footage of Wietrzyk, a world record-holder, went viral after it showed her competing in – and winning – Saturday’s event with demanding exercises and using communal equipment, despite having faecal matter running down her legs.

But she admitted in her post on Thursday night that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there was “more to life than racing”.

“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness,” Wietrzyk wrote.

“Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognise that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”

She said she would forfeit the points from winning the event.

“I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected. I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away. On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned.”

Hyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It made its debut in mainland China in late 2024.

In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

Hyrox earlier this week apologised and pledged immediate rule changes after Wietrzyk was allowed to finish and win the Beijing event.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologised in a statement on Instagram to everyone affected “directly or indirectly”.

“Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not,” Fürste said.

Infantino under pressure before presidential election

The Football Association’s chair, Debbie Hewitt, has written to Gianni Infantino demanding that Fifa releases all documents relating to his abandoned World Cup sell-off plan and the decision to lift the USA striker Folarin Balogun’s suspension during last summer’s tournament.

The Guardian revealed last month that Hewitt and other members of the Fifa council were lobbying for an independent review of the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off and the Balogun controversy. Their requests have been formalised in a letter sent to the Fifa president and his deputy, Mattias Grafström.

The letter, first reported by the Times, has been sent in advance of the Fifa council meeting in Zurich on 15 October. That is due to be the first time since the FFE plan emerged in July that Infantino will meet the other 36 members of the group that acts as Fifa’s board of directors.

A number of members of the council, which comprises 28 representatives of the six confederations, eight vice-presidents and Infantino, attempted last month to call an extraordinary general meeting to hold Infantino to account over FFE and Balogun.

The rebels were unable to get the 19 votes required to trigger such a meeting, however, and Hewitt’s call for the release of documents and an independent review is also likely to fail.

Infantino has not had any contact with the Fifa council since writing to it to withdraw FFE at the start of August and has been lobbying for support before next year’s presidential election, making visits to the Caribbean, South America, Morocco and Qatar.

Balogun’s ban was lifted after a phone call from Donald Trump to Infantino despite the player being shown a straight red card for serious foul play in the USA’s World Cup last-32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina. That allowed him to play against Belgium in the last 16, a match the USA lost 4-1.

Fifa has said it followed due process, with the decision taken independently by its ethics committee, but has yet to publish a written report on the hearing. A request from the Royal Belgian FA for an explanation went unanswered.

Hewitt’s letter is understood to make reference to other governance issues at Fifa, particularly its response to the crisis caused by the FFE controversy this summer.

The FA’s willingness to take the lead in holding Infantino to task comes with some risk because the UK is the currently sole bidder for the 2035 Women’s World Cup. A decision on the hosts of that tournament and the 2031 edition is due to be made at an extraordinary Fifa congress on 23 November.

The deadline for candidates to stand in March’s presidential election is five days earlier. Infantino is the only candidate to publicly reveal his intention to stand, with Uefa and Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – working to find someone to stand against him.

The FA sent a letter of endorsement for Infantino’s fourth term as president before the World Cup but, along with several other European countries, has since withdrawn its backing.

The Guardian view on EU-Canada relations: strategic ambition with lessons for Britain

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 17:48:38 GMT

Mark Carney’s response to the challenges posed by an unreliable US president contains a clarity of vision that is lacking in post-Brexit Britain

There is no “associate membership” of the European Union, nor any blueprint for what such a thing might involve. It is a political hypothesis, describing a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined.

This week, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, invited Canada to be the first country to enjoy this putative status. In her state of the union speech, she spoke of a future relationship elevated “to the highest level possible”, reflecting an affinity of interests and values. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, reciprocated the sentiment in a speech on Wednesday. Addressing the European parliament, he said the two sides should secure “strategic autonomy through deep cooperation” across a broad spectrum of interests: trade, defence, industrial capacity, science, space and AI. He proposed Canadian participation in the EU’s Erasmus student exchange programme and Horizon research scheme.

There is a vast gap between the declaration of those ambitions and their formalisation in any kind of treaty. Negotiating even a relatively straightforward trade agreement with the EU can be heavy going, given the need to accommodate the rival priorities of 27 member states. Creating a more multifaceted partnership is arduous work, bedevilled by technical detail, as Britain has found when trying to settle the terms of its post-Brexit relationship with mainland Europe.

That process has been complicated and slowed down by a deficit of trust. The Labour government has repudiated the venomous anti-Brussels ideology that drove the decision to leave the EU, but the Brexit deal inherited from the Conservatives was designed to work as an automatic ratchet, pulling the two sides apart. Reversing that mechanism takes a greater input of political energy and imagination than Sir Keir Starmer could muster. Andy Burnham has yet to rise to the challenge.

The UK prime minister could learn from his Canadian counterpart. Both find their global positions weakened by Donald Trump’s contempt for traditional US allies. Their circumstances are not exactly alike. Canada and the US share the longest land border on Earth. Mr Trump denigrates his northern neighbour’s sovereignty, suggesting it become the 51st US state. He has provoked a pointless, costly trade war. The UK has not been spared tariffs and other diplomatic indignities, but it has not suffered quite the same degree of sustained rhetorical and economic aggression.

Mr Carney has responded with a clear-eyed plan for geopolitical reorientation. He talks about a “rupture” in the international order and the challenge facing “middle powers” in a destabilised world shaped by rivalry between the US and China. He urges maximal cooperation between democracies that still value a system of multilateral alliances underpinned by international law and an understanding that reciprocal obligations can yield mutual benefits.

That is the animating idea behind the new acceleration in Canada-EU relations. It is alien to Mr Trump, and he doesn’t like it. He has warned of yet more tariffs should the Ottawa-Brussels axis evolve into anything he deems economically unfavourable to the US. For the time being, this is all happening in the realm of rhetoric. But Ms von der Leyen’s speech and Mr Carney’s response are important as expressions of serious geopolitical ambition. The time is overdue for a British prime minister to show the same clarity of purpose.

The Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: a spur to action on climate

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 17:47:01 GMT

New research links last month’s disaster to fossil fuel pollution. Supporting disaster-hit countries must be at the centre of climate politics

Following a familiar pattern, coverage of the glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border three weeks ago has subsided with the initial shock. But while the world’s attention has shifted, Nepal remains in the midst of an appalling tragedy. As well as at least 1,300 people who are known to have been killed, more than 5,000 are missing, some of them trapped in tunnels linked to the 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the floods. On Wednesday four bodies were recovered from one of these tunnels, with searches ongoing. Families of the missing people are desperate for news.

Last week the country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said that it would ask the UN’s loss and damage fund for $20m (£15m) towards a total rebuilding cost of around $5bn (£3.75bn) – including the replacement of up to 20,000 homes. The first academic study linking the disaster to the climate crisis will now be added to that application. Scientists at Imperial College London, along with international collaborators on the World Weather Attribution project, found that a number of drivers of the glacier fall had been made worse by atmospheric heating. While not the sole cause, fossil fuel pollution was judged to have destabilised the geology of the mountain environment.

Even before last month, Nepal faced huge economic challenges, due in part to instability in the Middle East. Its government has only been in power for six months, following protests that led to the collapse of the previous one. But inexperienced though they are, Nepal’s leaders are right to insist that other countries should pay towards its recovery. Nepal is estimated to be responsible for less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Like the small island nations in the Caribbean and Pacific that are most threatened by sea level rises and tropical storms, Nepal’s people are bearing the brunt of destructive forces that have been unleashed upon them as a result of decisions about resource use, energy and economic development taken elsewhere in the world.

The likelihood of any payment being made quickly is, however, low. Nearly 120 countries have already submitted claims adding up to a total of nearly $3bn (£2.2bn), which is far more than the fund, currently estimated at $400m (£300m), can afford. That is partly the fault of Donald Trump, who withdrew the US from the Paris climate agreement and put pressure on the World Bank to drop its climate finance goals. Other donors have also failed to meet targets.

The Nepal-Tibet disaster, coming as it did at the end of a summer of record-breaking temperatures, including in the Himalayas, ought to focus minds. Scientists have warned for years of the devastating consequences of melting glaciers, particularly for the millions of people who rely on them for water. But as well as a spur to accelerate the green transition and intensify decarbonisation, the plight of the Nepali people should be a wake-up call to the governments and institutions that must find a way to make a global climate finance system work – including in the aftermath of disasters such as Nepal’s. Turkey, which hosts the next climate summit in November, has positioned itself as a champion for developing countries. Boosting the loss and damage fund must be prioritised at those talks if climate justice is to remain a credible goal.

With Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, the Tories must hope for a bout of public amnesia

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 17:38:33 GMT

Andrew Griffith is keen on clearing red tape. Good job he wasn’t part of a Treasury team that abolished the Office for Tax Simplification

On days like this, it’s not hard to be overwhelmed by existential futility. At the current rate of progress, the UK looks on course to wipe itself out far sooner than it would with any interference from AI. Everything feels hopeless. Years of minimal growth and a cost of living crisis. The tech bros and the bankers may be getting richer. The rest of us? Not so much.

And there’s no end in sight. Andy Burnham may offer better vibes, but he is fighting a losing battle against global forces – wars, energy prices, borrowing costs – that he can’t control. You can feel the hope drain out of him as each day passes. Mr Congeniality is not quite so congenial as he once was. All the economic forecasts suggest things are going to get even worse in the next year.

Even Labour allies are preparing the ground for a tough budget next month. The chancellor, John Healey, has been making it known that even he is surprised by just how bad things are. Can’t think why. The rest of us have known for a while, and he’s had the benefit of sitting at the Cabinet table with Rachel Reeves for the past two years. Perhaps he dozed off while she was speaking. He wouldn’t have been the first.

Still, the government does have one thing going for it. There is currently no one better. That might not be much comfort to some people, but it helps Labour sleep a little easier. Reform members seem determined to take themselves down. If not by financial scandals then by their own stupidity.

That’s why Richard Tice has such a prominent role within the party. Only on Wednesday, Dicky was at it again. Responding to the news that Healey had made the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, a non-executive director of the Bank of England, Motormouth Dicky immediately declared Britain had descended into a socialist hell. Were he better informed, he would have known it’s been a tradition for the last 40 years or so that the TUC head honcho gets a gig at the Bank. One started by that well-known Commie apparatchik Margaret Thatcher. But why let that get in the way of an ill-thought through social media clip.

Usually, Dicky is in a league of his own in the competition to be the dimmest and least competent MP in Westminster. But this time Kemi Badenoch was keen to join in with a similar post. As much to remind everyone that the Tory party was still not ready to be taken seriously or forgiven for its 14 years of unmanaged decline as anything else. And where Kemi led, Andrew Griffith followed with his own statement insisting the unions would soon be running the country. You’d have thought that a shadow chancellor, with experience as a junior minister in the Treasury, would have inside knowledge of the Bank of England’s conventions.

There again, Andrew will be Andrew. Living proof of Kemi’s currently insurmountable problem. She can say all she wants that she has changed the party, but all the country sees is more or less the same faces promising that this time everything will be different. Something that’s more or less inevitable when you have a party of fewer than 120 MPs. It takes some cheek to appoint a backer of Liz Truss’s mini-budget as your shadow chancellor. Two fingers to everyone.

Right now, Griffith’s main function appears to be to make people yearn for the return of Mel Stride. The Melster may have been a bit useless, but he always looked as if he was trying to be decent. The Tories have set a lot of store by the fact that Andrew made a lot of money in the private sector before becoming an MP. Yet there is no sign that he can translate those skills into the public sphere. In Westminster, he is most noted for having loaned his £9.5m house to Boris Johnson’s leadership campaign team, for declaring that Elon Musk had saved humanity by buying Twitter and that too many Lib Dems were vegans.

On Thursday, Griffith chose to make his debut speech as shadow chancellor at a college in north London. He can only hope that not many people were listening because it rapidly became apparent that he didn’t have much to say. And what he did say was – not to put too fine a point on it – half-arsed and intellectually dishonest.

Where to start? The optics weren’t great. Looking like you’ve been locked in the boiler room by the college principal isn’t the best of looks. Though maybe it would have been better if he had been. There were no apologies, no acknowldgement of the Tories’ part in the current economic state of the country. It was as though July 2024 had been year zero. Everything had been just fine until then and Labour had ruined everything.

“The chancellor must rule out raising taxes,” he said. Something he, himself, is unwilling to do. The Tories have committed to keeping the current tax thresholds until 2028, a stealth tax that raises billions more for the Treasury each year. It was breathtaking. But there was more. Griffith was determined to simplify tax regulation and red tape. Another astonishing feat of amnesia. It had been Andrew who played a key role in the Treasury abolishing the Office for Tax Simplification while in office. He must think we’re stupid.

Surprisingly, he had nothing to say on the one tax cut that Kemi has actually committed to exploring. The abolition of inheritance tax. A proposal that would benefit the wealthiest 5%. So much for being the party of small business and the self-employed. Sometimes, it feels as if the current iteration of the Tories just can’t help themselves. They are their own burial ground.

There was just time for Griffith to reiterate that Nowak’s appointment to the Bank of England was a death knell for the country – you’d have thought he might have wanted to rethink this after a night’s sleep – before he brought the event to a close. Astonishingly, he thought it had all gone brilliantly.

Greens urge Zack Polanski to take stance on proposed policy declaring ‘Zionism is racism’

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 17:06:14 GMT

Exclusive: The Green leader has not spoken publicly about the motion, which is likely to be debated at the party’s conference in October

The Greens are pushing Zack Polanski to take a stance on a potential party policy stating “Zionism is racism”, with some fearing it could alienate Jewish supporters if it was passed.

Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, has not spoken publicly about the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference in Brighton at the start of October, and is thus almost certain to feature.

The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – with racism, would call for a single Palestinian state, and would risk members who supported Zionism being disciplined for racism.

While Polanski is believed to have reservations about the motion, some in the party believe he is wary of speaking out publicly to avoid angering left-leaning members who have joined the Greens in large numbers under his leadership, a number of whom have strong views on Gaza and Israel.

“Zack can try to be everything to everyone, and that doesn’t always work in politics,” one senior Green said. “But he is in a difficult position. Some of the supporters of the motion can be quite aggressive.”

A motion with the same title was submitted to the Greens’ spring conference but was never debated due to time constraints.

If the motion had been debated, it is understood that the party’s MPs and Polanski would have opposed it.

Polanski has not given a view yet this time but is understood to have concerns about any motion that could leave Jewish members feeling unwelcome in the party, or which could be seen as not helping a peace process.

Some in the party view the coming weeks, and whether Polanski takes a stance or not, as a test of his leadership, and whether he is willing to challenge some of the new Green members, particularly those who were formerly in Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour.
