The motion calls for “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants”, and says the Palestinian people have the full right to “resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” within international law.

If passed, Zionism “will be treated as any other form of racism” by the party, it adds.

Two amendments to tone down the motion have been tabled, which one Green source said Polanski appeared to support.

A Green official said that many activists loyal to the party’s leadership might not be at the autumn conference because it takes place a week before voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which Polanski hopes to take Keir Starmer’s old seat from Labour, potentially leaving more scope for others to push through the motion.

“The risk is that if it passes as it is we are alienating ourselves from the Jewish community in the UK, a lot of whom are not big fans of the current Israeli government,” a Green source said.

There was, they added, a parallel worry about internal splits, with some Green activists in leaked WhatsApp chats warning that Polanski was “struggling to overcome Zionist indoctrination”.

They said: “In the past, even highly contested policy debates in the Greens have always been conducted in a mature and sensible way, even [a] boring way. Now it’s changed.”

Sway, Mobo-winning British rapper, dies aged 44

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 16:35:28 GMT

Rapper won prestigious award as an unsigned artist before breaking UK Top 10 and nurturing artists including KSI

The British rapper Sway, who proved inspirational to a generation of Black British musicians thanks to his independence and frank, dextrous storytelling, has died aged 44.

The news was announced by the Mobo awards, with whom Sway won best hip-hop act in 2005, the first unsigned act to do so. “Proud to have him as part of our history. Our love goes out to his family, loved ones and fans,” the statement read.

It was confirmed to the Guardian via a close friend, who said he died at his home in Ghana. No cause of death has been announced.

Born Derek Safo, and later known as Sway Dasafo, he was born in Hornsey, north London, to Ghanaian parents, and as well as training as a producer, he honed a versatile rap flow that could be deployed on high-tempo grime and club tracks as well as thoughtful hip-hop leaning material.

That versatility meant that he didn’t fit into any one scene: “UK garage was big at this time but I just couldn’t do it because I never felt the vibe of the scene suited me,” he said. “British hip-hop was just so dry and grey, hiplife was a no-no ‘cause I couldn’t rap in Twi, drum’n’bass just hurts my head sometimes and I can’t sing good so R&B was out the question! I never felt at home anywhere.”

He started out in the groups Phynix Crew and One, before going solo and releasing a series of mixtapes. Breakout single Up Your Speed was a minor hit, but follow-up Little Derek – a manifesto for his own greatness, celebrating how “he ended up in HMV instead of HMP” – broke the UK Top 40 in 2006.

It became a cornerstone track of his debut album This Is My Demo, which accrued critical acclaim – including a four-star review in the Guardian – and his Mobo award, where he beat the much more established likes of 50 Cent and the Game. The album was also nominated for the Mercury prize, losing out to the Arctic Monkeys’ debut.

Safo continued to release via his own Dcypha Productions label but entered into a partnership with Konvict Music, the label from Senegalese-American pop star Akon, who was one of the guests on the next Sway album, 2008’s The Signature LP.

He later admitted difficulties as his fame grew, citing “ego, too many lights, and too much confusion” around the time of The Signature LP, but continued to embrace a more commercial sound and generated his biggest chart successes: the Ride on Time-sampling Still Speedin’ became his first Top 20 hit in 2011 (and featured a guest verse from Kano), then was outdone by Level Up, produced by dubstep star Flux Pavilion, which reached No 8 the following year.

Safo also collaborated with Riz Ahmed, appearing on the Riz MC track Shifty; Ed Sheeran, appearing on his No 5 Collaborations Project EP; was courted for tracks by the US rappers Lupe Fiasco and Chamillionaire; and worked with other British rappers including Tinchy Stryder, Akala, Mitchell Brothers and Donae’o. He also crossed into other genres, guesting on Kaiser Chiefs’ third album Off With Their Heads.

He nurtured artists on his own label and was instrumental in developing the career of KSI, who went on to have huge success as a YouTuber and musician. Safo and KSI had a minor hit together in 2013, No Sleep, featuring another young charge of Safo’s, the rapper Tiggs Da Author.

He and his wife Helen married in 2013, and had four children: Jalil, AJ, Inaya and Imara. In a recent social media post Safo described himself as a single father.

The complaint claims that for more than two decades, Epstein, who died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges, possessed, transported, produced and distributed “child pornography and/or child sexual abuse material of countless children”. It alleges that Epstein “acquired by theft” nude or partly nude images of the first plaintiff, referred to in the document as Jane Doe, and that he transported the material across state lines and retained it.

The lawsuit argues that many of those depicted in the CSAM that they say was possessed by Epstein have never been identified or notified through the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s victim-identification program.

With regard to the second plaintiff, identified in the complaint under the pseudonym “Amy”, the lawsuit alleges that “upon information and belief, Epstein acquired CSAM images” of her.

The complaint alleges that beginning in the 1990s, Epstein “created and kept” in his locked safe in his New York City home a “‘modeling book’ of sexualized images of children”. It further alleges that beginning in “at least in the 2000s, Epstein had his assistant take nude, sexualized photographs of multiple children, paid them for the images, and then used those photographs for his own sexual gratification and perhaps that of others”.

Jane Doe alleges that she was around 12 years old when Epstein stole photographs of her partly nude, which the complaint claims had originally been taken “as part of an artist study for and catalogued, numbered and maintained by the artist in a lockbox”.

The lawsuit alleges that Epstein also “stole nude or partially nude photos of another minor” and transported these images across state lines. The complaint also alleges that “despite contemporaneous reports made to law enforcement, specifically alerting law enforcement that Epstein had obtained these photos of Jane Doe, and similar photos of another minor, no one in law enforcement took action to prosecute anyone or even investigate these reports”.

It adds that “upon learning that Epstein had possessed sexualized images of her as a child, Jane Doe suffered and continues to suffer severe emotional distress”.

“Amy” alleges in the complaint that she is a victim of “actively traded CSAM which has been in distribution since the late 1990s to present day”. The lawsuit alleges that “on information and belief” images of her are contained within the CSAM collection seized from Epstein’s properties.

In a statement to the Guardian, one of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Margaret Mabie, of Marsh Law, said that according to the released files, a report completed on Epstein’s collection identified 15 or more hits of known series like Amy’s and that “to our knowledge, none of the victims identified in that report, or in any other CSAM discovered in Epstein’s collection, have ever received notice”.

The complaint also alleges that other people, “including Epstein’s employees and/or coconspirators, had access to, viewed, or otherwise received from Epstein, the CSAM images in his possession, including images of Jane Doe and ‘Amy’”.

“We want the estate to preserve and account for everything seized from Epstein’s properties, and we want a real, court supervised process to identify and notify every survivor depicted in that collection,” Nappi said. “Many of them have no idea their images exist in his files, and they deserve to know, and they deserve the chance to seek justice.

“Survivors have waited years for accountability, and this case opens the door for others depicted in his collection who don’t even know they’re in it,” Nappi added.

So it’s a place that I enjoy and it’s always good coming here.” Indeed, Rai’s score tied the early lead with Joakim Lagergren. The lead is one from Ryan Gerard and Adam Scott.

McIlroy remains in the middle of technical changes as he seeks to remove bad habits from his swing. “It definitely still looks better on the range than it does when I get out there on the course,” said the Northern Irishman. “But over time, if I just keep to what I’m doing, it will hopefully start to bed in.” McIlroy had been five under inside 10 holes before having to settle for minus three.

Patrick Reed’s 68 was significant as he looks to hold off McIlroy in the DP World Tour’s season-long order of merit. Reed and McIlroy have jousted in plenty of environments before, yet on this occasion the American insists it is not personal.

Keely Hodgkinson reveals how freak canal accident ruined world record bid

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 16:00:52 GMT

Hodgkinson tripped and fell on canal cooldown run

Runner shares her unique genetics of split tendons

Keely Hodgkinson has lifted the lid on how plans to chase the 800m world record this summer were ruined by a freak accident that her team has likened to whiplash.

The Olympic champion will run her final race of the season in the Athlos meeting in London on Friday, having returned last week from a hamstring tear sustained at the European Championships in August.

However, Hodgkinson believes the root cause of the injury was actually a fall during a cooldown run in July, when she tripped heavily on a metal grill while jogging along a canal.

The fall was so sudden that the 24-year-old was unable to get her hands down in time and was left with bloody knees and a jarred back. Hodgkinson now suspects her hamstring issue at the Europeans was likely a consequence of the fall.

“In the Europeans I was in the best shape ever, but sometimes it doesn’t always translate,” she said. “When I fell over, that kind of messed me up way more than I thought it did. And I think that’s what’s contributed to my hamstring, because I couldn’t really use my quad for a while.”

The freak accident has parallels with Steve Ovett, who after breaking the world mile record in August 1981, tripped and fell through metal railings four months’ later, badly injuring his knee and severely impacting his season the next year.

Hodgkinson also revealed that she suffered a tear in her hamstring during the European Championships final, having felt a twinge 10 minutes before the race. However, because of her unusual genetics, she was still able to train after the injury.

“My body’s quite literally built different,” she said. “So where everyone has one tendon, mine split, so I have two. We found it last year on an MRI scan after I tore it.

“We’re trying to figure out if it’s a strength or a weakness. So when one of them tore, I still had another one. It meant that I didn’t feel the injury until later on when it got a bit tight. I was like: ‘Oh, something’s not quite right,’ but it didn’t affect me during the race.

“The pro is it means that when one is down, I can still run on the one that works. But maybe it’s slightly weaker than the one that’s attached. But it’s a weird one: you can still run and I haven’t missed any training the last three weeks. I’ve just had to alter my approach.”

Hodgkinson can still look on her 800m season with pride, having broken the indoor world record in February, won the world indoor title in March, and then set a personal best outdoors in June.

“Obviously I would have loved to tick every goal that I wanted to do this year, but I’m 24,” said Hodgkinson.

Asked why she had decided to run at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest and at Athlos, despite having done little speed work, Hodgkinson replied that she wanted to prove to herself she could compete in far from ideal circumstances.

“What if it happened in an Olympic year? I’m not saying it will and, touch wood, it doesn’t. But I know that I can do this, regardless of if stuff goes right or wrong, and I can still perform with the best in the world. That’s given me confidence.”

Hodgkinson is one of the headline acts at the all-female Athlos meeting, which also includes the Paris 2024 200m gold medallist Gabby Thomas and the former world 100m champion Sha’Carri Richardson.

Athlos’ acting president, Kayla Green, said that with the event having a red carpet, multiple celebrities in attendance, and DJ Trauma on the decks, it would feel different to a typical athletics meeting.

“Fans are going to walk away and say the competition and athleticism on the track was second to none, but the experience itself was something that made them really have a great time,” she said. “It will also be epic to watch on TV.”

Revolut reportedly facing $3m ransom demand after hackers steal hundreds of customers’ data

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 15:58:56 GMT

Europe’s largest financial technology company confirmed it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam last week

Revolut is facing a reported $3m (£2.2m) ransom demand after hackers posing as government officials accessed the data of hundreds of the bank’s cryptocurrency customers, including one victim who says he fears for his safety.

Europe’s largest financial technology company confirmed last weekend that it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam in which hackers compromised an Italian government email system to contact Revolut staff and request personal customer details.

While the data breach only affected about 680 of Revolut’s 80 million global customers, it is believed to have targeted customers with suspected cryptocurrency holdings.

It is not clear how the scandal might affect Revolut’s much-anticipated stock market debut, with Revolut’s founder, Nik Storonsky, telling Les Echoes on Thursday that there were plans for a dual listing in both London and New York.

One of the alleged hackers has reportedly threatened to publish the customer data unless Revolut pays a $3m ransom, according to the Financial Times, which has been speaking to the purported hacker. A Revolut spokesperson said the bank “has not received any direct contact or demand from the individuals or group making these claims”.

But some victims have said they fear they could end up being forced to face ransoms.

The former chief executive of failed bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox, Mark Karpelès, said he was one of the victims of the data breach and is now worried about his family’s safety. “I have kids, we’re living together. My address is in those files, so of course I’m worried about this,” he told the Guardian.

He has since contacted law enforcement in Tokyo, where he lives, after saying in an X post earlier this week that he feared he could be “kidnapped or dead” by the time Revolut gave him more substantial information about the breach.

Karpelès said he was relieved that Japanese officials were taking the threat seriously, “but I might still have to travel overseas or be in places that may not be as safe”.

The French businessman, who has been a Revolut customer since 2023, said that hackers may have mistakenly targeted his account, thinking he was wealthier than he actually is. He said he was forced to declare bankruptcy in the wake of a high-profile court case in Japan.

Karpelès is a controversial figure in the crypto world. He was charged, but later acquitted, of embezzlement by Japanese courts, following the collapse of the crypto exchange platform in 2014. He was found guilty of falsifying data.

Karpelès said he has joined a victim chat group on X in the wake of the data breach, where customers having been sharing information and support. “We’re all in the same situation, which is: we don’t know exactly what happened, or how it happened, so we’re trying to get as much information as possible,” he said. He added that one of the victims got in touch with the purported hacker, who showed they had the victim’s personal details on hand.

The hacker then said they would delete the information, but only if they were sent $50,000, Karpelès said.

While Karpelès was frustrated with Revolut, which was valued at $115bn in a secondary share sale earlier this summer, he does not believe the bank should pay the $3m ransom, which ultimately gives no guarantee that the data will be deleted.

It is still not clear how many hackers are involved, and requests for the ransom to be paid through a platform known as Monero, meaning there would be no evidence or receipt of payment, allowing the hacker to claim they never received the money in the first place.

Karpelès hopes Revolut will share more information about the breach.

A Revolut spokesperson said:“Revolut recently identified a sophisticated external impersonation scam where an unauthorised third party utilised a legitimate government agency domain email to submit fraudulent requests for information.

The Bank of England is shaking up its bond sales – why does it matter?

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 15:45:42 GMT

What the plan to sell £146bn in gilts back to the Treasury means for the public finances

Bank of England holds interest rates

Burnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future rate rises

Mixed in with the Bank of England’s decision on Thursday to hold interest rates at 3.75% was a surprise announcement that it was shaking up its programme of quantitative tightening.

So why is this apparently arcane change to QT important, and what does it mean for the public finances?

It is the Bank of England’s controversial process of selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds that it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing (QE) during the financial crises of 2008 and Covid.

The Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) sees QT as the necessary unwinding of the massive balance sheet it built up. Its stockpile of bonds, known as gilts, has already been reduced from a peak of £895bn in February 2022, to £488bn.

But critics on the right and left have complained that selling off significant quantities of government bonds costs the Treasury, as they are being sold at a loss.

There have also been concerns that in a febrile bond market, large-scale sell-offs risk depressing prices – and thus driving up the yield, or interest rate, the government has to pay to borrow.

Instead of looking for private-sector buyers for its stock of gilts, the Bank plans to sell them directly to the Treasury instead.

The Treasury’s debt management office (DMO), which has the job of doing the government’s borrowing for it, will then issue new bonds to cover the costs of those it has bought from the Bank.

The Treasury sees this as simplifying what can be a messy process. As the chancellor, John Healey, put it in a letter to the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, on Thursday: “This sales model … would see a return to a single public-sector supplier of gilts to the market.”

It also has the advantage of allowing the DMO to tailor gilt sales to market demand, which currently favour gilts that mature over a shorter period, rather than the Bank having to sell off the 20- and 30-year dated gilts it still has on its books, for which there is less investor appetite.

The yield, effectively the interest rate, on 30-year gilts dropped sharply on Thursday after the decision was announced, to 5.745% – and was on course for its biggest drop since 2020.

No final decision has been made, however, despite the fact the Treasury, Bank and DMO have apparently been discussing the idea for a year. Healey has promised to make a final ruling in April – and until then, QT will be paused.

Yes. The Bank has run down its stock of gilts by £70bn this year. That included £20bn of actual sales; and another £50bn worth that reached their maturity date.

Over the coming years, it plans to sell off £20bn of government bonds annually, alongside retiring gilts that reach maturity.

That’s because the Bank is keen to avoid the risks of exacerbating already-fragile bond markets. The minutes of the MPC meeting revealed that members discussed offloading bonds at a faster rate; but “at a time when bond markets globally had been volatile, this risked destabilising markets”.

The Bank also announced it would set aside about £120bn of the longest-dated government bonds it holds, as these are used to back the issuance of the UK’s bank notes.

In total, the Bank expects to sell a total of £146bn of gilts between now and 2034 – at a steady pace of £20bn a year – back to the government, if Healey gives the plan the thumbs up.

Analysts expect it to be modest. The Treasury may be able to finance its borrowing a bit more cheaply when the Bank is not selling a slew of long-dated bonds into the market. As analysts at the investment bank Jefferies put it: “Taken together, the changes imply a materially lower future supply burden, particularly for [long-dated gilts].”

And to the extent that the pace of sales is slowing, the losses on those bonds, which is borne by the Treasury, will crystallise more slowly – another marginal upside.

Jefferies also suggested that, by making its future plans clear, the MPC’s decision could “ease some of the pressure that had been building for changes to the Bank’s QT approach”.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story review – it’s like Ryan Murphy’s new series was written by adolescent boys

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 15:42:03 GMT

The latest Monster instalment, about the 1892 Borden axe murders, is packed with periods and beheadings, and feels like it was made up as they went along

Okaaay – here’s what I think must have happened. Some time in the past year or two, Ryan Murphy discovered that women menstruate. Incredulous but enthralled, he rushed off to share the news with his soon equally incredulous and enthralled little friends. After confirming the basics they all looked at each other for a moment in silence as they contemplated this crazy, secret habit of the wimminz. And then Ryan said: “You guys? We have got to make a show about this!” The others nodded in fervent agreement and off they all ran.

The result is the utterly bonkers, blood-soaked, borderline-fetishistic fever dream that is The Lizzie Borden Story – the latest entry in Murphy’s popular anthology series Monster. This one is written by Ian Brennan and directed in the main by Max Winkler, the pairing responsible for the series’ previous offering, last year’s lamentable The Ed Gein Story. As, I presume, a gesture to the sex of this one’s subject, there is a female director for two of the Lizzie Borden episodes – Sarah Adina Smith – but it doesn’t really dent the vibe. Think: the gleeful disgust of a roomful of adolescent boys being taught about the female reproductive system in PSHE. It is now an eight-hour miniseries starring Rebecca Hall. We live in strange times.

So, then, to late 19th-century Massachusetts where the world’s most famous axe murder is, as we open, taking place in an affluent but otherwise unremarkable household in Fall River. Lizzie (Ella Beatty) gives her stepmother Abby (Hall) then father Andrew (Charlie Hunnam, who previously played the eponymous Ed Gein) multiple whacks and we then rewind to four months earlier to find out why.

Now, in real life, the why (even if you agree on the who, and there are those who point the finger at other Borden relatives nearby) was endlessly disputed. Some think she was angry about various property disposals Andrew had made to family members that she deemed unfair. Others think she had long-harboured resentment towards the victims for usurping and betraying her late mother (Andrew remarried quickly, and Lizzie and her sister Emma always referred to Abby as “Mrs Borden”, not “Mother”). Later theories include possible abuse in the family or a relationship with a suitor Andrew didn’t like and so on, but Messrs Brennan and Winkler have a simpler take: women be crazy!

Especially women who menstruate! Most of the first episode centres on Lizzie’s heavy periods. I actually looked at the credits to see if her womb got separate billing. First Lizzie loses a suitor by clutching at her cramping parts, then enrages Abby by bleeding all over her precious mulberry silk fainting couch. A new maid, Bridget (Vicky Krieps), is hired, whose duties include dealing with Lizzie’s bloody problems. “We keep her on a bed of wooden planks and muslin sheets she’s free to befoul with her putrid clots,” says Abby, presumably while Hall is mentally firing her agent. Bridget tells Lizzie that blood is good (“It means no man’s seed has taken hold”), hands her a hand-cranked vibrator she picked up in Amsterdam for the relief of cramping and reads her stories about multiple murderer the Countess of Báthory who used to bathe in the blood of her servant girls to preserve her youth. The vibrator is later upgraded to a Chattanooga medical massager when Bridget diagnoses an unbroken hymen as part of Lizzie’s menstrual torments. Which suggests that either Brennan wasn’t listening very attentively in PSHE class or that he saw the phrase “Chattanooga medical massager” somewhere and worked backward from there.

Unlike the team behind The Lizzie Borden Story, I have not made any of the above up, and it only gets madder from there. Bridget soon sets up a sex-for-lesbianism-in-the-miniseries relationship with Lizzie and a sex-for-money-for-keeping-the-many-axes-in-your-axe-cupboard-in-good-nick relationship with Andrew (a coffin-maker, who uses them to trim down corpses to a standard casket size, in case you were wondering). An avenue of cherry trees leading to a dovecote is mined for all the symbolism it’s worth, and soon the episodes are wall-to-wall decapitations (from birds to Báthory maidens, no one is safe), good sex (mostly between lesbians in the dovecote), bad sex (“the same ballbag slapping against you forever”), poisoned dinners, neighbours chatting genteelly over tea about “bitchcocks and pearly showers”, abortifacients, cameos from Sarah Paulson as Aileen Wuornos and much, much more. As I believe the Chattanooga medical massager ads used to say: I don’t know quite how they fit it all in.

Bonkers, as I say. Stylish – it has an almost Wes Anderson feel at times – and it’s got brio, energy and is absolutely full of great performances, especially from Hall in one of those roles that an actor shouldn’t have touched with a bargepole, despite being the only one who could possibly have carried it off. But the latest Monster has nothing to say about Borden, the times that shaped her or the prejudices most think helped secure a not guilty verdict in the end – all of which remain interesting and pertinent to the modern era, and which might have made it an illuminating companion piece to Murphy’s flagship show The People v OJ Simpson. It’s a bunch of boys on a dare who should have been called back after class and made to get down to some real work.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is on Netflix

Darkling review – Stranger Things’ Linnea Berthelsen confronts a gruesome Indian disaster

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 15:00:52 GMT

Bush theatre, LondonTitas Halder’s coming-of-age monologue is set against the 1984 Bhopal toxic gas leak – but the poetic script doesn’t quite capture the horror

Ominousness permeates Darkling. In Titas Halder’s dramatic monologue, we witness a young girl’s coming of age set against the backdrop of the 1984 toxic gas leak in the Indian city of Bhopal, an environmental catastrophe that remains one of the worst industrial disasters in global history, leading to thousands of deaths.

Actor Linnea Berthelsen – best known for her role as Kali in Netflix series Stranger Things – makes her UK stage debut and gamely takes on the singular role in a tightly wound, physical performance. Leaping across Simon Kenny’s artful, soil-filled set, Berthelsen embodies childlike wonder as she recounts her early years playing in the rain, savouring bowlfuls of plain rice and idolising her older sister.

So far so good. Except, alongside her emotional growth, the silhouette of a new factory rises in the background – effectively portrayed by lighting designer Rajiv Pattani’s projection – foreshadowing the calamity to come. When it eventually arrives, we hear of the horrors she witnesses, stepping over maimed bodies, facing blinded relatives and breathing in toxic fumes, all relayed through increasingly frenzied description.

Herein lies the main issue with Darkling. By using a monologue format – especially one where our narrator is never dramatically questioned – all the audience receives are streams of poetic description, a barrage of words that never feel emphatic or adequate enough to match the gruesome scale of such a tragedy. Coupled with Halder’s uneven pacing, which lingers in childhood for too long before alighting on trauma and then descending into a hectoring denouement that places the blame for the disaster on individual shoulders, Berthelsen is faced with a gargantuan task to maintain a sense of dramatic tension.

As Matthew Xia’s production draws to a close, with a strangely repeated narrative beat that equates female worth to motherhood, you are ultimately left feeling that this is a tragedy told without the requisite horror. Darkling is a worthy reminder of an often-overlooked disaster – but one that may well fail to take root in the mind.

At Bush theatre, London, until 24 October

I’m nearly 30, a virgin and feel lonely. The manosphere is trying to draw me in – where else can I seek assurance?

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 15:00:52 GMT

The manosphere says this type of suffering is targeted neglect, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But your suffering gives you the ability to make your part of the world better.

Read more Leading questions

I’m approaching 30 and I’m still a kissless virgin.

I’ve suffered with depression and anxiety since childhood and my family isn’t the most functional or supportive. I don’t really have friends either, as I find it hard to connect with others due to being bullied and feeling that I’m not worthwhile or wanted. I was also homeschooled from 14 and moved to a different part of the country at 15 and a few more times since then, so I feel quite rootless and alienated.

I attended university but struggled to cope, and my time coincided with Covid – after which I never returned to live in my university’s city.

I have tried dating very tentatively in the past but I feel like an impostor and as if I need to be perfect. I don’t feel attractive and I tend to feel invisible.

I’m working in a job which I enjoy and I get on with my colleagues, although I am often riddled with thoughts that they secretly dislike me. The town where I live is also starting to decline and I’m deeply worried about the future.

I’ve managed to avoid most of the manosphere but I have been gravitationally drawn into it in my search for guidance and advice, as well as to soothe my need for certainty and assurance. I abhor it but I don’t know how to go forward as a misfit man.

My question is mainly how do I manage with all this? Am I missing something? And should I forget about meeting someone and accept I might be one of those people who’ll never find anyone?

Eleanor says: Here’s the validating part: this is an awful lot to bear. You have lived through a terrible period of loneliness and isolation, and your depression and anxiety are as serious and potentially debilitating as any physical ailment (and, it goes without saying, as deserving – and requiring – of ongoing treatment).

Now for the tough part. It’s not that you alone lack certainty and assurance. There’s not a party that only you were uninvited from. It is hard for so many people right now.

The manosphere tells us this suffering is unique, targeted neglect, contrary to your entitlements. It positions you as the temporarily embarrassed fortunate. It tries to restore one group’s position in the pecking order, rather than asking why anyone has to lose. To the extent that it positions itself as a movement interested in wellbeing and loneliness, it is telling that it has complete disinterest in other people’s suffering or other kinds of loneliness. It is not a desire that these things be fixed. It is a desire that it does not happen to me.

That’s a mistake that would forfeit one of the greatest gifts available to you. Suffering like yours gives you understanding. Life made you purchase that understanding at great cost, but you now know what it’s like to be lonely. You know what it is to feel overwhelmed, adrift, unsure of yourself. That means you can give other people what you yourself are looking for: understanding and acknowledgment.

Many of the most beautiful souls in the world did not become that way by having great family, an easy ride and no anxiety. Being a good person is often about ratio – what-did-you-endure to what-did-you-pass-on. What-were-you-handed: what-did-you-make. Some people are handed two mothballs and a piece of string, and make things better in their corner of the universe.

Your suffering and your anxiety gives you the ability to make your part of the world better, partly by seeing and meeting other souls, sometimes at their most vulnerable: at their most scared, most lonely, least sure of what’s going to happen.

Admittedly, that kind of connection is not the same as getting numbers at bars. The fact that you are kind and thoughtful and responsible may not show up in digital spaces that prioritise facial structure or banter. So you might be down a few smooches. Smooches are great, don’t get me wrong – but compared to the depth of possible human connection, they are ultimately flotsam.

But for that deeper connection, you don’t want to be attractive to people writ large. You want to be attractive to the handful of people with whom you’d be a good match.

I can’t take away your uncertainty about whether you’ll find that person, I wish I could. But if you find them, you’ll find them in the spaces organised around your interests, and you’ll find them by being you on purpose, not by being a pastiche of other people’s ideas about a “man”, or a collage of your fears about yourself. You want to be loved for you.

You have been dealt a hard hand. It’s no wonder that you – like so many people right now – feel adrift and hungry for certainty.

But it’s not about finding assurance and certainty. It’s about learning to live and make things better for other people, even without it.

We are paying a high price for a university education

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:52:19 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Zoe Williams in which she argues that university has become a scam

Having read Zoe Williams’ article on student loans (Why has university become such a scam?, 14 September), I went and checked my student loan statement. What a depressing read that was. I went to university in 2012 as a slightly older student, at 22. I had been to drama school before that, but decided I wasn’t cut out for the harsh reality of show business and that a law career – a barrister perhaps – was more up my street. I wanted to keep the performance element.

After one law degree totalling £56,000, a career development loan of £15,000 to cover the cost of my bar course and a £12,000 postgraduate loan to cover my legal practice course (solicitor training), my student debt remains at £70,000.

I am now a solicitor for the NHS, working four days a week to manage childcare costs. The £150 in loan repayments out of my salary each month mean very little when £1,500 is added in interest each year. That £150 could instead be going into the pocket of my landlord as he hikes the rent again or towards the high private nursery fees for my son so that I can go to work. When his time comes to consider higher education, I will very much be encouraging an alternative route. Nerys Cookson-WilliamsLlandogo, Monmouthshire

As the mother of a new undergraduate, the student loans farce makes me livid. With about £24bn paid out yearly and only around £5bn returned in repayments, it will never pay for itself, so why put young people through this horrific system?

More importantly, it’s working-class and middle-class young people who are affected by what has effectively become another tax – as the rich don’t need loans, they aren’t affected by it. Until this is sorted, universities will once again become inaccessible to the majority of young people. Surely free university education for all is the way forward, alongside a fresh focus on vocational training?Emily MillerMildenhall, Suffolk

Zoe Williams is right to highlight the scandal of student debt. However, it is even more sinister when you consider the free labour propping up the NHS. Last month, after three thankless years, I finished my final 12.5-hour night shift as a student midwife. Having worked tirelessly for over 2,300 unpaid hours, I am graduating into unemployment with a £50,000 debt and a heavy heart.

Universities continue to host large cohorts of midwifery students, each paying £9,750 per year for the privilege, despite the crisis in recruitment. NHS trusts are paid to host students who work gruelling hours for no pay. This is nothing short of exploitation. Zoe GreenLondon

I wholly agree that students are being done a huge disservice. But as an employer, I disagree with casually blaming employers for the drop in graduate jobs. First, the economy is in the doldrums and the cost of employment has risen. With low growth the default, when national insurance goes up it directly hits our margins and reduces the amount of new starters we can afford to take on or pay rises we can afford.

The courses that students pay a fortune for are also a problem. As a digital marketing employer, digital marketing degrees are not desirable. An education system that delivers more capable staff, or incentivises employers to provide them with meaningful training, would do wonders for graduate recruitment. Name and address supplied

With regard to the unfairness heaped on today’s graduates, there is a simple answer out there – a (smaller) graduate tax on all graduates. If all graduates are asked to share the burden, the marginal tax rate could fall to 3% or 4%. Most, if not all, those currently paying student loans would favour it (with the option of staying on the current plan to anyone who has repaid in full or is about to), and it would be likely to appeal to many older graduates with children or grandchildren caught up in the current system.

Anyone who says this is impractical because there is no list of all graduates is being disingenuous. The Student Loans Company has lists of all graduates since 1998; a tick box on self-assessment forms would cover millions more, and asking employees to self-declare via their employer’s PAYE scheme would do likewise. Sufficient penalty deterrents could mop up most of the remainder. Given current funding solutions for higher education are generally considered a mess by all interested parties, I’m surprised that this hasn’t been given wider consideration. Alan TerryExeter

A fresh approach to supporting unpaid carers

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:51:54 GMT

Social care reform must reflect the variations in the type, intensity and duration of care provided, says Dr Louise Lawson

Patrick Butler’s article on the rising number of people leaving employment to provide unpaid care resonated with me, both as an unpaid carer and as a researcher in this field (About 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, 16 September). The juggle between paid work and caring responsibilities is a daily reality for millions. The report from Carers UK is a welcome reminder of this often-hidden issue, highlighting not only the growing care needs of older people but also the increasing numbers of younger people who rely on unpaid care. The midwife Jacqui Hylton’s observation in the article that caring for her mother is “harder than working in the NHS” deserves serious attention.

What is often missing from these debates, however, is recognition of the diversity and number of caring responsibilities. There is no such thing as a typical unpaid carer. Caring roles vary enormously, whether supporting a disabled child, a working-age adult with a progressive condition or an older relative with dementia.

Caring is also not fixed. There can be the onset of caring, often triggered by illness or crisis; ongoing care; and the end of caring, each with implications for work and financial security. Some people leave work to provide care and struggle to re-enter the workforce when caring ends. Others remain employed, but find the demands of combining work and care unsustainable.

These experiences reflect variations in the intensity and duration of care, the availability of support, the flexibility of employers and the nature of work. Social care reform must engage with these complexities. Politicians must recognise not only the value of unpaid carers but also the diversity of caring experiences. Effective support requires a more nuanced approach than policies built around a single model of care. Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy, University of Glasgow

Children’s care homes rely on committed people

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:51:32 GMT

Without the unflinching commitment of managers, social workers and those who work in them, they won’t be proper homes, writes John Burton

I congratulate the Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism for exposing the disgraceful state of residential childcare and the use of illegal children’s homes (Councils pay more than £125m a year placing vulnerable children in illegal care homes in England, 8 September). However, this is a symptom not a cause.

While there are good private children’s homes (I’ve worked with some), they are defined by personal and family commitment, not profit. The same relationships are required whoever runs a children’s home, whether a charitable organisation or local authority. Without the personal, unflinching commitment of councillors, managers, social workers and, crucially, the grownups who work in the home, it can’t be a loving home.

We have been led to believe that regulation and inspection ensure good care. Do they? No. A reliance on such “quality” standards and monitoring has in part led us to this absurd situation. These profit generators are a result of our reluctance to accept the responsibility and risks of giving children love and real care. Things will go wrong, they do in any home, and often it’s putting things right again that produces the greatest therapeutic effect.

Homes are not created by rules and regulations, but by families and communities, ie people. No good home exists without direct, personal commitment and relationships, and the internal and external organisation that enables and supports such relationships. John BurtonAuthor, Leading Good Care

Money in people’s pockets is the key to economic recovery

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:50:43 GMT

David Redshaw responds to a letter on the bond markets and economic pressures afflicting the UK

Neil Kinnock’s timely letter (9 September) reminds us that we are not alone in suffering high gilt yields and borrowing costs. We are still feeling the fallout from Covid, and it needs mentioning that our national debt is similar to America’s and much less than Japan’s, and it never gets mentioned that Italy routinely runs 100% of GDP debt. But as Kinnock observes, the policies of several Conservative governments (including Brexit) have made things worse, and the problem for us is not so much the actual debt but our direction of travel. The aforementioned will make the bond markets view us with a more jaundiced eye.

It was predictable that Jamie Dimon would pop up at this point (JP Morgan boss meets Burnham and Healey to warn against bank tax rise, 10 September). He talks about potential lack of investment by the banks. What investment? We aren’t even a nation of shopkeepers any longer; we’re a nation of pizza deliverers.

The economist JK Galbraith comes to mind here. He said that when push comes to shove, it’s the regular spendings of the working masses that keep the high street going. The spendings of the mega-rich involve either luxury goods or investment in plant, both of which are erratic and subject to the ups and downs of the economic cycle. Some might say, after the events of 1990 and 2008, that the banks have more money than is good for them.

Money in people’s pockets and the confidence to spend it has always been the recipe for recovery. Might we start by housing policies to reduce the 40% of rent that many are paying out of their salary? And a bedroom tax for the rich to make better use of the existing housing stock? You can go on raising the minimum wage, but you’re simply chasing your tail. David RedshawSaltdean, East Sussex

Charles’s rebuttal of Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana offers rare glimpse into palace thinking

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:47:02 GMT

From ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phrase

As denials go, King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegations that Charles said after Diana’s death, “We’ll forget her soon enough”, was a masterclass in the diplomatic royal rebuke.

Rarely has Buckingham Palace responded to claims in countless books on royalty. But it was straight out of the block on this one.

Little over an hour after the Daily Mail, which is serialising Spencer’s memoir Swan Song about his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, had published its first extract online, a statement was issued.

Charles, the headline claimed, had told Spencer days after Diana’s death and during a heated row over funeral arrangements: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.”

The king’s swift countering, that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, will enter the canon of carefully constructed regal pushbacks.

As rebukes go, it is up there with the late Queen Elizabeth II’s “some recollections may vary” in response to a torrent of allegations from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in their Oprah Winfrey interview.

Senior courtiers are often drawn from the diplomatic service and thus highly-skilled in couching the passive-aggressive denial. Deploying delicate language to devastating effect is a stock in trade at the Foreign Office.

But it is a weapon to be used sparingly. The royal mantra is, usually, “never complain, never explain”.

However, Charles’s former communications secretary Julian Payne said: “This is a much more personal situation, given its author, and therefore has a greater ability to do harm.”

That is why the palace “felt the need to set the record straight and deny these remarks have been made”, Payne told the BBC’s Today programme. Given the amount of things the palace don’t comment on, “you can imagine the strength of feeling”, he added.

Payne remains close to the king and was due to be sitting alongside him at Thursday’s AI summit just hours later, so the fact he felt able to speak so freely suggests his robust defence of Charles came with official sanction.

What is said behind palace doors usually remains private. The language may be less sensitive. But a carefully chosen phrase in public pulls back the privacy screen.

When Diana, in her highly controversial Panorama interview, said “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, she reaped public revenge on her then husband and Camilla.

In return, Diana found herself on the sharp end of Elizabeth’s ire weeks later. After Diana failed to respond to the queen’s request that the couple divorce, a palace spokesperson issued a statement: “After considering the present situation, the queen wrote to both the prince and princess earlier this week and gave them her view, supported by the Duke of Edinburgh, that an early divorce is desirable.” The matter was now, officially, out of Diana’s hands.

White fury was behind the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s statement in February 2021: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.” It was read as a succinct and direct challenge to the late queen’s insistence they could not keep their public service roles after stepping down as working royals.

Meghan was less direct in a 2019 interview with ITV’s Tom Bradby in which he asked her if she was OK juggling life as a royal with a newborn, Prince Archie. “Thank you for asking, because not many people have asked if I’m OK,” she replied. Was it directed at the palace and the institution? A huge number of the claims the Sussexes later made, in TV interviews and in Harry’s memoir Spare, were that the duchess had been unsupported throughout her time as a working royal.

One royal famously deficient in the art of the diplomatic royal rebuke, however, was the late Duke of Edinburgh. Philip was renowned for his gaffes. When a BBC journalist politely asked the queen at a banquet at the Élysée Palace if she was enjoying her stay in Paris in 2006, Philip dispensed with tact to snap: “Damn fool question!”

Baby found wrapped in 1910 newspaper was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:06:48 GMT

‘Terrible thing’ happened to infant boy found under the floorboards at a house in Bishop Auckland, says coroner

A baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and wrapped in a 116-year-old newspaper was unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded.

Crispin Oliver on Thursday said the child, known only as Baby Auckland, had been garotted by an unknown person.

He said it was an “unusual case, legally and evidentially”. The whole story, he added, was “very sad and singular”.

Oliver said: “Clearly, this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant. It happened in our community. But it happened over a century ago, and it is heartwarming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.”

The inquest heard that the skeletal remains of the baby had been found during renovations on the second floor of a late 19th-century house in Bishop Auckland, County Durham, on 29 July 2024.

They were found by the house owner, Peter Moody, while he was laying a new floor. In a statement he said he had made the discovery when he lifted up a floorboard. He contacted the county council, unsure of whether he needed to call the police.

DCI Mel Sutherland told the inquest he had been on duty in Bishop Auckland when he was alerted to the discovery of skeletal remains in a town centre house.

After they were confirmed as human, he supervised the sealing of the house to keep it forensically sterile, while a forensic anthropologist was contacted. That scientist, Dr Micol Zuppello, travelled up that evening and spent two days at the house investigating.

The baby’s skeleton was mostly complete, the inquest in Crook heard, bar a missing toe tip. The remains were partly mummified. Carbon dating could conclusively establish only that the baby died between the 17th century and 1955.

A postmortem of the skeleton was carried out by Zupello and Dr Louise Mulcahy, a Home Office pathologist for north-east England based at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle.

Mulcahy said the baby had been 38-40 weeks, with no signs of traumatic injury, and had twine looped around his neck. She said it had been looped around the neck three times, knotted, and then looped again.

It was not possible to say, she added, if it had been tight or loose. The medical cause of death, she said, was “unascertained”.

The skeleton was too old to be able to confirm or refute the presence of natural disease, she said. In the absence of soft tissue it was not possible, the inquest heard, to say if there had been any assault or trauma. Equally, it was not possible to say with any certainty if the baby had been stillborn or not.

Oliver said police had “had to think laterally” during their investigation. He praised Sutherland for “leaving no stone unturned”.

Sutherland described some of the techniques they had used to investigate further, including DNA testing. All were inconclusive.

He said the newspaper was very brown, but articles could be seen. It was called The Umpire and dated June 1910.

Sutherland said that in 1911 census data, the building was described as dining rooms, meaning “a cafe-type establishment”.

A public appeal was made for people who thought they might be related to come forward. Two sisters came forward who believed they were related to a servant at the house, but DNA testing revealed no match.

During the whole investigation, Sutherland said, there had been “very little to go on”.

Oliver asked if the twine might have been used for a religious artefact, but nothing like that had been found, Sutherland said. There was also no evidence to suggest any link to midwifery practices of the time.

A knot specialist could not be used, the inquest heard, because the nearest person was in the Netherlands and would have been too expensive for this type of investigation.

Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April this year, with professionals involved giving their services for free.

Sutherland said it had been two years of investigating, “challenging and frustrating at times, but heartwarming to see the send-off he got at the end”.

Beck: ‘What does a devil’s haircut look like? Anything with a lot of architecture and wild flights of fancy’

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 14:00:51 GMT

The genre-fluid singer answers your questions on being funky v lonesome, his infamous MTV interview with Thurston Moore and why he said yes to performing with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot

Read Alexis Petridis’s 5* review of new album Ride Lonesome

You’ve been performing since the late 80s. What keeps you going? AmongstTheWaves It’s a good question. I don’t really know any other life. I’ve spent a lot of my time trying to create a body of work, and out of that, maybe there’s a few songs at the end that are not bad. So I just keep going down into the mine, trying to come back with a couple of things worth keeping. It’s a lot of digging. If I had to stop and get a job painting houses or something, I would still make songs just for myself, because that’s how it started.

You tend to alternate between styles from album to album. What do you feel is closer to your intrinsic self, funky Beck or lonesome Beck? MazziniProbably lonesome. But the other side of things gets me out of my shell, stops me from being a little too ponderous, which I’m apt to do. The other side of what I do – Loser or Odelay – was more of a fluke. At the time that was what people liked. Now it’s kind of reversed – they prefer the more introspective, quiet songs, and stuff that’s a little more genreless. I don’t have any songs that they play at weddings, like Uptown Funk. I remember telling Mark Ronson, “Hey, you made a wedding song.” He was like, “Yeah, finally.” That’s a very elite category of song.

Your interview with Thurston Moore on MTV in 1994 is one of the most gloriously ramshackle interviews ever. Were you both doing a bit? LoftyDog

We filmed a bunch of things they wouldn’t air because they thought they would get in trouble or get sued by people. I’d brought an old-fashioned telephone and at one point we pulled out some baseball bats and destroyed the phone. I don’t remember what the bit was – who was calling us? Whatever it was, we decided to smash the phone in reaction to a call. We were kind of doing performance art. I met a lot of resistance and ridicule for being like that on my first album. I would do interviews and say wild things because so much of it was boring, just rote questions – and I thought if my friends are reading this, they’d be bored to death.

A lot of the things on TV were just going through the motions. As a kid, every once in a while I’d see something that jarred me. Like, wow, there was a glitch in the system and something real broke through. Something genuine that reminded us that this is all a construct, this smooth oiled machine that provides content for us. It was a very youthfully exuberant attempt to try to disrupt everything that was very pre-programmed and uninteresting. Thurston and I both came from underground art backgrounds, so it was preposterous to be allowed on mainstream TV. We were like, let’s seize the moment and do something.

Given how productive you were right from the start of your career, how did you feel about being tagged with the “slacker rock” label? SalfordianBlueI thought it was a reductive term. There was this influx of all this underground music that had been bubbling through the 80s and early 90s, and it all hit the mainstream at once. One day it was Vanilla Ice and hair metal and Whitney Houston, and then the next day it was Nirvana and all the stuff that you would see at your local dive bar. The 80s had been very curated and airbrushed and brightly coloured – I remember the first time I went to a record label, they told me I looked messy and rough, and it would never work. Whoever that was missed the point. We were reacting to how cleaned up everything was, and going back to something a little more raw and real.

To many, Loser felt like a classic one-hit wonder. Did you always have faith that you’d have a long career in music? StayPositiveI never had any expectations. I think the thing that supersedes everything is whether you are writing good songs. The people I came up with who wrote good songs – they’re the ones that are still around and playing arenas and stadiums. And it was tricky when I was coming up, writing a catchy song was frowned upon. If you had anything that was too poppy or catchy, you were selling out, it wasn’t real art. What’s funny is the catchiest, poppiest songs from that time are the ones that everybody loves now.

What would a devil’s haircut look like, and have you ever seen someone sporting one? StayPositive

It’d probably have a little bit of a rockabilly edge. Somebody showed me a video once of these proto-punk type people in Australia called sharpies, and they had a bizarre version of a mullet. It was really short bangs and kind of draped in the back. Something like that, maybe. I have a book of hairstyle photos that they would use in 80s hair salons – there are a lot of devil’s haircuts. I think any haircut that has a lot of architecture to it, with wild flights of fancy.

In their 1998 hit You Get What You Give the New Radicals threatened to kick the asses of Hanson, Courtney Love, Marilyn Manson – and Beck. Did they ever catch up with you? Dave_RowlinsonI ran into [New Radicals songwriter Gregg Alexander] in an Erewhon [health food supermarket] at the time, and he said: “I’m a big fan. We should write together.” And I just looked at him like, “What do you …? What’s happening here?” I thought the song was a little corny at the time, but it’s probably a classic now. It’s pretty catchy. I think the chords, to me, were a little too fancy for the aesthetic of the time.

Are you still in touch with [producer duo] the Dust Brothers? You’re one of the last artists who worked with them, on Guero in 2005, before they vanished into thin air. I genuinely wonder what happened to them! CoopertapesI did actually see them about a year ago. I see them from time to time. We have unfinished records that were never put out, so who knows? Maybe there’ll be something down the road. I’ve never asked, but I’m guessing they don’t really need to work in music, they’re doing other things. They worked with Hanson right after Odelay – people thought we were related [Beck’s surname is Hansen]. I remember they were working on that, the Rolling Stones and the Fight Club soundtrack. So that’s why my next two albums were not fully produced by the Dust Brothers, after the success of Odelay they became too busy.

Looking to the future, do you see yourself sharing the stage with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot? AKA how did you come to be a guest star on Futurama? vammypThey wrote a script and sent it to me, and I said no. Through that whole era, I said no to pretty much everything. I was asked to do the theme for Austin Powers 2 and 3, and Shrek, and I was even saying no to, like, Amores Perros and Y Tu Mamá También and Run Lola Run, all these classic movies. They wanted me to act in High Fidelity and Ghost World, and I just decided that I didn’t want to “go Hollywood”.

They sent me this cartoon and I thought, well, if I did something like this it would be The Simpsons – a lot of people have done that, Sonic Youth have done that. The script was sitting on the tour bus, and my band got a hold of it on a long drive and said, “What is this?” And I said, “Oh, it’s this show, Futurama. I’ve never heard of it, but they want me to do this ridiculous thing.” And they said, “You have to do it!” They all ganged up on me so I did it.

Beercan is my go-to “shake your ass” number. What is yours? TeeDubyaBeeI would say anything from the early 80s funk era. Anything Sly Stone, James Brown – and early 80s Prince era, Talking Heads. Classics.

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is one of my favourite films, and your recording of Everybody’s Got to Learn Sometime is a sublime part of it. How did you get involved with the film, and why that song in particular? CybillserviceI did a music video with Michel Gondry, the director, and we became pals. I was having dinner over at his house one night, and he described this convoluted plot that I couldn’t quite follow. I said, “I don’t totally understand what this is, but when you make it, I want to see it.” Three or four years later, he called me up and said, “I made the movie.” My buddy Jon Brion was doing the score. It’s one of the only things, again, that I said yes to. But it was because it was a personal relationship. It’s become one of my songs that people love the most. I had just done Sea Change, which I think is one of the reasons they called me. That album had met so much shock from my fans that I swore to never make a record like that again. And now it’s beloved. It’s probably the main thing that people care about. I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years, it’s all Sea Change and Midnite Vultures.

‘Amazing community’: how people are making new friends and connections as adults

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 13:53:28 GMT

As concern about loneliness and social isolation grows, we spoke to people who have joined groups and set up activities

Amid growing concern about loneliness and social isolation, new research from the Institute for Public Policy Research found the number of young people in England with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, with one in 20 now reporting having none at all.

Making new friends as an adult is not always easy. We spoke to people who have taken deliberate steps to make new connections about what worked for them.

For Rhiannon, a 35-year-old ghostwriter from East Sussex, joining a local knitting and crochet group has become “a lifeline” after separating from her husband and moving a few towns away, and finding connections harder to maintain.

In February, she joined the Yarners, a weekly group in Mayfield. Having only started crocheting a month earlier, she was “absolutely terrified” they would judge her for being a beginner. “But they didn’t care.”

The group quickly became an important part of her life. “No matter what is happening at home, I know for two hours a week I can just sit in a calm and supportive space with people who share my hobby. It’s more than just a group. It’s a real community.”

Having local friends to rely on is one of the biggest perks. “If I needed something, if I was in trouble in some way, I’ve now got people I could actually call and say: ‘Hey, can you help me?’”

Ria, 27, moved from Mumbai to London five years ago, but after later moving to Reading, she found it harder to maintain the friendships she had made in the capital.

“I faced acute loneliness,” says Ria, who now works in mergers and acquisitions in London. “When people move away from their home, it gets tough at this age to make friends.”

In May, she created a WhatsApp group to bring her London friends together. It soon expanded through friends of friends and Instagram. “It just blew up. There are 70 people in the group now.”

The London Coffee Club holds meetups in cafes for groups of five to 10. “I’m slightly introverted, so I don’t prefer big groups. It’s a relaxed vibe. There’s no agenda.”

Working from home left Rebecca, a 31-year-old NHS project support officer in Bristol, missing everyday social interaction. “I completely underestimated how much I would miss face-to-face contact, even informal conversations such as: ‘How was your weekend?’”

A few months ago, she joined exercise classes at her local leisure centre “as a way to make friends”. Although “absolutely terrified” at first, she now attends pilates, weights and body conditioning classes about three times a week.

“Even though you’re doing an exercise class, there’s that informal aspect where you are having a bit of a joke and a laugh. Working from home, you don’t get that sort of office banter. To me, this is my new equivalent.”

Rebecca has also met a new friend through Bristol Girls, a local Facebook group, and encouraged her to join the classes. “She’s helping me, and I’m helping her,” she says.

After leaving his job as a primary school teacher Ben, 35, suddenly had more free time so thought he would use it to “meet new people” and get back into stage performance.

“It was something I loved at school and at university,” says Ben, who lives in Gateshead and works in education.

In 2017, he joined the People’s Theatre in Newcastle upon Tyne, a non-professional community theatre company, and has since performed in about 20 productions.

“The first year was non-stop as I jumped from play to play and met so many fantastic people,” he says. “It’s been nearly a decade, and I count some people, even people I only met less than a year ago, as some of my closest friends.”

The friendships now extend well beyond rehearsals and performances, with regular social gatherings.

“It’s a huge community, and everyone involved, whether it’s performing, set building, or costume design, does it for the love of it,” he says. “It’s so inspiring.”

Chris, 32, says a combination of growing older, the isolation of Covid and having no similarly aged peers at work led to a point where he “essentially had no local friends any more”.

The systems manager from Kent decided to revive his interest in board and card games and found a local games shop holding £3-a-session games evenings. Although “terrified” before his first event, he “couldn’t have asked for a better environment”.

“I feel like it’s not the impossible feat I thought it was to make new friends as an adult on your own,” he says. “The joy it brings me to be able to take part in a fun activity while getting to know people and enjoying good humour is priceless.

“I think it’s vital for mental health for people to have a safe third space where they can develop relationships, skills and experiences without being dependent on work or partners to fill that void.”

When Chloe, 27, moved back to Hertfordshire after living in the Midlands, the change left her feeling lonely.

But instead of joining a group, she created one.

“All I wanted was just a friend to go for coffee or go to the cinema with,” she says. “I thought: there’s nothing for local women to make local friends. It’s so important to have that community.”

With this in mind, Chloe, a content creator, and her friend Sarah, 30, a nail technician, created the Girls Collective, organising activities where women can meet while trying something new, from keyring making to line dancing.

To drum up interest, they posted content on social media which caught people’s attention.

“We had 65 people for our first event just from our TikTok videos,” she says.

Engaging in an activity, Chloe and Sarah believe, helps to cut through any nerves and awkwardness.

The group now has 500 women in its community chat, and more than 250 have attended events. “They’ve made their own friendships and hang out outside of us [too], which is brilliant,” says Sarah.

Chloe adds: “I had thought having to move back was the worst thing. But now I’m like, no, because it’s brought me this amazing community.”

‘Songwriting instead of doomscrolling’: project inspires Welsh valleys towns to tune into their heritage

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 13:46:11 GMT

Community groups and schools work with Wales’s folk arts organisation to set stories of the area’s people to music

Growing up in Wales, Liz Puleston-Jones was familiar with the country’s rich heritage of storytelling and traditional music, but none of it ever seemed to have much of a connection to her life in Swansea.

Researching the history of the area as part of Cân y Cymoedd (When Valleys Sing), a project in nearby Port Talbot, she came across the story of Isabel Thomas, a 14-year-old girl in the 1940s who left school and lied about her age to work in a tin plate works to support her family.

“Her story really spoke to me,” said Puleston-Jones. “Before I did this, I didn’t really have a connection to the history and storytelling aspect of folk music, and how much it’s about community and telling the stories of normal people … Anyone can be part of a tune, and write a tune, and share it.”

Thomas’s story has now been celebrated in song form as part of the project from Wales’s national folk arts organisation, Trac Cymru. At Cân y Cymoedd community and school workshops, musicians, historians and volunteers have helped each group uncover stories at local heritage sites and museums, and channelled their findings into the creation of two dozen new compositions about local life in Rhondda Cynon Taf and Neath Port Talbot.

For many participants, the workshops have rekindled a sense of cultural pride and belonging in the community.

Jenny Pope, who took part in the sessions in Port Talbot, said: “For me, it made the Port Talbot area feel like a real beacon of folk music – somewhere people might once have just driven past but now feels full of life and culture. Creating something we can pass on to the next generation has been amazing.”

Puleston-Jones added: “I was terrified at the idea of having to write or produce something on my own but it was a collaborative experience. Now instead of watching rubbish TV or doomscrolling I’m being drawn to songwriting and playing my violin after years and years. It feels much healthier.”

At Llwyncelyn primary school in Porth, in the Rhondda valley, a year 6 class has been busy learning the song about their village composed by last year’s cohort with the help of a fiddle player, Aneirin Jones, before recording a music video at Rhondda Heritage Park, a former colliery.

Their song, Ein Cân Fach Ni (Our Little Song), references the area’s mountains, mines and chapels, as well as the activities and places that make up the children’s day-to-day lives, such as the recycling centre and the playground.

Ifan, 10, said: “I knew Cwm Rhondda before but I didn’t really know anything else about folk music before this, it’s been really fun. My sister is annoyed because her class wrote the song but my class is going to make the video!”

The original songs are being professionally recorded for an album Trac Cymru hopes will be accessible to a wider audience and become a resource for future generations.

The project manager, Antwn Owen-Hicks, said: “Cân y Cymoedd is about making sure that traditions continue to evolve. Magic happens when people explore all of this and begin to see where they’re from in a different light. It doesn’t matter what musical level you’re at or what language you speak. If you’ve got a story, you can write a song, and we help you do this.”
