Robert Kraft, once the NFL’s good guy, is just another billionaire silencing Macklemore

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 13:14:41 GMT

The Patriots owner’s decision to ban the rapper from performing at the team’s stadium brings back memories of the blackballing of Colin Kaepernick

Six years ago, in the middle of a “racial reckoning” that never was, a White House that had begun out of control reached its chaotic apex. Federal officials were sweeping citizens off American streets in unmarked vehicles, surrounding the Lincoln Memorial with armed guards and rolling military vehicles through residential neighborhoods in a fascist reaction to protests against the murder of George Floyd. It was at this point that NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, realizing it had all gone too far, appeared on a Zoom and admitted his league was “wrong” for not listening to its players when they had protested against police brutality.

The implication was clear: more than any other sports league, the NFL was harshest in its reaction to the protests that began with Trayvon Martin in 2012 and continued with Ferguson, Baltimore and Colin Kaepernick. By blackballing Kaepernick, sitting by while broadcast partners refused to air the national anthem to undermine the protests, and, most embarrassingly, Goodell’s draconian announcement that teams would be subject to fines if players showed dissent, the NFL had proven itself to act in the most un-American of ways.

This week, New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft showed he has learned nothing from those years. He banned Macklemore from supporting Ed Sheeran at the Patriots’ Gillette Stadium over the rapper’s vocal support for Palestine – something that has become a career-threatening political position as dangerous as kneeling during the national anthem. Kraft imposed his own version of authoritarianism: Macklemore claims that Kraft not only banned him from his stadium, but appeared to influence other NFL owners to stop the rapper from appearing at most of Sheeran’s other stadium dates. For his part, Kraft says his decision to stop Macklemore from performing at Gillette was due to both Macklemore’s “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”. In 2014, Macklemore apologized after he wore a wig, beard and hooked nose at a Seattle concert, which critics said was an anti-semitic caricature.

No NFL owner has worked harder to be seen as reasonable and socially conscious as Kraft. He has appeared on the surface as a shrewd businessman, power-neutral, making political donations to Republicans and Democrats alike. New Englanders recall him fondly as the man who rescued the Patriots from the misogyny and vile incompetence of the Victor Kiam years; from the threat of the team relocating to St Louis when he bought the Patriots from James Orthwein in 1994; and, of course, the man who saved them from all the losing.

Kraft was eventually given the benefit of the doubt as the hero in his stadium battle against disgraced former Massachusetts legislature speaker Thomas Finneran that nearly led to Kraft moving the Patriots out of the Commonwealth. He did so by building the only 100% privately financed stadium in the NFL – even though in 1998 Kraft himself had agreed to take a lucrative offer of public money from the Connecticut legislature and move the Patriots to Hartford. It was under Kraft’s ownership – led by his late wife Myra – that the Patriots took a stand for women, renouncing the rights to Christian Peter a week after drafting him, when multiple domestic violence accusations and convictions against the player surfaced.

As the NFL collectively destroyed Kaepernick’s career (the former quarterback says the same tactics of collusion are now being used against Macklemore), it was Kraft who tried to appear sympathetic to those who suffered under systemic racial injustices. He supported Patriots Devin and Jason McCourty in their advocacy of criminal justice reform, helped the release from prison of rapper Meek Mill, and following the deadly 2018 school shooting in Parkland, Florida, loaned the Patriots’ plane to students traveling to Washington to protest gun violence. Despite a president who called the pandemic a hoax and encouraged citizens to inject bleach to immunize themselves against the coronavirus, Kraft sent his private plane to China to help transport shipments of N-95 masks to the United States. Bob Kraft has always believed he’s one of the good guys.

In the Macklemore situation, he is not. While he has been lauded by his supporters, all Kraft has done is follow a familiar script of a rich man applying power. He has undermined his everyman persona as a guy who sat on the cold metal seats at Schaefer Stadium alongside his fellow Patriots fan but was fortunate enough to eventually buy the team. Now he is just another billionaire using his power to stifle words – to do exactly what his fellow owners did to Kaepernick a decade ago. Nor should it be forgotten that no matter how many rappers treat Kraft like the cool old white dude, Bob Kraft, hater of hate speech, lover of peace, is a prominent part of a league that conspired to ban a player from playing football for telling the truth: cops are getting paid leave for killing people. That’s not right. Hardly hate speech.

The end result is an old man threatened, unable to maintain the facade that he is any different, any better, than the moral rot around him. While truth often belongs to those who get to tell the tale, who control the airwaves, who get to do the blackballing and destroy the careers, it also belongs to the silenced. Both the overstepping Kraft and the tattered Sheeran – whose supporting acts have resigned from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore – know that now. One looks like a dictator, the other a wimp.

Kraft is also displaying a perverse, pervasive strain of American exceptionalism normalized by Donald Trump where might makes right. His supporters have attempted to argue that Kraft hasn’t violated the first amendment over Macklemore because he owns Gillette Stadium, the land under it and paid for it with his money rather than with public funds that would be better spent on potholes, bridges and better schools. Along those narrow grounds, Kraft can certainly decide who gets to say what on his property – although even that argument is a specious one if he cares about community and not oligarchy. By then extending his influence from his private bubble of Foxborough to allegedly use that influence to blackball Macklemore from the rest of Sheeran’s tour by calling ahead to Philadelphia, Dallas, Tampa, Charlotte, Indianapolis and Atlanta, Kraft engaged in yet another collusion, for each of those venues are largely publicly financed. They do not belong privately to Kraft, or the rest of the football oligarchy, but to the taxpaying public. Public space is protected by the first amendment. Kraft has either forgotten what the pregame flags and flyovers are supposed to be about, or like so many other foundations in this country, has simply decided to stop caring.

Where does Kraft stand today? The lover of peace and hater of hate speech is now backpedaling, remembering his position as one of the good guys, offering to throw money at the bad publicity – he suggested he would pledge $2m to unspecified charities in the Middle East without reinstating Macklemore – but he really stands with Trump, that most seasoned practitioner of hate speech, who once called Kaepernick and the NFL players who smash their bodies into a million pieces every Sunday “sons of bitches”.

Kraft gave Trump $1m for his first inauguration then said in 2024 that he hadn’t spoken to the president since the January 6 attack on the Capitol. But there he sat this January in the Kennedy Center presidential box next to Trump for a screening of the Amazon Studios bomb Melania. As Trump petulantly destroys the arts, Kraft’s wife Dana Blumberg sits on the Kennedy Center board, part of the unanimous vote to close the center unless Trump’s name is added to the building. Kraft has his name on another blackballing, but he’s headlining the marquee this time. For people who decry anti-democratic behavior, the Krafts seem comfortable in its company and quick studies at mastering it themselves. They’ve had a lot of practice.

Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including Full Dissidence: Notes from an Uneven Playing Field, and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America. He also writes on Substack

Margaret Busby: ‘My friend Bonnie Greer fearlessly spoke out and forged connections’

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 13:12:06 GMT

The writer and editor shares memories of a creative powerhouse who was generous with her time and expertise

Bonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77

Bonnie Greer personified courage, humour, principle and generosity. Before knowing her in person, I met her work. Her 1994 debut novel Hanging by Her Teeth – about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search of her father – was sent to me for endorsement by its publisher, and I commented unhesitatingly: “Writing with sharpness, wit and poignancy, Bonnie Greer gathers the sequestered memories behind one Black woman’s bitter-sweet blues.”

The scope of Bonnie’s own life is beyond anything fictional, encompassing highs and lows, triumphs and challenges, her trajectory starting in the West Side of Chicago and ending up navigating iconic areas of London – whether Holland Park or Covent Garden or Soho – as if to the manor born. It was an honour to become her friend, sharing many a good time, offering a consoling shoulder if needed. An added bonus was to meet her husband David Hutchins. What a wonderful mutually supportive team they made.

Bonnie’s activism marched side by side with her creativity and powers of persuasion. Friendship, support, empathy and behind-the-scenes involvement were all part of who she was. She could be effervescently sociable. There was an era when she relished get-togethers of a sort of ladies-who-lunch club that she would organise, where we might chat for hours, exchanging memories, planning dreamy never-to-be-fulfilled projects. I recall one gathering that took place at the House of Commons – with Diane Abbott, Verna Wilkins, Maya Jaggi and Nana Ayebia Clarke – when Bonnie suddenly made us all pause to reflect on the fact we were all sitting there, with a view of the Thames and London’s landscape, given where we had come from.

Seemingly ready to re-invent herself, she was perhaps defying anyone to easily label her. She could be public intellectual, television pundit, dramatist, librettist, academic. Her repertoire was wide-ranging and ever-expanding, with fresh ideas emerging at every opportunity. She fearlessly spoke out, forged new connections, took on weighty burdens.

She lent expertise to numerous national cultural institutions – including on the boards of the British Museum, the Royal Opera House and the London Film School, and as vice president of the Shaw Society and chancellor of Kingston University London. She shared her vision with such ventures as the Black Theatre Co-operative and Talawa Theatre Company (where, during her stint as artistic director, she mooted an ambitious dramatisation of my 1,000-plus-page anthology, Daughters of Africa). We were both patrons of the SI Leeds Literary Prize for unpublished fiction by Black and Asian women in the UK.

It was pure delight to accompany her anywhere to experience music, art, drama, film or anything intellectually stimulating.

In June 2019, we went to a lecture by Lonnie Bunch III at the British Library – then newly appointed to secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, the first African American and first historian appointed to do so, who recently announced his intention to retire at the end of 2026. Dr Bunch’s recent communication with me echoes my own feelings: “I have been made better by my interactions with Bonnie. She was generous with her time, with her contacts and with her friendship. Her passing is an immeasurable loss. I am crying but also smiling because of her impact on so many. She was simply amazing. Her ability to speak truth to power made her such a unique voice in both the UK and the US.”

We will all miss her.

Watching NAZA was like peering through a window – and seeing the machinery of killing in Gaza

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 12:30:49 GMT

For so long I wondered why I survived while family and friends were killed. Now I know the only difference between life and death may have been an AI algorithm

The lights go down, and for a moment I forget I’m watching a screen. It fills with a rooftop in Tel Aviv at night, black and grey. The camera pans down. Through windows, we see people watching screens of their own – couples holding each other close, following the news, eating food. They appear absorbed in their own worlds, and why wouldn’t they be?

That’s the thing I can’t get past as a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, watching this apparent tranquillity: this must be it – this must be what safety actually looks like. Just an evening uninterrupted, with no military aircraft flying overhead or drones buzzing incessantly. Meanwhile, men and women on the rooftop above them calmly talk about how they decided how many Palestinian civilians would die on any given night.

These are the soldiers, mostly intelligence officers, who helped Israel carry out its destruction of Gaza. Their testimonies form the basis of NAZA, a documentary whose title comes from an Israeli military acronym used to indicate how many civilians are likely to die in an airstrike on the territory.

What surprised me in the film wasn’t the massive scale of the killing, or even the coldness of it, but the proficiency of the soldiers who coolly described destroying people’s lives as if they were discussing a routine errand. One described the work simply as a “mission”, while another compared it to a “video game”.

One soldier described knowing exactly what some of the people were doing in the moments before he killed them. He recalled hearing a man talking to his wife in bed. A baby crying. The sound of the TV. Despite taking all that humanity in, he quickly gave permission to drop the bomb.

The soldier explained how he would then go out with friends in the evening, and come back the next morning to do it all over again. For these Israeli soldiers, killing Palestinians was simply a task that could be paused and repeated.

There was no hesitation in their voices, no sense that they were describing something that should be difficult to say aloud. They spoke with the ease of people who had learned how to do this, how to talk about it and how to carry on afterward – as one of them put it, with “zero” consideration for the lives they annihilated.

NAZA makes visible the targeting systems and planning decisions that precede a strike. But this is only part of the story.

Some of the perpetrators were on the ground in Gaza, where the same violence became much more immediate as they moved through Palestinian neighbourhoods, entering homes, setting them on fire and enforcing “kill zones”.

Yet for every act shown on film, there are many others that were never recorded and so will never be reckoned with – the constant surveillance, the restrictions on movement, the displacement of entire populations. NAZA opens a small window into the machinery of killing in Gaza, but it is something much larger than any film can capture.

Throughout the screening, I could not stop myself from putting names back into the places where the film placed numbers. When one soldier described how Israeli forces massacred Palestinians at aid distribution sites, I thought of my cousin, 35-year-old Raed Majed Mushtaha, killed in the “Flour Massacre” in early 2024 as he searched for food for his family. I remembered my friend Youssef Maher Dawas, killed in the first week of the genocide, whose body was later found beneath rubble.

Other soldiers described how the army authorised the killing of 20 civilians in pursuit of a single junior target, and as many as 500 in pursuit of a senior target. These targets, however, had predominantly been “incriminated” by an AI system that, the soldiers admit, was known to err in about 15% of cases – yet they killed them anyway, along with their whole families.

I felt stuck on that. I thought about my uncle, Hisham Zafer Mushtaha, his wife, Hanan, their sons, Basel and Mohammed, and their four grandchildren, Raged, Hisham, Lana and Abdrahman, aged between three and 12 years old. I imagined them being killed because an AI algorithm assumed there might be a target there.

For the soldiers, these moments are merely part of a daily “mission”. But Raed, Youssef, Hisham, Hanan, Basel, Mohammed, Raged, Hisham, Lana and Abdrahman were people I knew and loved, whose calls I waited for, whose absence will for ever be felt.

For so long, I had asked how these people I knew were killed. Watching the film, my mind kept returning to the opposite question: how did I survive? I had spent so much of my life in Gaza thinking that, because I did not belong to any faction, I would be safe. I believed that if Israel was justifying its killings to the world by portraying those it killed as military targets, then I would make it out alive, because I was not one of them.

But the difference between me and the people I’ve lost may have been nothing more than what an AI algorithm flagged, and what someone decided, through a screen in Tel Aviv, would be an acceptable amount of NAZA. I realised, perhaps for the first time, that there was no precaution that I could have taken that would have guaranteed my survival. The fact that I did survive was completely random. And when I think about that, my heart sinks.

What I want, watching this, is not catharsis. I have had enough of that. I want to attach names to the soldiers themselves – the ones who said it was “fun” to destroy Gaza, who viewed Palestinians in Gaza as mere data points. This is the only way that the “systematic” nature of Israel’s killing machine stops functioning as a shield, one that allows those responsible to feel as if they were mere cogs.

When the film ended, I called my family in Gaza, as I do every night. I have rung them often to tell them where to move and which road to avoid, hoping to keep them safe amid the ongoing senseless destruction. But having watched the film, I kept thinking about surveillance and systems that track their movements and could turn them into targets.

But sitting there after the film, a new thought took over: what if the soldiers watching them know more about where my family are than I do? What if they can see what I cannot? My family might be sitting together, drinking tea, laughing at something one of my brothers said, while, somewhere far away, those same moments could already be data on a screen.

And as I spoke to them that night, for a moment I forgot everything I had seen in the film. I did not hear coordinates, or surveillance, or AI. I heard my family. A familiar voice. A breath. And I understood, in that moment, what these systems can never account for: that each person on the screen is an entire world unto themselves.

After its screening at the Venice film festival, the film received a 25-minute standing ovation – an indictment, I couldn’t help thinking, of a western media that spent three years treating Palestinian journalists as unreliable narrators of our own deaths. A room rose to its feet, but that has not stopped the machine: the bombing hasn’t stopped, the machine on screen is still running even as the credits roll.

I’m glad the testimony exists; glad it’s believed now. But belief this late, costing us this much, is not safety. My people do not feel safer because a film about their killers received applause in a theatre they will never sit in.

Mahmoud Mushtaha is a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, and the author of Sobrevivir al genocidio en Gaza (Surviving the Genocide in Gaza). This article is based on a piece first published in +972 Magazine

Andy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 12:00:48 GMT

Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issue

British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it

UK politics live – latest updates

The UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050, Andy Burnham has argued in his strongest comments yet on the issue, saying it is no longer possible for Britons to believe they are not already affected by a changing climate.

Writing for the Guardian about new plans for a mass of community-led local green energy projects, the prime minister said the UK must “believe in itself”, and set out his determination to reach net zero targets, which have been rejected by the Conservatives and Reform UK.

The tone marks a contrast to the summer, when Burnham faced criticism for a seemingly muted response to the heatwaves, droughts and wildfires that affected the UK, with his main initiative being a ban on portable barbecues.

“I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050,” Burnham said. “I want Britain to believe in itself again.”

Saying he wanted to connect local communities to green power projects – to reach net zero targets and make energy more affordable – Burnham said: “I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record.”

He went on: “Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead.

“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.”

The issue is still a tricky one for Burnham, who is facing significant pressure from both sides over whether to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea.

A number of Labour MPs believe approving the projects would send a negative signal on climate efforts, and would provide a boost to the Greens, who argue that Labour is insufficiently serious in tackling the climate emergency.

A seemingly imminent decision to approve Jackdaw has been delayed until later this autumn, prompting the Greens to accuse Labour of wanting to bury the issue before the high-profile Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, is challenging for the seat vacated by Keir Starmer.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the field off the coast of Aberdeen, but it has been put off. Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank closed last month, with Fahnbulleh since considering her response.

Approving either or both projects would place renewed pressure on Burnham over his commitment to net zero.

No 10 officials point out that Burnham discussed the climate emergency in his first Commons statement as prime minister at the start of the month, and when he visited Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August after fires there. But in August, a series of climate organisations accused him of being silent about the subject during the heatwave.

In his Guardian article, Burnham tied net zero plans to devolution, setting out funding for so-called people’s power projects, where communities will have a stake in local green energy projects, such as solar panels, windfarms and hydro schemes.

He wrote: “Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland of community energy schemes, which keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home.

“These projects work and we want to take them nationwide … The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, the way we build homes and the way we produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.”

British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 12:00:48 GMT

With nearly £30m of funding, I’m giving communities power over local energy. They know the gravity of global heating, and they want to be part of the solution

Andy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050

On the day I became prime minister, I pledged to bring power to every postcode. Today, we begin to make good on that promise in the most literal sense. With nearly £30m of funding for People’s Power projects, communities across every nation of the UK will soon have the chance to build and control their own clean energy supply.

This investment means villages, towns and cities can harness the natural resources around them with solar panels on libraries, publicly owned windfarms, hydro schemes in their rivers, or whatever else works for them. The purpose is to put money back in people’s pockets while giving them a direct role in tackling the climate crisis.

Every council and community group awarded funding will have at least part-ownership in its renewable energy projects. That means, in the years ahead, more and more communities in Britain will do more than simply host solar panels and wind turbines. They will own a stake in them and retain a share of the wealth they create.

Today’s announcement is part of this government’s sustained effort to make energy more affordable. In my first week in office, I said I would remove VAT from household electricity bills. From the beginning of October, that policy kicks in, giving families some much-needed breathing room. But the only lasting way to bring down bills is to produce more of our own clean, renewable energy at home, which People’s Power will achieve.

I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record. Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.

Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples across the UK of community energy schemes that keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home.

These projects work and we want to take them nationwide. Today’s investment is the first down payment on a £1bn Great British Energy programme, the biggest investment in community energy ever, which will eventually fund more than 1,000 People’s Power projects.

The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, build homes and produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.

With this in mind, I believe there are two routes we can follow. There’s the traditional Whitehall way: make people pay for the change with more regulation and higher costs, and allow private companies to reap the rewards. Or we can pursue a different route: help people make the change by creating jobs, lowering bills and bringing power back to them.

That is the approach I took as mayor of Greater Manchester. When we brought the buses back under public control, we capped fares and made the fleet cleaner. The result was a transport system designed around the needs of the people who pay for it and rely on it. We are applying the same principle to community energy.

I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050. I want Britain to believe in itself again. That will not happen by asking people to stand still while the world spins around them. Everyone should have a say and a stake in their future. That is what No 10 North is all about. It is what today is about – it is community power in every sense. Power owned by local people, power generated by local projects and power returned to every postcode.

Human harps, massive bananas and dogging: the 20 best Busby Berkeley dance routines – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 11:48:25 GMT

To mark 50 years since the director and choreographer’s death, we count down his best fantastical, kaleidoscopic numbers, from erotic silhouettes to sinister tap dancers

So you thought Cats (2019) was tacky? Wait until you see Ruby Keeler (AKA Mrs Al Jolson) gambolling around as a fluffy white feline, being wooed by an ogling tomcat, or chasing Billy Barty, a child actor with dwarfism, costumed as a mouse.

Joan Blondell (seven months pregnant during filming) livens up workaday laundry tasks by fantasising about the men whose underwear she hangs out to dry. And the underwear flirts right back. Who cares if you can see the wires?

If this were a tap dancing Top 20, Eleanor Powell would be at No 1, but Berkeley wisely stands back and showcases her epic skills with minimal fuss. All the tricksiness took place out of frame, where stagehands were pushing grand pianos out of her way.

Berkeley’s first colour film as both director and choreographer stars “Brazilian Bombshell” Carmen Miranda in her signature fruit-laden headdress. The fruity motif continues in a musical number set on a fake tropical island where chorus girls wield giant bananas. Nothing salacious to see here, move along.

This quintessential backstage musical was a huge hit and established Berkeley’s approach to choreography. An initially stagebound song with innuendo-laden lyrics, belted out by lecherous Dick Powell, blossoms into revolving geometric formations of young women shot from every conceivable angle, culminating in a travelling shot through their spread legs. This is cinema!

“Mr Berkeley, I’m not raising my daughter to be a human harp!” was one critic’s reaction to a vision of chorus girls plucking at harps fashioned from other chorus girls. Just before the Hays Code banished navels from Hollywood, blond-wigged beauties flaunt their belly buttons while performing the ultimate ostrich feather fan dance.

Before Dick Powell went all film noir as Philip Marlowe in Farewell, My Lovely (1944), he and Keeler regularly played sweethearts in Berkeley’s musicals. The camera glides around what is essentially a sex hotel, as attempts to consummate their hasty marriage are hampered by other guests, interfering relatives and an unnaturally precocious child.

Once again, Berkeley the choreographer stands back and lets Eleanor Powell work her magic. MGM failed to come up with a suitable dog to partner her for this number, so Powell bought a terrier mix called Buttons and trained it herself.

“What do you go for, go see a show for?” The answer is dames (male gaze, sorry) and here they are, not as scantily clad as in pre-code days, but forming a wide range of pleasing kaleidoscopic configurations and Bridget Riley-esque patterns until Dick Powell’s head bursts through their tableaux.

Keeler once again tries to consummate a marriage (to Clarence Nordstrom), this time on a sleeper train to Niagara Falls. Other passengers leer salaciously out of their curtained compartments, while worldly Una Merkel and Ginger Rogers predict the ingenue will soon be on a train to Reno for a quickie divorce.

Chorus girls, wired up to neon-tubed violins, twirl around on vertiginous walkways. Then the lights go out so all you can see are the violins, which rearrange themselves into the shape of one massive violin. So many ways this could have gone horribly wrong – and indeed, a 6.4 earthquake hit Los Angeles during filming, and some of the violins short-circuited.

One minute Alice Faye is singing as normal, surrounded by dancing children who are only marginally weird. The next, we are plunged into a Technicolor hallucination of neon hoops, more dots than DC’s Polka-Dot Man could dream of, and psychedelic effects that will have you wondering if you accidentally ingested LSD.

Before teaming up with Fred Astaire in the first of their 10 musical collaborations, Ginger Rogers played a golden-hearted broad in Berkeley’s first two backstage musicals. Heading a chorus line draped in silver dollars, she belts out an upbeat ode to capitalism, including one verse in Pig Latin.

Once again, a musical number opens out into an entire panorama that could not possibly be physically contained in a theatre. Keeler’s effortful hoofing (she’s no Eleanor Powell, but we love her anyway) gives way to rhythmic travelling shots of New Yorkers going about their business: traffic, newspaper sellers, hairdressers and, adding a touch of dirty realism, a murder.

Dick Powell is trying to get into Keeler’s knickers in an outrageously nudge-nudge number featuring snowball fights, erotic silhouettes, roller-skating cops and stocking tops galore, before she finally stymies her beau with a onesie made of metal. Enter leering child actor Billy Barty, with a can opener.

Powell loves Keeler so much he keeps seeing her everywhere. And so do we, thanks to lookalike chorus girls in Keeler masks, holding up cut-outs of her face, or pulling their skirts over their heads to form one gigantic Keeler tifo, all set to a Harry Warren-Al Dubin earworm that quickly became a standard.

After The Public Enemy, James Cagney was keen to avoid being typecast as a gangster and draws on his vaudeville roots to give us a tap dance that almost makes up for Keeler in yellowface. Get an eyeful of Hollywood orientalism in all its pre-code horror, complete with sex workers, opium smokers and half the US Navy on manoeuvres.

Audiences of the 1930s went to the cinema to escape the Great Depression, but numbers like this assured them that their pain wasn’t being ignored. Joan Blondell, with a sort of sprechgesang, and contralto Etta Moten lament the treatment of poverty-stricken veterans of the first world war. As the chorus swells, the number segues from a theatrical street into montages of men marching to war and limping home to the breadline and a treadmill of silhouettes. Lump in throat time.

Dick Powell and Keeler celebrate “love in a natural setting”. Berkeley illustrates this early 1930s ode to dogging with an astonishing aquatic ballet of 100 synchronised swimmers forming flowers, snake shapes and a human fountain, shot from all angles in a glass-walled pool that filled an entire soundstage. None of this, of course, would be visible to the theatre audience glimpsed at the start of the number.

You ain’t heard nothing until you’ve heard 200 feet stomping out a time step in unison. Of all the musical numbers he directed, Berkeley’s personal favourite was this 13-minute expressionist nightmare in which a young woman’s nightclubbing gets out of hand. From Wini Shaw’s disembodied head turning into the Manhattan skyline, to the most sinister phalanx of tap-dancers this side of Leni Riefenstahl, to the frankly rather shocking ending, it’s an intoxicating masterpiece. “Come and dance!”

Dear Ed Sheeran, fence-sitting is so last century: musicians can no longer opt out of politics

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 11:00:48 GMT

It’s all very 2026: with a stadium owner on one side and angry support acts on the other, the cornered star will have to pick a side

Ed Sheeran, seeking to stay out of politics, has become, in this moment, the most political artist in the world. And in trying to leave himself room to manoeuvre, he has backed himself into a corner. Since the rapper Macklemore was dropped as a support act on Sheeran’s Loop tour on Monday, every other opening act has pulled out. Finneas O’Connell kept it brief on Tuesday: “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. I stand with Palestine and its people.” Aaron Rowe was already out, saying: “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence … rightful voices.”

Beoga, Sheeran’s actual backing band, then pulled out, along with the Danish band Lukas Graham, who probably made the mildest statement, managing to not even mention any countries: “We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them.”

Sheeran said the decision to drop Macklemore was entirely down to venue owners and promoters, adding that there was a reason he didn’t talk about politics on stage: “My audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.” Both statements sound weak, but more importantly, it is not true that Sheeran doesn’t take political stances. He has taken part in a fundraising gig for Ukrainians, telling them, “I love you, I stand with you”; in 2017 he outed himself as a “Corbynista fanboy” (TM the Sun), and has been a vocal supporter of LGBTQI+ rights, on stage and off, throughout his career. More specifically, it seems unlikely he didn’t know the views of his support acts when he chose them: Macklemore had a song about Hind Rajab, the five-year-old killed by the IDF in 2024, on his set list; Beoga are founding members of Irish Artists for Palestine.

To try to psychoanalyse Sheeran, and say definitively whether he was trying to borrow the spirit of these artists while distancing himself from their beliefs, or in fact shares their views, would be premature; ultimately, he’s bound to declare himself. So far he has simply said he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine” and that the “suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy”. Just because he didn’t choose to speak publicly, he said, “doesn’t mean I don’t care”.

This omertà won’t hold. But what we can say for certain now is that the idea of keeping politics out of entertainment, music, or art, is last century’s fantasy. Censorship is swift – but often not as overt as in this case. It is simply a fact that if artists don’t studiously avoid voicing certain opinions, they will get caught up in politics. It’s unclear whether it’s possible to create art – at least art that will be seen by a mass public – in those conditions.

At the vanguard of the move to jettison Macklemore from the tour was the Israeli-American Council, whose chief executive, Elan Carr, told the Today programme on Wednesday that the rapper had “put forth a blood libel against the state of Israel and, by connection, the Jewish people”. He was pressed by Justin Webb on what Macklemore actually said: “The words free Palestine don’t necessarily mean … that anything awful should happen to Jewish people or indeed to the state of Israel.” “Free Palestine absolutely is a call for the extermination of the state of Israel and the Jewish people,” Carr replied.

So what kind of Palestine is it acceptable to want? The other difficult strand of Carr’s argument was that a concert audience was “captive … people have paid to be there”. If you’ve paid money to be somewhere, the logic runs, you shouldn’t be subjected to politics of any kind. Yet billionaires have no qualms about having a political agenda. Macklemore, both onstage and in his own statement, has rebuffed the argument that voicing support for Palestinians and criticising Israel and its actions in Gaza and the West Bank is antisemitic. (In 2014, he apologised for a costume he wore on stage, which critics said was antisemitic, saying: “I respect all cultures and all people.”)

The concern of many of the artists was that they were facing not just censorship, but censorship by billionaires: specifically Robert Kraft, who demanded Macklemore’s removal with the threat of axing the whole show from his Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts. Kraft has so far not commented on Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s charge that he put pressure on other stadiums to follow suit. In his own statement, he insisted his decision to ban Macklemore from Gillette was “not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf”, but that such advocacy, “should not … obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.

What next, Ocasio-Cortez asked an interviewer, rhetorically: “It could be speaking out about AI … you can now just get a handful of stadium owners to ensure that an entire person’s career can be jeopardised.”

Ultimately, now, the only acceptable thing to say is nothing: there is no statement mild enough about Israel and Palestine that can be made on a stage to a general audience. Even to wish for a world in which children aren’t killed is too political, and even the Sheeran fix – that there’s a lot of pain on both sides – which might or might not have been devised to soothe billionaire interests, does not meet their preference. They would simply prefer that everyone pretend the situation doesn’t exist, that they’ve never heard of it, that nothing has happened, and if anything ever had, they wouldn’t be able to find it on a map. The slippery slope argument, that an enforced public silence could spread to protests against datacentres next, is plausible but unnecessary: we don’t need this censorship to get worse before we take it seriously.

Take good care of your tailbone. I didn’t – and my derriere has never been the same since

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:00:46 GMT

My coccyx still hurts from an extreme cycling challenge almost two decades ago. Is there anything it’s good for?

‘Welcome to middle age.” This is what my GP said to me 10 years ago when I asked her why I needed this pill or that. Being then just shy of 50, that hit home. Now being just shy of 60, I mutter those words to myself at least once a day. There’s a long list of aches, pains and assorted maladies about which to mutter. High up on that list are my shoulders. Bloody agony, both of them. Picking something off a high shelf or fishing for something on the back seat of the car have had to become planned events to be undertaken only if absolutely necessary.

I interviewed Prof Alice Roberts this week. A writer, broadcaster, academic, anatomist, archaeologist and sometime medical doctor, she knows her bones, and no mistake. I noted with interest that her PhD thesis was titled “Rotator cuff disease in humans and apes: a palaeopathological and evolutionary perspective on shoulder pathology”. I’ve rarely felt so connected with my ancestors, so human, and indeed so ape-like. In an instant my shoulder pain became easier to bear, as I felt at one with a caveman wincing as he reached up to apply the finishing touches to some wall art.

After the radio show I was full of regret that I didn’t get time to ask her about another bone with which I’ve had my troubles: the coccyx. Mine has not been the same since I did some extreme cycling for Sport Relief with Alan Shearer 18 years ago. To this day, every so often if I sit wrong, I get a very nasty kind of electric shock shooting up from my derriere.

When I asked Roberts later about matters of the coccyx, she didn’t disappoint. As it happens, she, too, has had coccyx problems, damaging hers when she fell off a table on which she was dancing. Impressive. As, predictably, is her knowledge of this area. She told me the coccyx consists of tiny, fused vertebrae that finish off your vertebral column at the bottom, or rather, in the bottom. Given that this remnant of a tailbone can’t be wagged, you may wonder if there’s any point to this little pointy thing. Well, without it there would be nothing to attach the pelvic floor muscles to, at the back. And that, she said, would result in your pelvic viscera falling out, which sounds awful. So look after your coccyx, at all costs.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

How’s your apocalypse stockpiling coming on? Three weeks in, mine has hit a few snags

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 08:00:43 GMT

Cans of tuna, sparkling water and an old torch – if the end of the world came for me now I’d struggle, but it’s hard to know how to prepare for an unknown threat

It’s been three weeks since the government advisory urging us to start stockpiling in case of emergency – how’s your prep coming along? The Prepare campaign, backed by Wes Streeting, who one imagines gliding through the apocalypse, quiff undisturbed, listed nine essential items, among them wet wipes, first-aid kits and batteries. The World Health Organization, meanwhile, suggests budgeting for 15 litres of water per person per day, so a family of four will need to store upwards of 180 litres to cover the recommended period of three days. The chances of this actually happening seem to me, intuitively, to be considerably lower than the disaster they’re supposed to forestall. But hope springs, so let’s see.

The first step towards stockpiling is stocktaking. This is where I’m at: one mega-torch (uncharged), which I bought in prepper mode after surviving the terrifying New York blackout of 2019 when for about an hour we couldn’t charge our phones; lots of very large sticking plasters and a handful of small round ones, the normal sizes having long been used up; two cans of tuna, which will go down to one after lunch; two litres of sparkling water, so for the first hour or so after a nuclear strike, assuming it happens this afternoon, we’ll at least be able to enjoy some bubbles; and three OxyContin saved from my c-section almost 12 years ago, which are probably less powerful than homeopathy at this point but I retain a vague hope I can use for barter when money breaks down.

In other words, I’m not really prepared and the biggest deficit in my unpreparedness is, evidently, my attitude. On the evidence of what appeared to be a collective shrug, recently, when we were informed of the threats posed by AI, it’s an attitude problem that’s widely shared. It’s not that we don’t care, perhaps, but that it is hard to know what to do. By which I mean, it’s hard to know what to do that doesn’t involve giving over precious closet space to 40 two-litre bottles of water or disrupting our thought patterns to accommodate large, uncomfortable truths.

In other words, if this is a collective failure of imagination, then what’s needed is some rigorous thought experiments that address our inability to imagine the worst. It’s wild that this should be necessary six years after a global pandemic, but of course, if there’s one thing to be said about humankind, it’s our ability to go scorched earth on recent trauma and pretend like nothing ever happened. This is called resilience – and there are, I’m sure, good evolutionary reasons for it, yet in this case it’s unhelpful. From scratch, then, we must develop what the government calls “household resilience”, which in my house means learning not to go into meltdown when someone can’t find their favourite hoodie or we run out of Nutella, or the Russians aim a missile towards our area.

With this in mind, I would recommend browsing something called the local resilience forum, made up of regional lists of potential threats starting with “nuclear attack by a state on the UK mainland”, working down through pandemics, biblical droughts, floods, and the collapse of the National Grid, all the way to the threat posed by “space weather”. It’s very When the Wind Blows, and if it’s hard to square with real world scenarios, I suspect it’s because when you put something in local government language and stick it in a table, any sense of threat collapses beneath the sheer weight of boredom.

For real imaginative engagement, we must turn to the fiction writers. The scene I go to in my head is the opening pages of Emily St John Mandel’s Station Eleven, in which a character called Jeevan, tipped off by a doctor friend that a pandemic is coming that will kill 99% of the world’s population, runs to a supermarket, shackles seven big shopping carts together and buys enough food and water to barricade himself in his apartment for 58 days, until the first panic has passed.

So, as long as Tesco is open and I can beat the rush, perhaps things will work out just fine? I know there are some walnuts at the back of the cupboard. We could take the batteries out of the remote to use in the torch. Per The Day After Tomorrow, I have plenty of books for firewood, and worst-case scenario, can wear the cats for extra warmth. And while water is a problem, I think about that couple who survived in a tiny boat in the middle of the Pacific for 118 days, and imagine we will figure it out. I can catch the drips from the freezer as it defrosts and suck the gel from the aloe vera. See? Already thinking like a survivor. We’ve got this!

Raheem Sterling’s bleak tale a reminder of absurd path young footballers face

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 07:00:42 GMT

Winger was one of the first big-money academy transfers, part of a child labour market that has barely been questioned

“What’s your name?”

“Raheem.”

“What’s your surname?”

“Sterling.”

This is how a story ends. At 9.13 on a glorious May morning, by the side of the A327, sitting in the passenger seat of a wrecked Lamborghini, feverishly stashing canisters of nitrous oxide into the back, having to recite one’s name from scratch. A police officer asks him who was driving the car at the time it smashed into a metal pole on a country road in Hampshire. Sterling says nothing. There’s nobody sitting in the driver’s seat.

As it transpired in court in Basingstoke this week, Sterling had been up driving all night by the time police started getting calls from members of the public concerned that someone was bobbing and weaving up the M3 in an unpredictable, uncontrollable manner. And of course there is an acrid and tasteless irony in the fact that this was exactly what Sterling was known for on the pitch: weaving in and out of traffic, no order or reason to it, following a logic that existed only in his own head.

We can, and we should, and the district judge did, take an extremely dim view of the serious and life-threatening crime to which Sterling has admitted. We can also acknowledge that football is the one and only reason any of this remotely registered on our radar. You are not angry at the other dangerous drivers, whose names you do not know and will never look up. You are angry at this one in particular, a £50m footballer four years ago, now facing the possibility of prison and a sporting career that may just have come to a hard stop at the age of 31.

Yep: younger than Kepa Arrizabalaga, younger than Solly March, younger than Ariana Grande. And let’s be real, the end of Sterling as a going concern really happened much earlier, about the time his Arsenal loan deal ended and Enzo Maresca made clear he had no further use for him at Chelsea and he was made to train on his own after 8pm despite having young children, and Maresca said this was no big deal, because people in the fishing industry also work hard hours.

In a way, Sterling became a victim of the cycle he helped to catalyse. At the age of 15, he became one of the first big-money academy transfers when he moved from Queens Park Rangers to Liverpool for a fee of up to £2m. More than a decade on, the increasing emphasis on one‑on‑one duels, on straight-line speed and dynamic dribbling, on unpredictable and unmapped movement, has generated a kind of fetish for unscarred teenage footballers, a self-perpetuating market in child labour that nobody has ever really begun to question, much less challenge.

The Premier League’s centre of gravity has been shifting younger for years, to the point where last season half its players were 25 or younger. The three youngest Premier League debuts (Jeremy Monga, Max Dowman, Ethan Nwaneri) have taken place since 2022. Farther afield players such as Lamine Yamal (La Liga debut at 15) and Cavan Sullivan (Major League Soccer debut at 14) have begun to normalise the trope of the child footballer, the athlete propelled to global superstardom before they can legally buy a vape.

This week it has been widely reported that JJ Gabriel, a talented and highly coveted 15-year-old attacking midfielder, has demanded to leave the Manchester United academy. Let’s assume for the sake of argument that Gabriel didn’t walk into the offices of the Daily Telegraph and plant this story himself. So what we really have here, in essence, is an entire locus of gossip – briefings, counter-briefings, whispers, internet spume, back-page splashes – centred on a child.

And before we even get into the myriad safeguarding issues, it’s worth reflecting on the financial incentives involved here. As scouting networks broaden and deepen, as clubs increasingly remodel themselves as trading vehicles, the premium on exclusive young talent has become unignorable. Should Gabriel leave United he will undoubtedly have his pick of Europe’s top clubs.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Players and their representatives have also begun to recognise their rarefied value in this market. In a previous era Michael Carrick might have had the luxury of integrating Gabriel gradually into the United first team, taking a long-term view of his development, much as Mikel Arteta has done with Dowman at Arsenal. But of course if Lamine Yamal is playing first-team football at 15, then why not JJ Gabriel? If every big club in Europe is looking for the next big star, then who ultimately holds the power in this relationship: the kid or one of the biggest football clubs in the world?

And this is absurd, and it is intentionally absurd, and it is no defence of Sterling’s subsequent actions to point out that this is basically a ridiculous path upon which to dispatch a human being: festooned with unimaginable riches as a teenager, placed at the very centre of things, cast on to the scrap heap by 29. This is an unbelievably weird life, one that starts so wildly and violently beyond the boundaries of normative society that it’s a wonder anyone manages to stay remotely sane within it.

The life-changing money, the scrutiny, the lack of privacy, the intermediaries and handlers, the winnowing of trust, the noise beyond the windows, the strangers demanding a piece of you, at a time when – remember – you are still a child and this entire lifestyle has been sold to you as the ultimate aspiration. Remember, you’re supporting the whole family now. Gabriel’s original surname, taken from his father and agent, was reportedly changed from O’Cearuill to Gabriel because it was easier to pronounce and therefore more marketable.

I guess the point here is that nobody has as much agency over their career as they might like. The young modern footballer exists at the mercy of forces barely within their control. Their job is contingent on so many others: the coaches who train their skills, the medical staff who manage their workload, the teammates who pass to them, the support network that might just dissuade them from getting into a car with a load of nitrous oxide balloons in the early hours of the morning.

And by any measure, Sterling is one of the lucky ones. The teenager who made it, who scaled the peaks, won 82 international caps, four league titles, worked under one of the greatest managers of all time, who tasted the manna even if it eventually choked him. How many other thousands of lives you will never see have been fruitlessly and callously bent and twisted towards this world: skills you will never witness, names you will never hear? How much humanity are we prepared to fling into this machine in order for it to provide us with entertainment?

Perhaps in the post-Ronaldo/Messi era we are beginning to shake the idea that great individual players can bend the arc of history to their will, a fallacy we may as well call the Ballon d’Or Industrial Complex. Injuries, circumstance, tactical trends, physical shifts, the inevitability of time and tide: these are the handmaidens of talent, its trade winds, its lucky charms. Gaze at any footballing prodigy from afar and you’ll see a seductive blur of gift and privilege. But look closely enough and you’ll notice that the driver’s seat is empty.

Driving that’s too fast, too dangerous and utterly lawless: why do we tolerate this petro-masculinity?

The Guardian Thu, 17 Sep 2026 05:00:40 GMT

In towns and in the countryside, I see SUVs and pickup trucks driven without care or conscience. It’s the Magafication of transport

Where is lawbreaking not just visible, but designed to be seen? Where is antisocial behaviour worn as a badge of honour? Where is pleasure gained directly from causing distress? And where is reckless endangerment often ignored by the police or treated with the mildest of punishments? The answer is on the roads.

Last month, three men in the West Midlands were convicted of street racing. Two were driving at over 80mph in a 40mph zone. The third clocked over 90mph in a 30mph zone. The West Midlands has long been blighted by organised racing, sometimes involving 200 cars or more and hundreds of spectators. The result is a long catalogue of deaths and life-changing injuries, including some caused when racers have left the road and ploughed into onlookers or pedestrians. And there are plenty more accidents where the police have little idea whether racing is to blame, for as soon as they happen, the drivers disperse.

The West Midlands is one of the few places in the UK where the police are actively trying to stop antisocial driving. An injunction bans street racing and dangerous tricks such as “drifting” (long sideways skids) and “doughnutting” (making the car spin on the spot). The local police commissioner has warned that reckless drivers “will face the full force of the law … including seizure of your vehicle and imprisonment”. But are the courts listening?

Of the three men convicted at Birmingham magistrates court, one received a suspended sentence, a £272 fine, 150 hours of community work and a two-year driving ban. Another was handed a £1,275 fine and seven penalty points: in other words, he could step out of the court and back into his car. The man who did over 90mph in a 30mph zone got a £253 fine and a 56-day driving ban. He’ll be back on the roads in November. All appear to have kept their cars.

If these men had caused the same level of endangerment by any other means, it’s hard to believe they would have got off so lightly. But in dozens of ways, driving gets special treatment.

There’s a similar racing culture in mid-Wales, where I lived until 2012. Night after night, a convoy of cars with exhausts modified to be as loud as possible would race past, at 50mph or more in a 30mph zone. They would start at around 10pm and continue some nights until 2am, going round the nearby roads in a loop. As soon as I’d got my infant daughter to sleep, they’d roar past and wake her up again.

Calls to the police were useless: they told me to take down the number plates and “report the incident”. When I did so, they explained, in effect, that I was wasting my time, as I couldn’t prove the drivers were breaking the speed limit. In fact, their advice was counterproductive: when I went outside to take down the number plates, the young men jeered, gave me the finger and accelerated. It seemed that shock and disgust was what they craved. And this was before TikTok, where drivers can achieve much wider notoriety.

The first young man to “do a ton” (100mph) down my high street in Wales on his motorbike became a local hero. Soon afterwards, he rode into a wall and died. Other drivers killed their passengers, hit pedestrians or forced other cars off the road. When people were killed or injured, the drivers were prosecuted and lightly punished, but there was little effort to address the underlying culture. Some men went straight back into the convoys when they regained their licences. I’m told that nothing has changed, despite the default 20mph speed limit now applied to residential areas across Wales, and that every year a new cohort of young men joins the local urban racetrack.

Now I live in Devon, where there’s a different culture of antisocial driving. Here it’s mostly middle-aged men in “lifted” pickup trucks, which have been modified to be as loud and smoky as possible. Two local SUVs have been refitted to “roll coal” from twin exhaust towers mounted behind the cab, releasing a dense black cloud of soot when the driver hits the “smoke switch”. Adapting your truck for this purpose means buying a “delete kit” to bypass the vehicle’s emissions control system, retuning the engine and fitting bigger injectors. The practice emerged in the US, both as an anti-environmental protest and as a form of amusement. It is largely deployed against cyclists, pedestrians and electric vehicles. I’ve seen these two trucks doing it, blinding the drivers behind and choking everyone around. Of course it’s illegal. But it doesn’t seem to be a priority for the police in my area.

What we see here are manifestations of petro-masculinity: a violent, misogynistic, climate-denying version of manhood, expressed through an antisocial driving culture. Some of the modified trucks have decals saying “Stop the Boats” or “Save Our Children” (who are apparently being brainwashed by LGBTQ+ cultural Marxists). This is the Magafication of transport – a vehicle that carries some of the worst aspects of US culture and politics into the UK.

It’s the extreme end of a much wider trend. In the UK last year, 52% of the new cars on sale were SUVs. Not only do the ever-rising bonnets of these trucks make it harder for drivers to see pedestrians and cyclists, especially children, but higher and heavier cars are also more likely to cause deaths or serious injuries when they hit people: children under nine are three times more likely to be killed if they’re hit by an SUV than by a regular car.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And what are they for? On narrow country lanes round here, tourists in these “off-road” vehicles won’t back up if it means touching a hedge, in case the high-gloss finish on their Wankpanzer Childkiller SUV gets scratched. In one of the poshest parts of London, the Chelsea Truck Company advertises “iconic urban 4x4s”. “Iconic” appears to mean huge. But what the hell is an “urban 4x4”? And why is it legal?

Isn’t it obvious that selfishness on the road changes us as a society? The belief that a driver should be allowed to do whatever they please, regardless of the impact on others, mounts the pavement and travels deep into our lives. If this is to be a decent, inclusive country that values human life, then the law and its enforcement should match that aspiration. But when the roads are used to amplify and celebrate a dangerous, antisocial culture, we are driven towards a very dark place.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

A Provocative Streamer Creates Headaches for El-Sayed in Key Senate Race

The New York Times September 17, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Under pressure, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan this week rejected Hasan Piker’s argument that the U. S. has caused more terror than Al Qaeda.

By Tim Balk

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s pivotal Senate race, has labored for weeks to push past criticism of his relationship with Hasan Piker, a provocative streamer who campaigned with him during the primary.

Dr. El-Sayed has said that he disagrees with Mr. Piker on “many, many things,” and that he doesn’t plan to campaign with him this fall. But he has resisted calls to disavow Mr. Piker more fully.

This week, some of those calls grew, after Mr. Piker said the United States had caused more terror than the group that orchestrated the Sept. 11 attacks. Dr. El-Sayed swiftly rejected the assertion. And Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, issued a statement saying that “enough is enough” and called on Dr. El-Sayed to “condemn Piker once and for all.”

It was the latest episode to underscore the challenge Mr. Piker poses for Dr. El-Sayed, whose race could decide control of the Senate. Mr. Piker, who has a huge, young audience, has sway with the sorts of progressives who powered Dr. El-Sayed’s populist primary campaign. But other Democrats, who say they are appalled by some of Mr. Piker’s criticism of the United States and Israel, have pressured Dr. El-Sayed to go further and fully disavow Mr. Piker. And Mr. Rogers has used Mr. Piker’s incendiary commentary to cast Dr. El-Sayed as outside the mainstream and even un-American.

Dr. El-Sayed has said he campaigned with Mr. Piker during the primary because he wanted to reach Mr. Piker’s audience, which Dr. El-Sayed says is alienated from the political process. He has been repeatedly called to answer for Mr. Piker’s most provocative statements.

The latest came in an interview with Axios on Wednesday. Mr. Piker was asked if he continued to believe the United States was the “top dog” in terrorism, a view he has expressed over the years. The interviewer also asked if Mr. Piker believed the country was responsible for more terror than Al Qaeda, which planned the attacks that killed 2,977 people on Sept. 11, 2001.

“Pound for pound, as far as the number of deaths, yes,” Mr. Piker told Axios. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.”

Dr. El-Sayed disagreed.

“I do not agree with this statement, nor do I give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer,” Dr. El-Sayed said in a statement, adding that he was more focused on the price of gas, groceries and health care. “As I have said, this campaign speaks for itself.”

In a text message, Mr. Piker wrote that “mainstream outlets focus far too much on me as a way to attack” Dr. El-Sayed. He said he was “totally independent” from Dr. El-Sayed and his campaign. On social media, Mr. Piker also defended his comments to Axios, saying that he had given a “nuanced answer.”

In the Axios interview, Mr. Piker pointed to a U. S. strike that hit an elementary school in Iran in February. Iranian officials have said the death toll was at least 175 people, most of them children. A preliminary U. S. investigation determined that the strike on the school was the result of a targeting mistake.

“If you’re killing 140 schoolgirls, that is an act of terror,” Mr. Piker said. “This doesn’t mean that all Americans are terrorists. But the reality of the matter is we have to create an environment of accountability to ensure things like that never happen again.”

Mr. Piker has long criticized America’s engagement in wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, in which hundreds of thousands of civilians died, calling the conflicts “devastating.”

The race between Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Rogers, a former congressman and an ally of President Trump, is seen as one of a handful competitive races that could determine Senate control.

For weeks, Mr. Rogers has attacked Dr. El-Sayed over his ties to Mr. Piker.

Dr. El-Sayed campaigned with Mr. Piker in April at rallies on two college campuses. The two also appeared together in final days of the primary race in August, with Mr. Piker joining Dr. El-Sayed’s primary night party in Detroit. Dr. El-Sayed has repeatedly said he has no plans to campaign with Mr. Piker in the general election.

Jewish Democrats, in particular, have been pushing Dr. El-Sayed to disavow to Mr. Piker more forcefully. Mr. Piker is a fierce critic of Israel and has called the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, the “direct consequence” of actions by the Israeli and U. S. governments.

A group of Jewish voters in Michigan issued a letter on Wednesday urging support for Dr. El-Sayed. But other Jewish voters have said they are uneasy about his ties to Mr. Piker, and the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus has not endorsed him.

At a debate on Tuesday that Mr. Rogers did not attend, Dr. El-Sayed said he disagreed with many of Mr. Piker’s positions, citing, among other things, “his ridiculous comments about 9/11.” But, he said, “I resist the idea that we should play this cancel culture gotcha game that tells us who we can’t talk to.”

In the past, Mr. Piker said the United States “deserved” the Sept. 11 attacks. He later apologized.

The New York Times September 17, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

The health secretary spoke at a conference featuring misinformation about vaccines, including a claim that the success of the polio vaccines was a “fraud.”

By Christina Jewett and Teddy Rosenbluth

Reporting from Washington

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday told members of the anti-vaccine group he founded that they had “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House” and that he would “die with my boots on” pursuing answers about the risks of vaccines.

His remarks, to a convention of Children’s Health Defense, signaled a notable shift from earlier this year when White House officials and political advisers had pushed Mr. Kennedy to sidestep the vaccine issue, given widespread support among voters for protecting children against deadly diseases. They came just one day after President Trump’s nominee for surgeon general, Dr. Nicole Saphier, gave a full-throated defense of the safety and efficacy of vaccines during her Senate confirmation hearing.

But Mr. Kennedy, after spending the first part of his speech on the far more politically popular topics of food safety and nutrition, plunged headlong into vaccines, in a conference riddled with misinformation and references to discredited studies.

The speaker before Mr. Kennedy was Mark Gorton, the president of the MAHA Institute, who called the success of the polio vaccine a “fraud,” priming the audience for the remarks of their former leader, who railed against vaccines for two decades. The speaker after him was Andrew Wakefield, a discredited British doctor whose retracted paper linked the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine with autism. Decades of research have proved that finding to be wrong.

With the midterm elections less than two months away and Republicans struggling in the polls, Mr. Kennedy has been trying to rally followers of his Make America Healthy Again movement, some of whom have expressed impatience with the pace of his policy changes.

He promised the crowd that he would “be in this fight” to the end, and said the work he was doing was methodical. He added that his team was launching studies after which, he said, “we will take appropriate action.”

He also generated applause when he announced that he would be looking at the health effects of electromagnetic radiation and so-called chemtrails, the trails left by airplanes that the Environmental Protection Agency has said are actually condensation, not chemicals.

Despite worries from his political advisers, Mr. Trump himself has recently jumped into the vaccine debate. Last month he signed an executive order that called for limiting the number of vaccines given to children. In a White House signing ceremony filled with misinformation, he falsely described the measles shot as “lethal.” Under persistent questioning, Dr. Mehmet Oz, one of the administration’s top health officials, corrected the president’s statement in an interview on CBS’s “Face the Nation”: “The M. M. R. vaccine is not a lethal vaccine.”

The support from the president appears to have emboldened Mr. Kennedy to play a star role at the Washington conference of his former nonprofit.

Mr. Kennedy was absent from the group’s conference in Texas last year when Mr. Gorton, whose group works to advance Mr. Kennedy’s agenda, exhorted the crowd of about 1,000 “to be more boldly anti-vax. ” On Thursday, Mr. Gorton said that “the success of the polio vaccine was a massive medical fraud” and that widespread vaccination was a “public health disaster.” He received a standing ovation.

Mr. Kennedy spoke next, linking arms with the group even as measles cases continue to rise, surpassing a 35-year record with about 3,300 cases. Officials in Pennsylvania reported a fourth measles death this week, adding an 18-year-old to a list that included two infants and a woman who was 40. The adults were both unvaccinated, and the infants were too young to receive the vaccine.

After the announcement of the first deaths, Mr. Kennedy publicly questioned whether measles played a role and suggested the deaths may have been “fabricated.” The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which he oversees, has refused to acknowledge them and is currently reporting no measles deaths for 2026.

Mr. Kennedy’s appearance at the conference sparked a fresh round of criticism from Josh Shapiro, the governor of Pennsylvania, who he had sparred with Mr. Kennedy in recent days over the measles death reports.

“In the midst of the largest and deadliest measles outbreak in America in 35 years, RFK Jr. chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America,” Mr. Shapiro said in a social media post. “He needed to say one sentence: I urge all Americans to get the measles vaccine now to protect themselves and their families during this deadly outbreak.”

In his speech, Mr. Kennedy also discussed his administration’s effort to require more information about minimally tested chemicals and additives to food. He said they are likely linked to health problems in children.

“That has to be one of the culprits,” he said. “And we know that many of those foods are associated with obesity, with neurological disorders, with A. D. H. D. and many, many of these other injuries.”

About 290 people attended the conference in person at the Grand Hyatt in Washington, and another 230 streamed it online, according to a Children’s Health Defense spokesman.

Children’s Health Defense also focuses on toxic exposures, such as from pesticides, and radiation exposure from cell towers, cellphones and other devices. But much of its advocacy centers on vaccines.

Mary Holland, the chief executive of the group, testified in New Hampshire earlier this year in favor of eliminating requirements for children to be vaccinated before starting school, a widely popular measure. That bill and others aimed at vaccine requirements for school entry did not pass.

At the start of the one-day conference, Michael Kane, the director of advocacy for Children’s Health Defense, marveled at Mr. Trump’s show of support for parental and religious rights, often invoked to refuse vaccination.

“When have we ever seen a president take on vaccine reform like this?” he asked. “Never. It has never ever happened.”

He added: “Just a few years ago, we were the hated stepchild in the corner. It was hard for us to get anything to happen. Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.”

Christina Jewett covers the Food and Drug Administration, which means keeping a close eye on drugs, medical devices, food safety and tobacco policy.

Teddy Rosenbluth is a Times reporter covering health news, with a special focus on medical misinformation.

To a Binational Tribe, Trump’s Border Wall Feels Like Betrayal

The New York Times September 17, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

An escalating confrontation on Native land southwest of Tucson threatens to upend decades of uneasy cooperation between the Tohono O’odham Nation and the United States.

An escalating confrontation on Native land southwest of Tucson threatens to upend decades of uneasy cooperation between the Tohono O’odham Nation and the United States.

“It’s like me bulldozing right through the Arlington Cemetery,” said Verlon Jose, the chairman of the Tohono O’odham Nation. Credit...

Supported by

By Reis Thebault

Visuals by Anna Watts

Reis Thebault and Anna Watts reported from the Tohono O’odham Nation and Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. They traveled nearly the entire length of the tribal reservation’s 62-mile border with Mexico.

The first fence to slice through the Tohono O’odham Nation was simple barbed wire meant to keep cows from roaming south into Mexico. The second, which rose nearly a century later, was a sturdier steel barricade that stopped smuggler trucks from barreling north into the United States.

The binational tribe, whose land stretches from modern-day Arizona into the Mexican state of Sonora, has long been caught in the middle of disputes over a border between two countries that did not exist when the O’odham’s ancestors first settled here thousands of years ago.

The tribe’s leaders have adapted, working with the American government as it ratcheted up immigration security on their territory. But now they are facing the biggest wall yet, and they are drawing a line.
