The New York Times

The Trump administration wants to build a towering 62-mile barrier that would bisect the Tohono O’odham homeland along the international boundary with Mexico, and construction could begin as soon as October. Leaders of the Native American nation say it will restrict member movement, endanger wildlife, destroy sacred burial sites and undermine tribal sovereignty while doing little to tamp down illegal activity.

“It’s like me bulldozing right through the Arlington Cemetery,” said Verlon Jose, the chairman of the Tohono O’odham Nation. “We don’t matter to the U. S. government. They want to erase us. They want to take our land, they want to desecrate it, they want to hit us where it hurts.”

The tribe has sued to prevent construction, but the federal government is pushing ahead as it seeks to wall off most of the southern frontier. Last month, masked and armed Border Patrol agents escorted a group of contractors through the reservation to do survey work at the planned wall site. O’odham leaders accused the workers of trespassing.

It is one of many battles simmering along the southern border, where President Trump’s wall has drawn bipartisan outrage in national parks, on private ranches and among environmentalists and Catholic priests. But this escalating confrontation on Native land southwest of Tucson stands out because it upends decades of uneasy cooperation between the tribe and the United States.

The Tohono O’odham Nation, which occupies a reservation roughly the size of Connecticut, has for years allowed federal immigration authorities to operate bases and surveillance towers on its land. The tribe spends $3 million a year on border security, and its police force works closely with Border Patrol agents.

“We’ve bent over backwards to work with the federal government,” Mr. Jose said. “But we will never agree to a wall.”

During Mr. Trump’s first term, the tribe successfully lobbied against a wall. But since Mr. Trump’s re-election, O’odham leaders say they have found federal officials unwilling to compromise.

The administration, which has waived environmental reviews to speed wall construction, has argued that the tribe’s vast and varied territory is a hot spot for cartel-sponsored crime.

“The project will close one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border,” Rodney Scott, the U. S. Customs and Border Protection commissioner, said in a statement.

The Tohono O’odham, whose enrolled members number near 40,000, have long moved freely among the Sonoran Desert’s sky-scraping saguaros, Seussian ocotillos, herds of javelina and packs of coyotes.

In the 1850s, the Gadsden Purchase divided O’odham land nearly in half as a new boundary was drawn between the United States and Mexico. Today, Mexico is home to some 2,000 tribal members, as well as ancestral cemeteries and ceremony sites. But to cross, the O’odham must call a Border Patrol agent, who then checks documentation and unlocks one of three gates along the existing barrier.

Illegal immigration and drug smuggling through the reservation surged in the 1990s, raising fears among tribal members and prompting O’odham leaders to increase collaboration with Border Patrol.

“We’ve been homeland security,” Mr. Jose said. “We care about who’s coming through our borders.”

The tribe now says the federal government has betrayed that partnership. If the C. B. P. proceeds, Mr. Jose said the O’odham could seek to cancel leases allowing the agency’s offices and towers on the reservation.

The tribe sued in June, claiming the wall would illegally reduce the size of its reservation without congressional approval. Its lawyers asked for an emergency court order to stop construction. Last month, a federal judge denied the request, writing that the government’s security needs outweighed the O’odham’s concerns. The tribe is appealing.

Critical to the court challenge is a 60-foot-wide ribbon of federal land that runs along the border from California to New Mexico, known as the Roosevelt Reservation, where the Trump administration has claimed broad authority to build walls.

The tribe argues both that its borderland is exempt from the Roosevelt Reservation and that wall construction would inevitably spill beyond the strip.

A few feet from the border fence, a group of O’odham members has been tending a fire of creosote branches for weeks while praying for a halt to the wall construction. Tribal members at the prayer camp said the idea that C. B. P. would listen to them was far-fetched.

“We don’t trust the government,” said Wynona P. Larson Yazzie, a Marine Corps veteran who lives a few miles from the border.

Some see the dispute as a continuation of abuse and exploitation that dates back to Spanish colonization of the area.

“It’s just opening old wounds again,” said Samuel Fayuant, a cultural affairs specialist with the tribe. “They have never healed. It just continues and continues, and I don’t know if it’s ever going to stop.”

If the tribe loses in court, many members have said they would put their bodies on the line to stop a wall, citing the massive protests in support of the Standing Rock Sioux’s fight against an oil pipeline in 2016.

The tribe also has concerns about construction outside the reservation. In nearby Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, where C. B. P. built a wall during the last Trump administration, it is now building a second barrier that will run parallel to the first.

Bulldozers have already begun clearing miles of desert to make way for construction, and the tribe is worried the work will wreak havoc on a sacred site known as Quitobaquito Springs.

The spring, a rare desert oasis, hosts three endangered species — a fish, a turtle and a snail — and was long the site of religious rites for the Hia-C’ed O’odham, a band of Tohono O’odham.

“Quitobaquito is the aquatic, biological gem of that broader desert landscape,” said Russ McSpadden, a conservation advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. Because the Trump administration waived environmental laws, “contractors are pretty much working blind,” he said.

C. B. P. conducts cultural and environmental reviews before construction and hires monitors to oversee the contractors, said Hilton Beckham, an assistant commissioner at the agency.

Illegal immigration also threatens the environment, she said, when border crossers leave “trash, pollution and damage to natural resources.” Ms. Beckham said construction would “avoid Quitobaquito Springs and minimize impacts to sensitive resources.”

But activists and tribe members say the government has a poor track record. Six years ago, border wall construction in the area unearthed human remains and destroyed protected saguaros. In April, contractors plowed through a 1,000-year-old O’odham archaeological site.

Lorraine Marquez Eiler, whose great-grandparents lived near Quitobaquito Springs, fears the cherished place will not survive a second wall. “How much more damage can it take?” she said.

The atmosphere around the reservation is tense these days. On a recent afternoon, Mr. Jose was driving along the planned wall site to monitor construction preparation when a Border Patrol agent flashed his lights and swerved his truck in front of the chairman’s S. U. V.

“Why are you stopping me?” Mr. Jose demanded.

“I’m trying to get your attention,” the agent replied. He asked Mr. Jose to roll down his windows and identify the passengers in his car, saying he was checking for smugglers. “We don’t normally have a lot of vehicles coming down this way.”

Mr. Jose refused, saying: “This is my territory.”

The chairman fumed as he drove on, angry that a federal agent would accuse an O’odham leader of wrongdoing on his own land. Mr. Jose continued his survey until he reached a hill on the reservation’s eastern boundary.

Leaning on a dried saguaro rib for support, Mr. Jose walked to an overlook and gazed out. Far below, the old steel border fence faded into desert scrub, almost out of sight.

Bora Erden contributed reporting.

Reis Thebault is a Phoenix-based reporter for The Times, covering the American Southwest.

Kennedy Names New Members to Powerful Health Panel Whose Work He Has Blocked

The New York Times September 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Kennedy has repeatedly interfered with the work of the United States Preventive Services Task Force, whose recommendations guide insurance coverage for many Americans.

By Maggie Astor

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the appointments of eight new members on Thursday to a federal task force whose decisions affect health care access for most Americans, after more than a year of stymieing the panel’s work.

It is not yet clear when the panel, the United States Preventive Services Task Force, will convene with the new members, along with its eight existing ones. It has not met since March 2025.

The appointees were selected through an opaque process, during which officials at the Department of Health and Human Services refused to provide access to nomination and application materials, which were supposed to be available to the public.

The new members are Dr. Seth J. Corey, a pediatric hematologist-oncologist; Dr. Patrick K. Hunter, a pediatrician; Dr. Ronald P. Karlsberg, a cardiovascular expert; Dr. Venkatesh L. Murthy, also a cardiovascular expert; Stephen T. Parente, who works in health finance and is not a medical doctor; Dr. Goldie Stands-Over-Bull, a family medicine physician; Dr. Louis J. Wilson, a gastroenterology specialist; and Dr. Dennis W. Wulfeck, a diagnostic radiologist.

Members of the task force — normally experts in primary care and prevention — review scientific evidence for tests and medications to prevent conditions like cancer, diabetes and H. I. V., and make recommendations on how they should be used.

Those recommendations inform medical care for hundreds of millions of people, guiding when they get their first mammogram or colonoscopy, and whether they are screened for depression or osteoporosis. Because most insurers are required to cover services that the task force endorses, its recommendations also determine what care Americans can afford.

But the panel’s work has been hamstrung since the Supreme Court ruled in June 2025 that Mr. Kennedy could unilaterally remove its members and override its decisions. He has prevented it from meeting as scheduled four times, most recently this July. That has left the task force largely unable to make new recommendations or update old ones.

Mr. Kennedy also did not fill the vacancies left when the terms of a chairman and five other members expired months ago. (New members are typically chosen before their predecessors’ terms expire.) Then, in May, he fired the panel’s two remaining leaders, leaving eight of the normal 16 spots vacant.

Normally, those leaders would have helped the health department evaluate candidates to serve on the task force.

The selection process to fill the open seats officially began in April, when a Federal Register notice solicited nominations with a May deadline. When Mr. Kennedy postponed the panel’s latest meeting in July, Emily Hilliard, a spokeswoman for the health department, attributed the decision to “an unprecedented number of nominations received for Task Force membership” and said more time was needed to pick new members.

Materials on the nominees were supposed to be public. However, federal health officials did not make them available to The New York Times.

As directed by the Federal Register notice, a Times reporter sought access to the documents in person in June at the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, the health department branch that oversees the task force. She was turned away by Erica Moshtahedian, the AHRQ chief of staff, who said personal information like addresses and Social Security numbers had not yet been redacted.

Ms. Moshtahedian, Ms. Hilliard and other officials have not responded to repeated follow-up emails and calls since then.

The Times filed a lawsuit in August seeking the nomination documents. That followed Freedom of Information Act requests in June for the application materials, along with nominees’ names, the names of all people interviewed this year for membership on the task force, and recordings of the interviews.

Ms. Moshtahedian, Ms. Hilliard and Grace Davis Jamison, another spokeswoman for the health department, did not respond to a request for comment.

This is a breaking news article and will be updated.

Maggie Astor covers women’s health and the health effects of government policies for The Times.

Lawyers for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts told a federal judge on Thursday that the temporary closure of the center’s main building was urgently needed to protect the public after a five-foot section of plaster fell from the ceiling during a recent storm.

After the closure began on Tuesday, lawyers for a Democratic lawmaker from Ohio, Representative Joyce Beatty, accused the center of violating a judicial order that barred it from shutting down for a $257 million renovation project championed by President Trump.

The Justice Department pushed back on a request for an emergency hearing from lawyers for Ms. Beatty, an ex officio board member who is suing the center.

The department’s lawyers responded in a filing on Thursday. “There is no emergency caused by defendants’ temporary closure of the center,” they said, adding, “The only emergency is the risk to the public and the center’s employees and artists if it remained fully open without further safety assessment.”

The judge was expected to decide soon whether to grant the request for an emergency hearing on the center’s closure.

The Kennedy Center, in Washington, has been at the center of a legal and political maelstrom as Mr. Trump advocated its immediate closure and raged over a court decision that blocked his name, for a second time, from being affixed to the front of the building.

On social media this week, Mr. Trump threatened to cancel the renovation if an appeals court did not allow his name to be restored. He told reporters on Wednesday that the Trump administration deserved credit if it was going to commit to rescuing the center from physical and financial turmoil.

“The Trump administration should certainly have recognition,” he said. “Because, frankly, if we don’t do that it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down.”

Mr. Trump and the Justice Department have raised the prospect of demolition as an eventual necessity if the Kennedy Center is not renovated. Images captured by news photographers on Wednesday showed Mr. Trump, sitting aboard Air Force One, reviewing what appeared to be a rendering of the center being demolished — stoking fears that such a move could be a serious prospect.

In response, lawyers for Ms. Beatty asked Judge Christopher R. Cooper of Federal District Court in Washington on Thursday to “make crystal clear” that his previous order blocking the closure of the building also prohibits demolishing it.

The White House and the Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to requests for clarification on whether demolition of any part of the institution was being considered.

Matt Floca, the center’s executive director, has tried to calm such fears, saying in a video posted on social media this week that “this is not about demolition” but rather about safeguarding the building for the future. The video detailed what Mr. Floca has described as the center’s serious maintenance needs, including structural steel corroded by water infiltration and outdated stage equipment.

In a sworn declaration filed with Judge Cooper, Mr. Floca said the closure would last seven days, during which officials would evaluate the extent of the safety concerns. He said that other areas of the ceiling showed water damage, and that the possibility of extending the closure would be assessed on a “weekly basis.”

For months, Judge Cooper has assessed the legality of the Trump administration’s agenda at the Kennedy Center as Democratic lawmakers and historic preservation organizations have reacted furiously to his complete takeover of the institution.

The judge ruled in May that the Trump-allied board of the Kennedy Center had unlawfully renamed the arts institution after Mr. Trump, writing that only Congress — which dedicated the building to President Kennedy after his assassination — had the authority to do so. At the same time, the judge temporarily blocked the center’s plan to close for two years of renovations, reasoning that the board had not given the plan proper scrutiny.

The Next Gene-Editing Technology May Also Be the Oldest

The New York Times September 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Scientists have discovered a powerful gene-targeting system in viruses. Billions of years old, VIPR seems to predate CRISPR and may be even more powerful.

By Carl Zimmer

Over the past decade, the gene-editing technology known as CRISPR has become a familiar scientific tool, used to create lifesaving cures, make more productive crops, and even engineer allergy-free dogs.

But scientists didn’t invent CRISPR from scratch. They discovered it in bacteria and other microbes, which use it as a defense against invading viruses. On Thursday, scientists reported that they had found another gene-editing defense in nature, this one in viruses themselves.

This system, called VIPR, appears to be more than four billion years old, and it seems be the evolutionary ancestor of CRISPR, the researchers wrote in two papers published in Science.

It may prove to be the more powerful gene-editing tool, with certain advantages over CRISPR. VIPR seems able to target a wider variety of genetic sequences, allowing it to alter more of the genome.

And these molecules are smaller, making them potentially easier to deliver into cells.

“The incredibly small size of VIPR makes these systems transformative tools for genome engineering,” said Philip Kranzusch, a microbiologist at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the research.

Jennifer Doudna, a biochemist at the University of California, Berkeley, who is an author of the studies, shared the Nobel Prize in 2020 for harnessing the power of CRISPR. After that breakthrough, she began wondering how the natural version of the gene editor evolved.

“It had to come from somewhere,” she recalled thinking. “Maybe it was being used to do something else before, and maybe there’s still evidence of what it might have been doing.”

CRISPR is made up of proteins and RNA molecules that join together to shred viral genes. The RNA molecule consists of a sequence of building blocks that exactly matches the gene sequences of certain viruses.

The RNA locks on to viral genes, and the protein it has brought along cuts the DNA strand, disabling the virus.

Since the first CRISPR systems were discovered in the 1990s, scientists have found them in an ever-growing number of microbes.

By comparing their genes, scientists have gained insight into CRISPR’s evolution. In 2024, researchers concluded that the common ancestors of all living things carried CRISPR molecules.

But where did this DNA-shredding defense come from?

When biologists try looking back that far, the picture gets fuzzy. It’s like peering through a telescope: The farther away you look, the blurrier the stars become.

Two years ago, Peter Yoon, then a graduate student working with Dr. Doudna, set out to build a better telescope. Instead of examining CRISPR genes, he studied the molecules encoded by those genes.

A gene serves as a blueprint for a protein. When a gene mutates, the protein it encodes may also change — but sometimes, a gene mutation will have no effect. Its protein may still retain the same overall shape, even over billions of years.

The shape of a protein determines the chemical reactions it can carry out. Once a protein evolves to do something, it usually just keeps doing it. “Nature is very lazy,” said Dr. Yoon, who is now a member of the technical staff at Anthropic, the A. I. company.

Working with Kenneth Loi, a graduate student, Dr. Yoon sifted through 2.3 million proteins, finding hundreds that had resembled CRISPR molecules but were not part of that gene-editing systems in microbes.

No one had figured out what any of these CRISPR-like proteins were doing. But Dr. Yoon and Mr. Loi did discover one astonishing fact: Almost all of them came from viruses.

“It was a total inversion of what we were expecting,” Dr. Yoon said. CRISPR is a weapon that microbes like bacteria use against viruses. Now the scientists were finding viruses that seemed to carry a version of it themselves.

Dr. Kranzusch noted that this discovery would have been impossible just a few years ago. Artificial intelligence systems now allow scientists to uncover ancient connections between proteins that were hidden until now.

“It’s a beautiful demonstration of the power of these methods,” he said.

Dr. Yoon and his colleagues named these proteins VIPR and set out figuring out how they worked. That required running experiments on real viruses.

On their list of candidates, they noticed a strain that Dr. Doudna happened to have stored in her lab freezer for other experiments.

“We were so lucky,” Mr. Loi said. “We just thawed the virus and infected some cells and said, ‘Let’s just see what we find.’”

The infected cells made VIPR proteins, which then joined together with viral RNA molecules. And like CRISPR, these molecules targeted viral DNA, the researchers found.

While CRISPR proteins chop up genes, VIPR proteins wrap around them. The effect is the same: The targeted genes shut down.

Dr. Doudna and her students see in this biochemistry a weapon that viruses must be deploying against other viruses. “The whole thing starts to make sense,” she said. “This is some kind of ancient viral warfare.”

The idea is that when two viruses infect the same cell, they have to compete for control of the cell’s molecular machinery. A virus that carries VIPR genes can shut down its rival. The triumphant virus alone gets to replicate within the host.

Dr. Doudna and her colleagues propose that VIPR arose early in Earth’s history, well over four billion years ago. As viruses competed to infect the first microbes, they battled one another with gene-targeting molecules. That struggle continues today.

CRISPR arose from this viral weapon, the researchers suggest, when microbes seized the system for their own use. It’s fairly common for viral genes to accidentally wind up in the genomes of their hosts. (Our own DNA is rife with them.)

“You can imagine VIPR is a gun that viruses are pointing at each other,” Dr. Yoon said. “If the bacteria just steal that, it becomes an immune system.”

It remains to be seen if VIPR can be turned into a gene-editing tool. But its discovery has left scientists wondering if the long-running battle between viruses has produced other genetic weaponry not yet found.

“I would be very surprised if VIPR were the last unexpected targeting system we discover,” said Rafael Pinilla-Redondo, a virologist at the University of Copenhagen who was not involved in the studies.

Dr. Doudna said she felt humbled to think that an ancestor of gene-editing systems was sitting in her lab freezer for years: “It’s a great reminder of how little we still understand about biology.”

Carl Zimmer covers news about science for The Times and writes the Origins column.

Toxic Fracking Waste Bubbling Up in Ohio Is Becoming a Political Issue

The New York Times September 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Democratic candidate for governor backed restrictions on disposal of fracking wastewater around a hard-hit town, and called for a “thorough investigation” of the dangers.

By Quinn Glabicki

For years, Ohio has been a disposal destination for hundreds of millions of gallons of toxic wastewater produced by the fracking industry. The wastewater, which contains hazardous chemicals and radioactive material, is pumped deep underground into injection wells, where it’s supposed to stay.

But recently it has been bubbling up to the surface, raising fears about health risks and drinking water contamination. Now, as elections loom, the issue is gaining political traction.

On Thursday Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor in Ohio, pledged her support for a moratorium on this kind of fracking-wastewater disposal during a campaign stop in the town of Marietta, Ohio, where the water has been resurfacing, alarming the community.

The leaks are “destroying local businesses and potentially contaminating Marietta’s drinking water,” said Dr. Acton, a physician who formerly led the Ohio Department of Health. “This poses a serious threat to the safety and quality of life.”

Dr. Acton called for a three-year moratorium on permits for injection wells in Washington County, where Marietta is and a halt on further injection there while Ohio regulators conduct a “thorough investigation” on the effects of underground wastewater migration.

The announcement comes as residents, public officials and water-system administrators in the rural county have urged state leaders to halt the practice, which they say threatens the drinking water sources for 32,000 people. “In Marietta, we have a chance to prevent the worst from happening, and we need to act now,” Dr. Acton said Thursday, pointing to a potential billion-dollar cleanup.

In total, Ohio pumps about 1.4 billion gallons of wastewater underground each year, and as much as half of it comes from out of state, primarily from Pennsylvania.

Ohio has permitted more than 240 injection wells for the disposal of oil and gas waste statewide. By comparison, there are 19 such injection wells in Pennsylvania, and a few dozen in West Virginia, which also borders Ohio. The state became a destination for wastewater because decades ago it received permission from the federal government to regulate its own injection wells. As a result it’s easier to drill them in Ohio than in states where there is federal oversight, like Pennsylvania.

Washington County is home to 19 permitted injection wells, which is as many as the entire state of Pennsylvania. Over the past two years, 59 percent of the 562 million gallons of waste injected under the county came from out of state, according to state records reviewed by The New York Times.

Last year, the City of Marietta declared an emergency after state regulators approved two more injection wells just outside the city limits (a third proposed injection well nearby is pending). Local officials asked the state to halt injection within six miles of the city’s aquifer and to stop permitting new wells. By March, eight local water authorities in the county had also called for a moratorium.

“This is not an anti-energy position. It is a pro-drinking-water position,” said Susan Vessels, a Republican and the president of the Marietta City Council, appearing alongside Dr. Acton. Problems with fracking wastewater migrating to the surface have occurred in Oklahoma and Texas, with documented cases of water contamination.

Mike Chadsey, a spokesman for the Ohio Oil and Gas Association, said a three-year moratorium is “a broad response to issues currently being investigated on a site-specific basis,” adding that regulators already have “the authority to investigate, suspend operations and take corrective action when warranted.”

A campaign spokesman for Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy said Dr. Acton’s position is “hollow and can’t withstand scrutiny.”

Migrating fracking wastewater is also starting to affect natural gas wells in the region. When wastewater encroaches on gas wells, it can cause them to stop producing, according to Bob Wilson, who operates gas wells in the region and supplies a local utility, Knox Energy, with gas.

At least 50 of Mr. Wilson’s wells have been flooded by wastewater and no longer produce, he said, which is contributing to gas shortages at Knox.

In recent weeks, Knox has notified some residents that it will be “unable to provide reliable natural gas service,” and has urged them to seek alternate winter heating sources.

Quinn Glabicki is a climate reporter for The New York Times and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

A former superintendent in Joplin, Mo., is trying to apply what he learned to other shattered districts — and reckoning with the toll of the disaster on his own life.

C. J. Huff, former superintendent of the Joplin, Mo., schools. Credit... Eli Durst for The New York Times

Supported by

By Eve Fairbanks

The weather on May 22, 2011, was bright and cloudless in Joplin, Mo., ideal for a high school graduation. C. J. Huff, the superintendent of schools, had gotten to his office at 5:30 in the morning to put the finishing touches on his speech. That afternoon, the ceremony proceeded on a disciplined schedule, the way Huff liked it. He recalls walking out into the sunlight afterward, feeling relieved that graduation had gone smoothly.

In the parking lot, he heard a storm siren wailing. As he drove home, a meteorologist on the radio mentioned severe weather. But the sun was still above him. When he turned into his subdivision, though, he noticed something out of the ordinary, even physics-defying: A tree in the right of his field of view snapped in half, and the top part lifted away from the lower trunk and began to float in the air, like a leaf. He suddenly realized that a violent wind was rocking his car from the left. Just as he did, he felt the wind shift in the opposite direction. His windshield filled with grass and dirt.

A tornado was entering Joplin, a city of 50,000 people. Most of us imagine tornadoes as ominous but narrow funnels. This is not what the most dangerous ones look like. The Joplin tornado was a rain-wrapped wedge that expanded to a mile wide, making it hard to identify until it was nearly on you.

One resident, Callum Eldred, who had then just finished 10th grade, described it as the blackest thing he had ever seen — like a wall looming over his city, with what looked like “twigs coming out of the top of it.” The “twigs” were things like telephone poles, trees and bits of houses. “You don’t know what you’re looking at because you’ve never seen it before,” Eldred, now 32, told me recently, “like in a movie, when the Indians first see ships.”

The tornado touched down just southwest of Joplin, gathered steam, then carved a six-mile line straight through the city, its winds cresting above 200 miles an hour. It obliterated a hospital, crumpling steel beams like paper. It gobbled up nursing homes, churches, 500 businesses and nearly 7,500 houses, more than a third of the city’s housing stock. And it ultimately killed 161 people, making it the deadliest tornado in America in over half a century.

The intensity of a 200-mile-an-hour wind is not double what you would encounter if you stuck your head out the window of a vehicle traveling 100 miles per hour. When speed doubles, the force of wind quadruples, so that kind of tornado is not something humans or infrastructure experience in any other circumstance; nothing can really be built to withstand it.

At a bank, only the steel-and-concrete safe deposit vault was left upright. The rest of the building was blown clean away. Cars, manhole covers, even the hospital’s medevac helicopter turned to missiles; chairs embedded themselves in walls. The tornado scoured into the earth, tearing up asphalt. It dragged people out of their homes and ripped off their clothes, even their skin. About 30 minutes after it set down, it lifted. Thirty minutes after that, the sky was blue again.

Huff’s immediate instinct, once the storm passed, was to drive into town and take stock of the school buildings. Joplin High School’s principal, Kerry Sachetta, had that impulse, too. “The gym was exploded,” Sachetta recalled. “The performing arts center was exploded.” On the sports field, “it looked like God and the angels shot down splintered two-by-fours, like you see arrows coming down in movies set in medieval times.” Trees were sawed off. Tangled power lines were sparking all over. “It was like Armageddon,” Sachetta said. The sharp pine scent of cracked timber filled the air, along with the smell of natural gas.

The tornado had destroyed six schools in Joplin: the regular and technical high schools, two middle schools and two elementary schools, facilities that taught more than half the district’s 7,911 students. Three more elementary schools and an administrative building had obvious damage. The storm also killed seven Joplin students, including one who was handed a diploma by Huff hours beforehand. More than 100 students had been injured. Many had lost family members or homes.

A week later, Huff held a news conference in front of the ruins of the high school. School, he declared, would start on time in August. The idea had stunned Joplin’s school board, but it gave him temporary emergency powers to make decisions without its input. He salvaged a countdown clock from the practice field and set it to 87 days. Reopening on time would prove that the city still had a future.

Huff ultimately led a remarkable turnaround. The district barely lost enrollment, and over the next few years, it actually improved educational outcomes. Huff’s part in this set him on a new career path, designed to fill a void in federal support for school administrators: In 2017, he was hired to help the Department of Health and Human Services with its disaster-relief efforts, advising school leaders on how to rebuild their districts after devastating storms, wildfires and floods.

This work has become increasingly urgent in our disaster-plagued age. Though there is inconclusive scientific evidence that climate change causes or worsens tornadoes like the one that hit Joplin, the warming planet has led to more intense hurricanes, longer wildfire seasons and other severe weather phenomena across the globe. Forthcoming research from Brown University estimates that 25 percent of all American public schools are now in areas with “very high risk” of at least one kind of climate-related disaster. In the aftermath of these crises, superintendents trained in the minutiae of curriculum implementation are suddenly thrust into an entirely new role. This is where Huff comes in: His job is to deploy to other ruined districts and try to export the lessons he learned restoring Joplin’s schools.

The idea that schools should be central to a region’s post-disaster recovery emerged three decades ago after a brutal hurricane. Schooling had long been considered a priority below shelter. School buildings, with their vast gyms and industrial kitchens, were often converted into refuges for the displaced. Then, in 1992, Hurricane Andrew ravaged Florida, and leaders in the hardest-hit county, Dade, decided to find focus amid the chaos by throwing themselves at reopening schools as fast as they could. “We were the ones that brought this community back together by opening up the schools,” the Dade County superintendent, Octavio J. Visiedo, later told education researchers — thus undergirding the reboot of a whole society.

If you got children back into school, it freed up parents to return to work. It reassured families that a community would remain viable, making them less likely to move elsewhere. And restoring routine for children could safeguard the psychological health of a future generation. Other officials began to follow suit, racing to reopen schools in Grand Forks, N. D., after a major 1997 flood and across Florida during a ruinous 2004 hurricane season.

In 2005, Hurricane Katrina underscored this principle and expanded it. The extended tail of misery it wrought on New Orleans put a spotlight on the longer-term suffering that disasters inflicted, particularly on children. In 2010, nine months before Joplin’s tornado, the social and behavioral scientist David Abramson released an influential study called “Children as Bellwethers of Recovery.” Citing post-Katrina data, Abramson argued that young people’s mental health reflects the performance of all the systems around them — government, civic institutions, health care, schools. When children regain stability, that is evidence that a community is functioning again; if they don’t, that’s a “lagging indicator.” That means leaders should “prioritize kids” after natural disasters, Abramson told me recently; their flourishing can help the adults along.

In the years since, this has played out so often that it has become a national rite of passage: A school district is crushed by a storm or a wildfire, and overnight, a superintendent becomes a short-term crisis-response coordinator, first charged with overseeing wrecked infrastructure and traumatized children and then presiding over a district’s resurrection. Indeed, superintendents can end up determining whether an entire community rebounds or withers.

Even as more and more superintendents find themselves in this position, the help and training for educators has not kept up. In the United States, there is no centralized guidance for school administrators. For example, FEMA’s recovery framework involves encouraging communities to ask themselves questions in the vein of: Is your old transportation network actually the one you want to rebuild? What’s your big vision for the next 20 years? How can federal money help get you there? There has been no explicit federal guidance, meanwhile, for questions like: How quickly should children return to school? How should we rebuild damaged school buildings? This was true in 2011, when the tornado hit Joplin. It’s still largely true 15 years later.

Katrina also crystallized an emerging belief that the devastation wrought by extreme weather might present a chance to correct broader social problems. In 2006 testimony before Congress, Robin Jarvis, an acting school superintendent in New Orleans, called Katrina a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” to redesign a public school system that had already been teetering on the edge of insolvency and make it “world class.” State officials redesigned New Orleans’s public education system around charter schools.

Back in 2011, Huff was new to all of this thinking; he had received no training on post-disaster school operations. He felt, he said, as if he was “flying blind.” But he would come to seem, to many, like the ideal implementer of the principles that Abramson and other researchers had laid out.

On a late-June day, I drove with Huff from where he now lives in Springfield, Mo., to Joplin, to look at the path the tornado took and what had been created in its place. The foothills of the lush Ozarks emptied into dusty plains dotted with water towers. The region is patchworked with farms, but it has never had very good soil. Originally a hardscrabble frontier, Joplin became a boomtown at the turn of the 20th century after the discovery of lead and zinc. Its school football teams dominated state competitions.

Within a few decades, the best ore had been used up. The region started running on fumes. Today neglected cemeteries are bellied up to the Interstate. Slightly desperate signs beckon cross-country tourists, promoting attractions like a museum dedicated to an electric shovel or the Uranus Fudge Factory: “The Best Fudge Comes From Uranus!” When we got into Joplin, though, it looked much fresher — both appealing and a little eerie. The town center devastated by the tornado has front yards so treeless and identical houses so immaculately painted that it resembles the video game Animal Crossing.

When Huff decided that Joplin’s schools would reopen on time, other educators were reeling. “We looked for our kids for a whole week,” Sachetta, the former high school principal, who is now Joplin’s superintendent, recalled. “If a kid was on Facebook and they were posting, we marked them off the list. We used every method possible. Call their parents, call a friend. ‘Have you seen Joe? Are you sure?’” Then there was the question of how to hold summer school, replace torn-up textbooks and prevent students from going to the ruined school buildings.

The students were drawn there. When Randy Steele, then a school board member, drove by the high school at night, he would see lights faintly bobbing in the dark: flashlights wielded by teenagers who might be sneaking back to look for their cheerleading uniforms or just wander the wreckage. The site was more dangerous than they knew. In the first few days after the tornado, Steele and some district employees dug through what was left of the buildings, trying to salvage sheet music, instruments, desks, anything that still looked usable. But Huff heard from his facilities director, as he put it, “Asbestos is probably everywhere.”

Tests confirmed it was. “It’s not like the government or FEMA had a SEAL-team-type, education-focused, insertion team saying, ‘Here’s what to expect,’” he said. Instead of concrete advice, he mostly received warnings, the most dire from a FEMA official who said to expect the loss of at least a third of Joplin’s school-going population as families were displaced. A Department of Education administrator said there could be up to 150 student suicides. “It scared the heck out of me,” Huff said.

He worked to set up temporary facilities all around town: The wrestling team met in a fireworks store, emptied after the Fourth of July. The heavily damaged East Middle School was relocated to an industrial building on the far edge of Joplin, with no windows and a gravel floor. It was next to a dog-food plant, “and when the wind was out of the right direction, it just did not smell good,” Huff remembered. For the temporary high school, he negotiated to use a shuttered big-box store inside a shopping mall.

In 2011, Huff, at 41, was sandy-haired and baby-faced; he peppered his speech with “awesome!” As his national profile rose, he made a useful mascot for a city bent on an inspiring turnaround. His rousing TV interviews led to more coverage, more donations. Barry Manilow donated more than $300,000 worth of instruments to Joplin’s school music programs. The United Arab Emirates gave a million dollars to buy a laptop for every child, to replace the ruined textbooks. Huff hired nine new trauma counselors, who set up “weather school,” in which meteorologists gave presentations to assuage students’ anxieties.

When it came to the longer-term rebuild, Huff perceived a rare opportunity. With an influx of federal money and an infrastructural blank slate, he could change Joplin’s education system significantly. “We will rebuild better than before,” he promised the community in an open letter.

Joplin’s schools had been struggling already. About 65 percent of students qualified for free or reduced-price lunch; when Huff became superintendent three years earlier, the district had among the lowest high-school graduation rates in Missouri. The dropout rate had been aggravated by a class divide. Some children who lived in the wealthier pockets referred to working-class children as “the dirties,” Huff told me. So he wondered: Why not remake the schools in a way that might even out educational outcomes?

He dispatched more than 50 Joplin administrators and teachers to fly around the nation to visit institutions whose design and philosophies might be an inspiration, from vanguard charter schools to Apple’s campus in Cupertino, Calif. The idea of making public high schools “career academies” was sweeping education-policy circles, and, Huff said, “we wanted to have new 21st-century learning spaces. Just real, real new and fresh.”

Joplin High would be his most ambitious project. It had already needed expansion, and now he envisioned rolling the high school and technical college into one, offering a group of simulated workplaces like a restaurant kitchen and a nurse’s bay to train in. Ninth graders could enter one of five “freshman academies” focused on the arts, business, health, service and technology. Instead of long, “double-barreled” hallways lined with classrooms, the interior of the new school would feel like a miniature town, with dispersed cafes and little plazas. Storm shelters would be built into the design, with multipurpose rooms that could be used as gyms and performance spaces.

At first, the whole town came together. Residents stayed up all night to clear one another’s debris. FEMA employees “kept comparing us positively to New Orleans,” Tracy Clements, a former school counselor, told me — a fact that made Joplinites feel proud. The tornado had ripped the letters J, L, I and N off the JOPLIN HIGH SCHOOL sign, leaving O and P. One night, somebody added an H and an E in duct tape, so the sign spelled HOPE. Huff kept a roll of duct tape in his car, to repair the letters if they peeled off.

Over the course of that first year, school enrollment dropped only 6.5 percent, and the district did not lose a single student to suicide. Huff traveled the country telling the story of Joplin’s reborn schools. People magazine made him one of its six 2011 “Heroes Among Us”; in 2013, Missouri named Huff its superintendent of the year. But as Huff’s fame grew, backlash was brewing in Joplin. In the chaotic months after the tornado, residents had been excited about a major upgrade to the city. Now harder-to-fix frustrations were mounting: the slow rebuilding, the long toll of injuries. Grief fed a desire to put back what was lost, just as it had been. Callum Eldred, the former student, told me that it was initially “cool” to go to high school at a shopping mall — but over time, he started to feel like a guinea pig in somebody else’s experiment.

Some residents began to object to an underlying idea that Huff’s rebuilding plan seemed to convey: that the old Joplin, whose residents bravely survived disaster, was actually a backward, failing place. Tina Carl, Eldred’s mother, told me that in her view, the recovery started to “look like a class separation.” She thought Huff was capitalizing on the destruction to make Joplin and its schools more “bougie.” “I felt like, I don’t think they’re thinking the way poor folks are thinking,” she said. “They’re thinking like rich people.”

The complaints were not baseless. The temporary and new buildings were funded through insurance, government grants and donations, but Huff also had to ask Joplin residents to approve a $62 million local bond and was forced to borrow money while awaiting FEMA reimbursements. After a Missouri state audit criticized the district’s dwindling reserves and procedural opacity, residents began confronting him in supermarkets, accusing him of stealing Joplin’s money. Frustrated and hurt, Huff fought back in public, clashing with new school-board members. His office started a blog called “Real or Rumor”: “I am happy to report that there is NO $150,000 elephant tusk Italian chandelier in the new high school,” one post read. To his critics, the jaunty tone seemed condescending. An online petition demanded his removal; hundreds of signers called him “arrogant,” a “crook” and a “bully.”

Huff stopped sleeping. He gained 40 pounds. On drives, he found himself wondering what would happen if he flicked his wrist and sent his car into a tree. “Most days, my state of mind was that I wasn’t afraid of dying,” he told me. “In fact, I welcomed it.” Three weeks before Joplin won a 2015 award as a “future-ready school district” from the Department of Education, Huff resigned. “I was destroyed physically, mentally, spiritually,” he said.

One afternoon in Joplin, Huff and I stopped for lunch at a cafe. Huff is now 56, with salt-and-pepper hair and a more subdued vibe than he had a decade ago. As we ordered, a man Huff thought he knew walked past our table. Huff said hello, and for a second, the passerby didn’t recognize him.

“C. J.,” Huff prompted.

“Ah,” the man said. “The infamous C. J. Huff.”

After two years piecing together educational consulting work, Huff got a call: The Department of Health and Human Services was looking for someone to lead education-related disaster relief. It was 2017, and his basic brief was to do “landscape assessments” of shattered school districts: to figure out exactly what educators needed in order to reopen their schools. When he accepted the job, Hurricane Harvey had just made landfall, and he was deployed to Texas.

There, he was given a cubicle in a response hub that FEMA and state officials had set up in a golf-club-manufacturing plant. It held 1,200 disaster experts from dozens of federal, state and local agencies — “huge teams of people,” he told me, “to support health care, for instance.” But Huff was among only a handful of people assigned to support educators. Vast areas of the state’s coast had been underwater, and Huff realized how complicated and wide-ranging flood damage was compared with the more circumscribed havoc wreaked by a tornado.

The scale of flood damage set limits on how fast schools could reopen: In the worst-hit places like Port Aransas, a city on an island off the coast of Corpus Christi, even temporary buildings could not open their doors for nearly two months. But speaking to Sharon McKinney, the district superintendent, Huff felt overwhelmed by a sense of recognition. The grief, the exhaustion he saw in her: “I remembered that look on my face.”

Dozens of federal and state officials had visited McKinney and left her their business cards. She had become responsible overnight for building design and decoding government regulations, things she had little training for. But no one took the time to walk her through what she should actually do, she told me. She and Huff sat together in her office and talked.

Traveling to other districts, Huff learned that resource-poor parts of America struggled to implement even some of the most basic principles of school recovery. In Puerto Rico, school buildings were used as shelters months after Hurricane Maria hit; when Huff arrived eight months later, some were still missing roofs. When he got to Florida after 2018’s Hurricane Michael — which came on the back of a particularly destructive 2017 hurricane season — he realized that the local, state and FEMA leadership bench was “only staffed so deep,” especially when “large-scale disasters happen back to back like that.”

He has now been doing this work for nearly a decade, but new disaster zones still jolt him. Huff recalled looking out the window of his Uber from the Maui airport into Lahaina, Hawaii, a month after the 2023 fire, thinking about how the stripped toothpick trees reminded him of Joplin. The general emptiness of the landscape, though, was a shock; fire doesn’t produce debris in the way storms do. All four school campuses remained unusable, and many students had enrolled elsewhere. The blaze had done a different kind of damage, melting car batteries and timber treated with arsenic to resist termites. Even intact buildings were coated in toxic ash.

All these years after the tornado, he is struck by how little has changed procedurally. There are still no clear federal guidelines for restoring schools after a disaster. In my own conversations with superintendents whose districts were devastated by hurricanes, floods and wildfires over the past decade, I heard about how they felt left alone to manage crises that had damaged their own homes, put them at the front line of comprehensively caring for thousands of their most vulnerable neighbors — the children — and rendered them responsible for decisions that would determine whether their communities’ tax bases survived, whether their towns lived or died.

Josh Barnes, who ran the broader division within the Department of Health and Human Services that contracted Huff, left H. H. S. in 2019. But he told me that he still sees an acute need for better organized federal help. School leaders, Barnes said, are not “adequately able to benefit from the collective experience that we have as a country.” In his view, every time a new district becomes a disaster zone, “we are discovering the same lessons for the first time, for, like, 20th time. And it’s agonizing to watch, frankly.”

As Huff visited other school districts, he discovered another common thread: The backlash he experienced was not specific to Joplin. Devastated communities often fell into infighting following disasters. After a catastrophe defined by helplessness, finding a shared enemy gave people something they could control.

In Maui, for example, Huff was surprised by the intensity of the community’s anger, even the children’s. At one meeting of fifth graders he convened, a child was incensed that leaders hadn’t sounded a warning siren. Huff was also struck by the residents’ desire to retain the island’s “identity,” to put things back the way they were — what he called the “‘heart piece’ of recovery.” Lahaina’s jade-green elementary school had stood in the same spot since before Hawaii joined America. That location was in the island’s tsunami zone. Contemplating the site, Huff knew it was impractical to rebuild there. But some Lahainans fought to preserve the site nonetheless.

Seeing all of this helped Huff process his own experience. “Joplin’s cycle of recovery is very, very real,” he told me. Jarvis, the acting New Orleans superintendent, resigned less than two years after Katrina. After flooding in 2016 in Nicholas County, W. Va., local officials proposed to use the recovery money for an ambitious school-consolidation plan. Residents mutinied, and the debate over how to rebuild and how much to spend dragged on for years, eventually leading to resignations.

When superintendents didn’t face resentment, it was often because the whole community — local leaders and residents alike — had assigned blame to federal officials. When everyone felt abandoned by the same institutions, that failure could be strangely protective. In Port Aransas after Harvey, the demon was outside: Frustration was directed outward, at contractors and FEMA. “We were all in the same boat,” McKinney told me. For years she kept an email she had printed out on her desk, a FEMA reimbursement denial for hardware, to remind her of what victimized her town. (FEMA did not reply to a request for comment.)

One night in Texas, Googling disaster recovery theory in his hotel room, Huff came across a graphic. It depicted a line tracking people’s psychological response after a disaster: The line soared upward as survivors experience a “heroic” surge of optimism, the “honeymoon phase.” Then the line plummeted into the “disillusionment phase,” in which fatigue, blame and rage send a community far lower emotionally than it was before the catastrophe. Only long afterward would the real “recovery and reconstruction” begin.

When Huff first saw it, he thought: “Oh, my gosh, this is exactly what I went through. This is normal.” He sent it to other leaders from the time of the tornado, several of whom mentioned or showed it to me, too. It became cherished, like a talisman. When Huff described this graphic to me recently, he began to cry.

The central tension in disaster recovery — between rebuilding what was lost and creating something new — will always be hard for communities to reconcile. And complicating the research around school recovery is how time can change the picture. Two decades after Hurricane Katrina, the remaking of New Orleans’s school system is seen as a contentious case study: It prompted real and comprehensive academic gains, yet it also deepened some inequities in the schools. In Joplin, certain educational metrics, especially graduation rates, improved after the tornado; though those rates fluctuated over the longer term, they have shot up recently.

But several former Joplin students told me that their feelings about Huff’s rebuilding plan had evolved as they got further out from their high school years. Mariah Vazquez, whose home was destroyed in the tornado, entered the new Joplin High when it opened in 2014 and told me that she initially felt lost in the “extravagant” building. But, she said, “I would not be where I am today” — a professional photographer — without the career academy project. For a long time, Eldred, who stayed in the Joplin area and works at McDonald’s, felt as if he were still “living in the shadow of the tornado.” But now, he said, he can appreciate the citywide recovery that Huff’s flashy school renovation plan helped jump-start. He mentioned the modern library, the cutting-edge hospital, “things we probably wouldn’t have gotten if we stuck to the old-style Joplin.”

Today Huff works out of a co-working space in a former chicken-processing plant in downtown Springfield. When the plant was converted, the developers got rid of the equipment but didn’t change the architecture, so the floors slant in odd ways, a relic from when the builders wanted the blood of slaughtered chickens to run into easy-to-clean pools.

After the pandemic began to discourage in-person deployments, his government work became too intermittent. So he and his wife founded their own company in 2024 as “a turnkey solution” for shattered superintendents awash in problems after disasters, he said. “FEMA technical assistance. Grant writing. Grant management. Anything and everything that school leaders have to deal with.” When we spoke on the phone a few weeks ago, he was about to travel to central Pennsylvania to meet with a superintendent whose school was hit by a tornado in August. In theory, Huff is better positioned than anyone to do this kind of work. “It’s mystifying,” said Abramson, the social and behavioral scientist, that public officials don’t do more to “help affected communities quickly climb the learning curve” by imitating Joplin’s fast, ambitious school reopening plan. But over time, Huff himself has begun to think that his logistical advice goes only so far. After all, every school district is facing its own specific, regional obstacles. Now he tries to offer something more like solidarity. For two superintendents I spoke with who worked with Huff, that empathy was just as crucial as any recovery template.

Huff told me that in retrospect, he thinks all the TV interviews he did about Joplin, the crusading, visionary attitude, might have been a way to distract himself from feeling or processing his own grief. “Maybe part of the reason I kept the hero cape on was so I didn’t have to face those memories,” he said. “It was easier for me to just focus in on the work.”

Now he tells educators: “‘I’m not your knight in shining armor. I’m here to be your backup.’ I try to be a Swiss Army knife.” He encourages school leaders to spend more time listening than talking and to “take the hero cape off.” “I always kind of frame it as, ‘Do as I say, not as I did,’” he said.

One day in Joplin, Huff took me to the high school he once reimagined. For 20 minutes, we wandered all around the school’s imposing facade, from the triple-height entryway doors to the outdoor amphitheater, searching for a way in. Pressing his face against the tinted windows to try to spot someone within, Huff looked like a child locked out of his family home. Finally he spied a custodian and pounded the glass until she opened a door.

Inside, the windows filled the high-ceilinged space with a beautiful, gentle light, bringing the outdoors in. We visited the restaurant, the state-of-the-art black-box theater, the auto-body-work training area, the “think tanks” — small, soundproof rooms — that supported the development of clubs and organizations, “just to make sure kids felt like they’re part of something.”

As we wandered the school, Huff began speaking in the present tense. “We’ve got a great culinary arts program here,” he said, showing me a full restaurant where students can serve guests. “Kids have a lot of chances to just explore their passions.” We paused in the hall, where alcoves displayed striking wood sculptures that artists had carved out of tree trunks torn up by the tornado. He touched a wall. “I’m wandering around here, and I’m like, ‘That spot needs painting.’” Finally, we had seen everything we could. Huff pushed an emergency-exit door and walked out into the sun. It was easier to leave than to get in. In two months, the school would be full of students again, and he would be on to the next place.

This Rare Gene Drastically Raises Lung Cancer Risk in People Who Never Smoked

The New York Times September 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The gene is found predominantly in Southern Appalachia and may be one of the most powerful cancer-risk mutations ever found.

By Gina Kolata

Between 200 and 225 years ago, someone or several someones from the British Isles had a gene mutation that caused lung cancer. They traveled to America, settled in Southern Appalachia and transmitted the cancer gene to their descendants and their descendants’ descendants.

Today that lung cancer gene, known as EGFR T790M, is found largely in residents of the United States and mostly in Southern Appalachia, especially Tennessee and Alabama. It makes lung cancer 62 times as likely in those who have never smoked and 10 times as likely in smokers.

The gene is one of the most powerful, if not the most powerful, cancer-risk mutations ever found, said Alexander Gusev, a geneticist at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and an author of the paper.

Those are among the stunning findings of a new report, published on Thursday in Science by researchers at Dana-Farber and 23andMe Research.

Unlike other cancer genes that can cause cancer in a variety of organs, this gene is associated only with lung cancer. Researchers expect their discovery can help unlock secrets about the development of the disease.

For those with the gene, the hope is for early detection and treatment or even cancer prevention, said Dr. Raymond DuBois, the director of the Medical University of South Carolina’s Hollings Cancer Center, who was not associated with the work.

“This is a great story,” Dr. DuBois said, adding that he “read the paper like a novel.”

The variant was discovered in 2005, but because it is so rare, researchers were limited to studying families in which several members had the gene and got lung cancer. Studies like that could not reveal how much the gene increased risk.

Investigators did learn, though, that the variant was unusual. Lung cancer patients often have mutations in the EGFR gene, but those mutations arose by random bad luck later in life. If those mutations arise in embryos, they kill the embryos. But not the EGFR T790M mutation. People are born with it, and it is not lethal. It causes only lung cancer, but decades later.

Dr. Jaclyn LoPiccolo and Dr. Pasi A. Jänne, lung cancer experts at Dana-Farber, realized that 23andMe’s data might hold the key to figuring out how dangerous EGFR T790M is. Other databases had too few people — less than a million participants, only a handful of whom had the mutation. But 23andMe, a direct-to-consumer recreational databank that many use to find ancestors, was huge.

The database had more than 10 million people who had consented to participate in research, including the 3.37 million who had provided both genetic data and information on whether they had lung cancer. There were 641 who had the mutation.

Those data allowed the investigators to trace the origin of the mutation to the settler or settlers from the British Isles, to determine the cancer risk the mutation conferred and to discover that the gene was associated only with lung cancer.

They also found that about one in 15,000 people in the United States had the gene, but one in 2,000 in Southern Appalachia had it.

For those who have the gene, it can confer a grim legacy.

Caroline Blanchard, a 35-year-old nurse practitioner from New Orleans, said her story began about 15 years ago, when her very healthy aunt, who had never smoked, got lung cancer and died within a year, at age 45. “We didn’t question it,” Ms. Blanchard said. “Her doctors said it was just sort of random.”

Then, four years ago, her grandmother got lung cancer, at age 80. Her doctors, at MD Anderson Cancer Center, suggested genetic testing. Ms. Blanchard’s grandmother had the EGFR T790M mutation.

After learning that, Ms. Blanchard’s “very healthy” mother decided to get a lung scan. It revealed nodules in both lungs: She also had the mutation.

Next it was her turn, Ms. Blanchard said. She found out she had the mutation and nodules in both lungs.

“I’m so glad my grandmother lived to be 80,” she said. If she had died in her 70s, Ms. Blanchard added, no one would have thought to test for that cancer gene.

Dr. Jänne, a senior author of the report, said lung cancer could be found early with CT scans, but guidelines reserved them for smokers and former smokers over 50. The new findings raise important questions: Should doctors screen people with the mutation earlier? Or at least more often?

He would also like to understand why the mutation affects only lung cells.

“There’s a lot to learn here,” Dr. Jänne said.

All in all, “it’s a very cool story,” said Dr. Stephen Chanock, director of the Division of Cancer Epidemiology and Genetics at the National Cancer Institute, who wrote a perspective accompanying the article.

“We always thought this gene was causing cancer,” he noted. But, he added, only now it is clear how powerful it is.

Gina Kolata reports on diseases and treatments, how treatments are discovered and tested, and how they affect people.

The New York Times September 17, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Mistakes that led to the deaths of more than a hundred children “went beyond negligence,” investigators said. They also cited a separate strike the same day that killed a reported 22 civilians.

By Nick Cumming-Bruce

Reporting from Geneva

United Nations investigators said Thursday that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that two U. S. airstrikes on Iran in February in which at least 178 civilians died had been indiscriminate and amounted to war crimes.

The first of the attacks hit the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school on Feb. 28 and killed 157 people, including around 123 boys and girls below the age of 13, the investigators said. They cited what they described as credible independent information.

The second strike took place the same day and hit a sports center and nearby residential buildings in the central city of Lamerd. Iranian sources reported that 22 civilians were killed, including five children, the investigators said. They said a “credible organization” reported that close to 170 people were injured, among them children who sustained life-threatening injuries.

The findings were contained in an 18-page report by the U. N.’s Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran and are to be presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.

The report also details abuses it said amounted to crimes against humanity that were committed by the Iranian authorities in their crackdown on government protesters.

Addressing the strike on the elementary school in Minab, a town in southern Iran, the report said: “The mission finds reasonable grounds to believe that the U. S. committed the war crime of launching an indiscriminate attack resulting in loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.”

“The U. S. failed in its obligation to do everything feasible to verify that it was a military objective,” it said.

American officials refused to discuss the findings. “The Department declines to comment on a report conducted by an outside organization,” the Defense Department said in a statement. “Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment.”

In March, The New York Times reported that an analysis showed that missile fragments purporting to be from the school strike bore the markings of an American cruise missile. The remnants had serial numbers and other details that were consistent with how the Defense Department and its suppliers label munitions. They appeared to be from a U. S.-made Tomahawk cruise missile.

American officials have ascribed the school strike to a targeting error caused by outdated data.

The school was hit during an attack on a nearby Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps naval complex, but the U. N. investigators said it was clearly identifiable as a school. They also concluded that the site had been “the intended point of impact” and that it had not been hit by an errant strike. They also said it was not collateral damage.

The mission noted that a Defense Department preliminary investigation had acknowledged that the U. S. was probably responsible. The Pentagon has not published the results of its investigation.

“Nobody did that on purpose,” President Trump told journalists in June. “Mistakes are made. War is nasty.”

U. S. forces did appear to have relied on outdated intelligence, but the failure to verify their target “went beyond negligence,” the U. N. report said.

“Rather, the U. S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen,” it said.

The Lamerd sports center was adjacent to, but visibly separate from, a Guards Corps building, the report said. It said U. S. forces had employed a Precision Strike Missile that dispersed approximately 180,000 tungsten pellets over a wide area. The weapon’s use in a populated civilian area was “reckless as to the likely extent of death or injury,” it said.

The investigators noted that the U. S. military has confirmed use of the Precision Strike Missile in Iran but that it has denied hitting the sports center. U. S. officials say the attack appears more consistent with an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile. The American claim is at variance with evidence, the report said.

The investigators said they had written to the U. S. government requesting information on the airstrikes and meetings with American military officials. They did not receive a response, they said.

In reaching their conclusions, the investigators said they had taken into account public statements by American officials, including Mr. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, that were dismissive of U. S. obligations under international law to distinguish between civilian and military targets.

The investigators said they had also looked into Iran’s brutal treatment of protesters in the period before the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran. In December 2025 and early this year, the report said, the Iranian government engaged in killing of dissidents “on a staggering and unprecedented scale” across all 31 of Iran’s provinces.

The report noted official estimates that 3,038 people had been killed in the violence and some 25,000 injured, many seriously. But the investigators said they strongly believed the real number of people killed and injured was significantly higher.

In the ensuing crackdown, Iranian security forces arrested thousands of people. And since the start of the year, the government has executed at least 58 people on security-related charges, the report said. More than 70 Iranians, including at least five women and three boys, remain at imminent risk of being sentenced to death or executed over the protests, the report said.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting.

Fighting Intensifies in Yemen as Militia Advances on Key Provinces

The New York Times September 17, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Clashes between Iranian-backed Houthi fighters and Saudi-backed government forces have been reported near oil-rich Marib Province.

By Ismaeel Naar

Reporting from Dubai, United Arab Emirates

Fighting has intensified near two strategic provinces in Yemen, a sign that Iranian-backed Houthi militants are expanding their offensive after seizing the country’s Red Sea coastline, analysts say.

A sustained Houthi push into Yemen’s resource-rich eastern regions, including Marib Province, would threaten the economic lifeline of the internationally recognized government and risk triggering a fresh humanitarian crisis among millions of Yemenis.

While the Houthis have succeeded in taking much of northwestern Yemen since capturing the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, Marib has so far eluded them.

“It is the bastion and stronghold in the north for those who resisted the militia’s coup more than a decade ago,” said Mohammed al-Basha, a Washington-based risk analyst focused on Yemen. “If they capture it, it would be such a symbolic and strategic win for them.”

Marib, about 75 miles east of Sanaa, and the southern city of Taiz have emerged as the Houthis’ most likely targets after they captured territory near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital waterway for global trade. That advance has allowed the militia to increase its pressure on shipping in the Red Sea.

Pro-government forces have struck Houthi positions in both provinces with fighter jets and drones over the past month and say they have repelled the militia’s advances. The Houthis have countered by firing missiles at government-held areas.

The Yemeni government has been backed for more than a decade by Saudi Arabia, which has led a military coalition aiming to roll back the militia. The coalition carried out a devastating bombing campaign, but it ultimately failed to oust the Houthis from power.

Since then, Yemen has effectively been divided into two states, with the Houthis in control of large swaths of the country’s north and the government in the south, based in the temporary capital, Aden.

Marib is home to some of Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields. Its loss would deal a severe blow to the government’s finances as well as its claim to legitimacy. Marib’s fall would also open a route for the Houthis toward the eastern province of Hadramout, Yemen’s largest, which shares a long border with Saudi Arabia.

“If Marib falls to the Houthis, it would mean the militia would be in reaching distance to the Saudi-Yemeni borders,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group. “That would be unacceptable to Saudi Arabia and threatens their national security.”

A Houthi political official, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, said that tribal elders in Marib had called on the group to “liberate” the province. “Sanaa assures everyone that it is committed to liberating every inch of Yemeni territory,” he said in a phone interview. He said Saudi-backed forces had rejected de-escalation efforts.

Yemeni government officials and analysts describe the recent clashes as among the most intense since 2021, when the Houthis last mounted a major assault on Marib but were pushed back. The Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia both appear to be stepping up airstrikes to blunt Houthi advances, said April Alley, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute, where her research focuses on Yemen and the Gulf.

But she said: “The Houthis have the wind at their back for the moment. Government forces are deeply fragmented, and morale took a huge hit after the west coast losses.”

The Houthis said on Wednesday they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib with a locally made missile. The wreckage of the downed jet seems to be consistent with that of the F-15 jets in the Royal Saudi Air Force, a review of the images by The New York Times found. However, the exact location of the wreckage could not be confirmed.

In recent weeks, the battlefront has also extended to Taiz, which connects the Houthi-controlled north with the southern coast controlled by the government.

“What the Houthis are doing is trying to besiege the city of Taiz and choke off the last highway connecting Taiz with Aden,” Mr. Nagi said. “Who controls the city would matter strategically for both sides.”

The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported Saudi airstrikes on Thursday in the city of Abs in Yemen’s Hajjah Province that left one person dead and another wounded. The agency said that Saudi aircraft also targeted three telecommunications towers in Taiz Province. A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said that the Saudis had carried out 37 airstrikes using F-15 jets targeting Taiz and Hajjah over the past 24 hours.

Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense on Thursday said a Yemeni resident had been killed in the Saudi province of Taif, east of Islam’s holiest site, Mecca. They were hit by shrapnel from an intercepted Houthi drone, the Saudis said.

It was the first announced death in the kingdom since the Houthis intensified their cross-border strikes this month. A Pakistani man was injured and in critical condition, the authorities said.

Shuaib Almosawa Almosawa reported from Sanaa, Yemen.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.
