Review: Apple Watch Series 12

Wired September 17, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

9/10

On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t appear to be a major upgrade over last year’s release and, in many ways, it isn’t. But after a week of wearing it day and night, I noticed that the Series 12 feels more intuitive, putting fewer steps between me and the information I need from my everyday smartwatch.

Health tracking is more thorough, thanks to a new Health Sensing System and faster S11 chip. The watchOS 27 update, first announced at WWDC in June and finally available to consumers, gives the Apple Watch a cleaner, streamlined interface that positions Siri AI at the center of the user experience. The most notable addition is perhaps Audio Intelligence, a suite of listening tools powered by Apple Intelligence. Plus, in a fun return, the Series 12 also comes in ceramic, a premium finish Apple discontinued in 2020.

Not everyone needs the upgrade, though. If you’re coming from the Series 8 or older, the Series 12 is a generational leap, with a better display, longer battery life, and newer health features, including sleep apnea and hypertension notifications. Owners of the Series 9 or 10 have fewer reasons to swap, but the battery improvements alone (18 hours to 24 hours) may be compelling. If you already have the Series 11, Audio Intelligence probably isn’t going to be enough to justify replacing a watch that’s already capable of most of the same functions.

Visually, Apple isn’t fixing what isn’t broken, and I’m not mad about it. The Series 12 looks nearly identical to its predecessors, but Apple highlights it as its thinnest Apple Watch yet. The aluminum and titanium models measure 9.7 millimeters thick, and the ceramic option is 9.85 millimeters thick. I didn’t notice a difference during everyday wear, but the Apple Watch Series remains one of the most comfortable smartwatches I’ve tested. Aside from the new Hermès collection, there aren’t any new band designs this year, but Apple has added new colors to the existing lineup.

Apple Watch Series 12

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The new finishes are exciting, particularly the return of ceramic. Apple first offered a ceramic option with the Series 2 in 2016, and it was discontinued in 2020. Today, it’s available in pearl white and night blue, both of which give the Series 12 a softer finish that looks more like an accessory. The ceramic feels more like a fashionable move rather than a functional one, but Apple is following a trend seen across brands like Oura.

I’m testing the aluminum model in the new dark bronze finish, which has become my favorite. It complements most of my wardrobe and gives the watch a more cosmopolitan look than some of Apple’s sportier colorways. Aluminum models are also available in the standard light gold, black, and space gray; titanium comes in natural and a new radiant gold. The aluminum models are now coated with Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the previous Ion-X glass. I haven’t had enough time with the watch to meaningfully test that durability claim, but for someone who tends to knock their smartwatch on doors and countertops, it’s an improvement I’ll happily accept.

Battery life remains rated at 24 hours, which is slightly disappointing when competitors can go longer between charges. The saving grace is faster charging. Fifteen minutes of charging now provides up to 12 hours of battery life, and five minutes gets you up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. This has been the most useful upgrade for me. I can set the watch to charge while I’m getting ready for bed and put it back on for sleep tracking.

The Series 12 ships with watchOS 27, but most of the software changes will also arrive on compatible older Apple Watches. I particularly love the revamped app layout. Instead of having to hunt through a sea of icons or scroll through an exhaustive list, Apple now surfaces five Siri AI-suggested apps, the Siri app, and a shortcut to the full app grid. The apps I need most are immediately available without cluttering the display.

Apple Watch Series 12

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Apple is also making the watch easier to navigate with one hand, adding a single-tap gesture to Apple’s existing double-tap and wrist-flick controls. Tap your index finger and thumb together to select widgets in Smart Stack; double-tap lets you scroll through them. A wrist flick can return you to the watch face, silence timers, or dismiss notifications. These gestures are particularly handy (ha) when you’re multitasking or if you want to use your watch discreetly.

The new S11 chip brings the standard round of faster CPU and GPU performance, along with a more efficient Neural Engine. S11 also powers a remodeled pedometer to improve step counts and distance measurements, particularly during indoor walks and runs. Compared to Series 11, I didn’t notice much difference in numbers. I do, though, appreciate the new Steps complication, which puts my real-time step count on the watch face, so I can check my progress without opening the Activity app.

The bigger hardware upgrade is Apple’s new Health Sensing System. The Series 12 has 32 electrodes for improved skin contact during ECG readings, compared with two on the Series 11. The photodiodes have been rearranged in a ring configuration for improved optical sensing, and larger green LEDs have been added for more accurate heart rate readings.

The result, and one of the watch’s biggest selling points, is that it takes more frequent readings. The Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, even while you’re moving, whereas the Series 11 takes readings every five minutes when you’re relatively stationary. The Series 12 can also measure heart rate variability (HRV) as often as every five minutes, compared with every two hours on the Series 11, and it measures two variants: recovery HRV and overall HRV. For health-conscious people, the higher sampling frequency gives you a more continuous picture of how your body responds to stressors throughout the day instead of a handful of isolated snapshots. You can see those readings in the Heart Rate app or through the new live heart rate complications.

Readiness has at last arrived for anyone who has been anticipating a unified recovery score from Apple. The new Readiness app pulls together activity, sleep, and other health data to estimate how prepared you are for the day ahead. It takes seven days of sleep data before the score becomes available, which is standard for wearables to determine a baseline.

I like having the score as a quick shorthand instead of attempting to contextualize the individual metrics myself, but I stay skeptical of any recovery score that simplifies complicated physiological states using a proprietary algorithm. That said, Readiness is useful as a prompt to pay attention to your body, and I’m glad Apple finally has one.

Apple is also planning a redesigned Health app later this year, including a new Longevity tab and metrics such as Health Age, which compares your health data with that of your demographic. I haven’t been able to test those features yet, but I have a feeling my Health Age will either be oddly gratifying or immediately anxiety-inducing.

Audio Intelligence may be Apple’s most controversial addition. The suite brings four audio-focused features, including accelerated Shazam and Sound Recognition, the latter of which has been available on the iPhone since 2020. The more intriguing additions are Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which push the Apple Watch into murky waters by using its microphone to capture and process audio. I haven’t been able to test either feature yet; both are slated to arrive later this year.

Siri Recap is Apple’s answer to the AI notetaking boom. When enabled, it can transcribe conversations and generate summaries using Apple Intelligence. I can see the appeal for meetings and classes. During a briefing, I saw Siri Recap turn a PTA meeting into a detailed set of notes and reminders that seemed genuinely useful.

Apple Watch Series 12

Rating: 9/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Live Rewind is harder to wrap my head around. The feature maintains a rolling buffer of recent audio so you can ask the watch for a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Double-press the Digital Crown and, in theory, you can recover something you just missed without asking the other person to repeat themselves.

The privacy concerns are justified, and you can read more about them here. Apple says the audio is processed in a protected memory area called the Secure Enclave. The S11 chip has an isolated buffer for sensor data, and Apple says raw audio isn’t accessible to the operating system, apps, the user, or Apple. The company also says these features don’t create or store audio recordings.

That’s somewhat reassuring, but it doesn’t eliminate the always-listening worries. Live Rewind supposedly plays an audible chime when activated to alert people nearby. Whether a beep is sufficient consent is a personal judgment call. I will test these features myself once they roll out and will report back.

Apple has refined the everyday experience, added health metrics people actually want, and resisted the temptation to bury the watch under a pile of new features. It’s a thoughtful update, and that makes the Series 12 the best Apple Watch yet.

Which iPhone Should You Buy (or Avoid) Right Now?

Wired September 17, 2026

Apple

Apple

Apple

Apple (Pro)

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Apple sells seven iPhone models, from the $699 iPhone 17e to the $1,999 iPhone Duo, but which iPhone is best for you? This is a good time of the year to buy an iPhone if you need to upgrade, since Apple just released its flagship models. (We don't expect the more affordable iPhone 18 models until spring 2027.) We've tested nearly every model and outlined their strengths and weaknesses so you can get the right one for you. (The iPhone Duo is coming soon, but we have some initial hands-on details.)

Check out our other Apple buying guides, including Which iPhone 18 Models to Buy, Which iPhone 17 Model to Buy, Best iPhone 17 Cases, Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Chargers, Best MagSafe Wallets, and Best Apple 3-in-1 Chargers. Wondering what's new in iOS 27? We have details on that, too.

Updated September 2026: We’ve added the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, and the Apple Upgrade option that replaces the iPhone Upgrade Program. We’ve also added the latest features from recent iOS updates and updated pricing across the board due to Apple’s price hikes.

But First, Sell That Old iPhone!

If you’re upgrading from an iPhone, you can trade it in to Apple for a small discount. Before you do that, check whether you can sell it elsewhere for more money. iPhones hold their value incredibly well, particularly if they’re in mint or good condition. We have a guide that runs through the process of selling your phone, and we generally recommend you use websites like Swappa, Gazelle, or Back Market.

We also have a handful of setup guides you should follow:

Buying From Apple vs. a Carrier

Most people in the US purchase iPhones from carriers, which means the devices are locked to that network. If you bought an iPhone from Verizon, you can't easily switch to another carrier without breaking a contract and paying extra fees. It also poses headaches for travelers who want to use international SIM cards or eSIMs.

The easier approach is to buy directly from Apple, though there are some things you should know:

Connect to any carrier later: Choose this option for the most hassle-free experience. You get an unlocked iPhone, then all you need to do is transfer the SIM card or eSIM from your old iPhone to the new one to get started. This might be painless, though you may need to contact your carrier if the iPhone can't complete the eSIM transfer. In the US, Apple hasn't included a SIM tray since 2022's iPhone 14.

Choose a carrier: If you choose a carrier through Apple. com, you will get an unlocked iPhone, no matter which carrier you choose (except if you purchase with AT&T on an installment plan). The downside is that Apple doesn't have the same offers as the carriers, so you may lose out on a deal. However, carrier offers often require new lines, trade-ins, or an upgraded plan, and the savings come in the form of bill credits, so these deals aren't as amazing as they may seem.

Finance: You can finance your iPhone either with Apple's credit card via monthly installments or as Apple iPhone Payments via a Citizens One loan. You need to choose a carrier here, but Apple confirmed these devices are all unlocked. You have to fill out a credit application to see if you qualify. If you opt to finance through a carrier on Apple. com, only the T-Mobile and Verizon models will be unlocked. The AT&T and Boost Mobile options are locked iPhones, so it's no different from buying it on an installment plan directly from those carriers.

Apple Upgrade: Buying directly from Apple also nets you access to the Apple Upgrade leasing option. Is it worth it? Broadly speaking, no. Most people do not need to upgrade to a new iPhone every year or two. It's expensive, and you must return your leased iPhone in good condition to avoid additional charges. AppleCare is not included, as it was with the discontinued iPhone Upgrade Program.

What Is Apple Intelligence?

The most hyped-up feature from the iPhone 16 range was Apple Intelligence, which rolled out in iOS 18.1. This is Apple's suite of AI features, following the wave started by the likes of ChatGPT and Google's Gemini. Apple Intelligence is available on the iPhone 15 Pro/Pro Max and newer, including the iPhone 16e (not to mention select iPads and MacBooks).

What exactly is Apple Intelligence in the first place? It's a collection of features that draw on the power of large language models to introduce “smart” capabilities. For example, in the Voice Memo and Notes app, you can now start a recording and get a real-time transcription. You can even record a call and get the transcription saved in the Notes app. Siri has been redesigned to understand when you misspeak and can even plug into ChatGPT for more powerful responses to open-ended questions. There are writing tools available throughout the operating system that let you change the tone of your emails or proofread text so you don't make an unnecessary typo on Threads.

This is just a small sampling. We've boiled down many of the Apple Intelligence features here, and additional features keep rolling out in iOS updates. For example, Genmoji—which lets you create your own emojis—debuted alongside the AI image-generation app, Image Playground, in iOS 18.2. In iOS 27, Apple added the revamped, conversational Siri AI assistant. Siri now understands personal context and can retrieve information from your messages, emails, and photos. It can also act on your behalf to draft a message with a particular tone or find a good restaurant for your partner's birthday dinner. Here's everything you can do with Siri AI.

If you don't care for Apple Intelligence and want to turn it off, you can! We have a helpful guide detailing the exact steps.

What Is MagSafe?

Magnetic MagSafe wireless charging is available on the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, iPhone 17, and iPhone 18 models (except the iPhone 16e), and it allows you to magnetically attach various accessories to the back of the iPhone. (iPhones support Qi2, which is the open standard, whereas MagSafe is proprietary; you can use Qi2 accessories just like MagSafe.)

You can get first-party accessories like Apple's MagSafe Wireless Charger, which sticks to the back for faster charging. Or snag the MagSafe Wallet so you can keep your credit card attached to your phone. There are plenty of third-party accessories (you'll find quite a few in our guide), and MagSafe doesn't just have to be charging accessories like power banks or wireless chargers. There is a wealth of useful tools, from wallets, tripods, and camera cages to notepads and ring lights that can attach to the back of the iPhone and add extra versatility.

If you plan to use a case, get one that has MagSafe embedded inside to ensure a strong magnetic connection with Apple's accessories (non-MagSafe cases can interrupt MagSafe and make the magnetic connection weaker). All of the cases in our case guides are MagSafe-tested. And yes, a case is a smart investment because iPhones are made of glass, and glass breaks, even if Apple uses ceramic to strengthen it. We cracked an iPhone 16 Plus after a 4-foot drop to the pavement—that model's ceramic glass was supposed to be twice as strong as previous iPhones, too! Ouch. See our favorite cases for the iPhone 17, iPhone 16, iPhone 15, and iPhone 14 ranges.

The iPhone 17 is nearly the perfect phone, and it's what most people looking for a new iPhone should buy right now. With this model, Apple finally upgraded the screen's refresh rate to 120 Hz. This might not sound like the snazziest feature, but you'll immediately notice everything feeling smoother and more responsive as you use the phone, especially if you're coming from an iPhone with a 60-Hz display. The slightly larger display can also hit up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness, which means you shouldn't have any trouble reading it in sunny conditions, and the new anti-reflective coating should also help cut glare. It's protected by Apple's new Ceramic Shield 2 glass, which supposedly is three times more scratch-resistant than before.

More excitingly, the selfie camera has been upgraded to 24 megapixels (binned down to 18 MP). It's the same across the entire iPhone 17 lineup (excluding the iPhone 17e), and Apple is using a square sensor for the first time. It's smart and helpful because you can keep holding your iPhone firmly in portrait orientation, but digitally switch to landscape or portrait orientation when taking a selfie without having to rotate the phone in your hand. It'll also automatically zoom and rotate orientations when it detects more people in the frame (Apple calls it Center Stage). You can also natively shoot video with the front and rear cameras simultaneously with Dual Capture.

Storage was bumped to 256 GB (finally!), and the ultrawide camera was upgraded to 48 megapixels, delivering sharp results even in low-light conditions. There's a slightly bigger battery, too, and the results have been very impressive, easily lasting through a full day with more than six hours of screen-on time. I only wish Apple added a telephoto zoom camera here—Android phones at this price are starting to see more optical zoom options, like the Google Pixel 10 and Samsung Galaxy S26, and it would make this iPhone more versatile. (At least the “optical-like” 2X zoom is decent.)

All in all, this is one of the most well-rounded and feature-rich iPhones in years, even if it doesn't feature the fun Camera Plateau design of the pricier iPhone Air or Pro models. Sadly, Apple increased the price of the iPhone 17 (and every other older model) by $100 when it unveiled the new 18 line-up.

There's a single camera on the back—it's decent but not as versatile, and it struggles the most in low-light conditions. This iPhone doesn't have the ultrawide-band chip, which allows for precision guidance when hunting for your AirTag. (You can still locate your misplaced item, just with more vague instructions to its location.) Oh, and the screen is stuck at 60 Hz, so it doesn't feel as responsive as the other iPhones here.

If those flaws don't seem like deal-breakers, then the iPhone 17e will be more than sufficient. It's powered by the A19 chip like the iPhone 17, except with one fewer graphics core, so there's a small hit to performance. However, I booted up Genshin Impact and didn't have much trouble playing it, even after maxing out graphics; you'll just see more stutters here and there.

I appreciate that Apple has installed its Ceramic Shield 2 glass to protect the screen, meaning improved durability, and there's a bump in base storage to 256 GB. Battery life has been reliable, easily lasting me a full day even with heavy use, but the biggest upgrade is the addition of MagSafe. A strange omission on the iPhone 16e, this capability means you can take advantage of the wealth of magnetic MagSafe accessories on the market, whether you want faster wireless charging or just an easier way to mount the smartphone on a tripod or car mount.

If the iPhone 17e's single-camera system turns you off, then take a look at the iPhone 16. (Or maybe you prefer the bright and bold colors here.) Apple still sells this 2024 phone but has increased the price to $799 and discontinued the larger iPhone 16 Plus. I would try to find it for cheaper at other retail channels if possible—I wouldn't pay $799 for the iPhone 16. (There is no new iPhone 17 Plus model; Apple replaced it with the iPhone Air.)

The 6.1-inch iPhone 16 can get you through a day, but heavy users may need a top-up before bedtime. It features the Action Button, which replaced the mute switch on older iPhones, but you can bring that functionality back or customize this button to do something else. There's also Camera Control, which launches the camera and doubles as a shutter button. A light amount of pressure on this button lets you switch camera modes or photography styles, and you can slide your finger to cycle through them. (I hate this secondary function, so I always disable it; Settings > Camera > Camera Control > Customize and toggle off Light Press and Swipe.

The iPhone Duo may have dominated the headlines recently, but Apple's true flagships are the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. If you want the best battery life on a smartphone, this is it, particularly the Pro Max, because it packs a denser battery. You can easily make it through two days on a single charge. The smaller Pro generally had around 40 percent left by bedtime. These are also the most powerful smartphones, with the Apple A20 Pro chip backed by an improved vapor chamber design for cooling—ensuring the smoothest performance even when you're playing a AAA game like Control.

The Dynamic Island is a little smaller this year; it can now display three activities, making it a little more useful. There's no orange color option, but Apple is offering a lovely new burgundy. Perhaps the biggest enhancement is with the already versatile, triple 48-megapixel lens camera system, thanks to a new variable aperture in the main lens. Changing the aperture gives you more control over how much light you let in, allowing better low-light performance, and allows you to capture that coveted bokeh effect for blurred backgrounds or narrow it down to keep more of the scene and background in focus. It also adds enhancements to the already excellent video capture capabilities.

This minor refresh over the iPhone 17 Pro also comes with a price bump (an extra $100 across the board), and some handy new features in iOS 27 (though the iPhone 15 Pro and newer will get these, too). The revamped Siri AI is far more capable than previous versions, with more contextual understanding of what's onscreen and the ability to delve into your messages, emails, and photos.

Apple

Apple

Breaking the trend of incremental annual updates, the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foray into foldables. Instead of the book- and flip-style foldables that have dominated the market so far, Apple went with a passport-sized form factor, similar to Samsung's recent Galaxy Z Fold8 (our current pick for the best folding phones). The Duo sports a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, but unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display inside that feels like an iPad Mini.

With a tough titanium frame, a precision hinge with magnets for that satisfying snap-shut, and an IP68 rating, this promises to be one of the most durable foldables on the market, but not the slimmest or lightest (it's bigger and heavier than Samsung's Fold8).

There are trade-offs with folding phones, and the Duo drops Face ID (Touch ID is in the side power button instead) and makes do without a telephoto lens (you get a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide). On the upside, it has the biggest-ever iPhone battery, promising 24 hours of mixed use.

Apple's take on the software is what we're most excited about, as the company will surely find unique ways to take advantage of the new form factor. From our brief look so far, controls have been stacked vertically, there's plenty of split-screen support, and transitions look typically smooth. Features like Kid Cue, to help you catch your kid's attention for photos, and enhanced StandBy support to use the outer screen as an alarm clock, while the inside display gently pulses with light to wake you, will set this iPhone apart.

Whether it's worth the considerable premium, when the iPhone 18 Pro models are more capable (on paper), remains to be seen. We'll find out soon when we get to spend more hands-on time with it. Preorders open on October 16.

The iPhone Air is the first model of its kind. Borrowing from other Air models—the original MacBook Air and iPad Air—it's the thinnest iPhone ever made at a mere 5.6 mm and one of the lightest at 165 grams. The difference is palpable, especially considering its large 6.5-inch screen. Use the iPhone Air for a day, and the iPhone 18 Pro will feel like a brick.

It's not for everyone. Think of it like an early-adopter iPhone, as the design innovations no doubt informed the folding iPhone Duo. But there are a few too many compromises considering the price. Namely, the camera system. We're all used to multi-camera setups on our smartphones, and a single-lens design for a $1,100 handset is too limiting. It sports the same 48-MP main camera as the iPhone 17, though the cheaper iPhone sometimes delivers sharper results. You can use the 2X “optical-like” zoom, but that's it. There's no ultrawide and no telephoto camera. I even tried to take a close-up photo of a flower, and the lack of a macro mode meant I couldn't move the iPhone Air as close to the subject. Thankfully, it has the same great 18-MP selfie camera as the rest of the iPhone 17 lineup.

The other major compromise is battery life, though this depends on how you use your phone. I was pleasantly surprised by the iPhone Air's runtime, which often hit more than five hours of screen-on time. That's better than I expected. With average use, it lasted me a full day, and I didn't feel too anxious about it dying on me. However, on busier days, I needed to top it up in the afternoon. If you're a heavy user, relying on various battery-sucking apps like Maps or gaming, the iPhone Air's battery won't impress.

This, alongside the iPhone 17e, has Apple's custom C1X modem, which is more power efficient, and one of the ways Apple can max out the battery life on the Air. The downside is that it doesn't support millimeter-wave 5G (mmWave). It won't impact you much since the dominant form of 5G is sub-6 (we have an explainer here), but mmWave is deployed in dense urban areas and high-traffic areas like airports and stadiums. It's weird to not have it on a flagship smartphone in 2025.

If you barely use the camera and are regularly near a charger, there are plenty of cheaper smartphones that will serve you well. But if you must have an iPhone and want to try a super-thin and lightweight device, I think you'll be happy with the iPhone Air.

Apple no longer sells the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, but you can find them at alternative retailers. As long as you're not paying MSRP (anything close to what the new iPhone 18 Pro models cost), they're great buys.

They are some of the thickest iPhones in recent memory because Apple stuffed them with big batteries. For the first time, we didn't always need to charge an iPhone every single day. We routinely hit close to seven hours of screen-on time and had 30 or 40 percent left, depending on the device. Outside of battery and screen size, these two iPhones have the same features.

The second biggest upgrade in the iPhone 17 Pro models wasn't a sexy topic: thermal conductivity. Apple switched to aluminum and added a vapor chamber cooling system to manage heat better. By dissipating heat across the back of the devices, these iPhones stay cooler for longer and eke out more from the A19 Pro chipset. We played Assassin's Creed Mirage for more than an hour, and while the iPhone was warm, it had no hot spots. We saw no stutters or lag at max graphical settings, a step up from its predecessors. Meanwhile, the iPhone Air got uncomfortably hot in one spot, and we saw more stutters after prolonged play. If you plan to play demanding games on your smartphone or tackle processing-intensive tasks, buy one of the Pro models.

The cameras didn't just get a fun new redesign on the back. Apple upgraded the telephoto to 48 megapixels, so now every rear camera is 48 MP. It zooms up to 4X, though you can get optical-like quality at up to 8X. If you're wondering, yes, the iPhone 16 Pro offered 5X optical zoom, but the larger sensor and higher megapixel count mean you'll get sharper, brighter zoom photos on the iPhone 17 Pro. If you capture a lot of video with the rear cameras, that's another reason to buy these iPhones, because they offer some of the best native video quality on a smartphone. (We have plenty of examples in our review!)

The iPhone 17 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro Max are still plenty powerful for most folks. The new 18 Pro models slightly strengthen already strong areas of these phones (see above for what has been upgraded). But only the 17 Pro models come in orange!

While last year's iOS 26 debuted the divisive Liquid Glass, iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 focus squarely on quality-of-life improvements, with a redesigned and much improved Siri AI assistant, easier Shortcuts, and lots of little tweaks to enhance speed and stability.

Siri AI doesn't just look different—now resembling a glass orb—it can also understand your personal context, pulling info from your messages, emails, or even photos, and helping you draft messages or find the right wine to pair with your dinner. Siri can also now pop up in the camera app to help you choose your next book or split a bill with friends.

Apple says iOS 27 is faster than ever, with app launches up to 30 percent faster, newly captured photos in your Photo Library loading up to 70 percent faster, and AirDrop transfers completing up to 80 percent faster. For more details, read our guide on the top features in iOS 27 and how to download it.

Most of these are 30-watt chargers that will fast-charge most iPhones. If you want the fastest speeds on the iPhone 18 models, you'll need a 40-watt charger, and we have some picks for you.

Avoid These iPhones

The iPhone 14 and older iPhones are probably available somewhere, but you shouldn't take the bait. They don't have the processing power to keep up with the latest software, and even if they do, they will have a much shorter software shelf life or lack modern features like USB-C. The only older iPhones worth considering at the moment are the iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 series, even better if it's the Pro models, if you can find them at low prices. The iPhone 16e is also another option, though only if you can find it at a steep discount.

The iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, and iPhone XR are cut off from receiving the iOS 27 update, so they're especially ones to avoid. Without software support, your device will slowly become less secure and could become a slow, buggy mess.

The iPhone's Charging Port Is USB-C, Not Lightning

The iPhone 15 range ditched the long-standing Lightning port for USB-C, and it's in every iPhone since. This is the same charging port on iPads, MacBooks, Android phones, Windows laptops, and many more personal tech gadgets. USB-C is often called the “universal port” because it can technically handle various responsibilities. For example, you can plug in external displays and extend the iPhone's screen or connect the same USB-C accessories you might be currently using on your laptop, like SD card readers. Sadly, it does mean your Lightning accessories won't work unless you get dongles.

You can read more about what the port does here, but there are two important things to note:

The iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Plus, iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16e, iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, and iPhone Air support the USB 2.0 standard just like the iPhones before, so you'll max out at 480 megabits per second of data transfer speeds.

The iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo support the USB 3.0 standard and are capable of up to 10 gigabits per second of data transfer speeds.

What’s the Deal With eSIMs?

All iPhone 14 and newer devices completely ditch the physical SIM tray in the US, meaning you can no longer just pop your physical SIM inside to turn on cellular connectivity. Instead, you'll have to rely on an eSIM. You can read more about them here. This tech has been available in iPhones since the iPhone XS and XR, but now you have to use it. Apple has also started switching more global models to eSIM only, like the iPhone Air.) When you're setting up your new iPhone, you'll automatically be asked to transfer your number from your previous iPhone, and the whole process should take a few minutes without any hassle. (eSIMs are more secure than physical SIMs.) Once you transfer your number, your physical SIM card won't work anymore.

There's a chance you may still run into some issues, especially if you're coming from an Android phone (or want to switch back to an Android phone). You'll have to check with your carrier to get your cellular connection working again. It shouldn't take long, but it's not as simple as popping in a physical card.

How to Replace Your iPhone's Battery

If you don't want to spend the money to get a new iPhone, consider a fresh battery. If the biggest issues with your aging iPhone revolve around how long it lasts in a day, replacing the battery might make it feel brand-new. (Apple's iPhone 16, 16 Plus, and 16e have an easier-to-replace battery.)

Replacements for older iPhones are $89, and $99 or $119 for newer models. If that doesn't do the trick, read our guide on ways to fix your iPhone's problems or our guide on selling your iPhone to get the most money for it.

What Is the Action Button and Camera Control Button?

The Action Button debuted on the iPhone 15 Pro models, and it's now standard on every iPhone in the lineup. It sits above the volume rocker on the left edge of the phone. It effectively replaces the old Mute Switch, but think of it as just a configurable button. You can have it still control the mute function of the phone, or customize it (Settings > Action Button) to trigger the flashlight, a Voice Memo, or even launch an app or Shortcut.

Camera Control is another newer addition that debuted on the iPhone 16 series. On the right edge of the phone below the power button, press it to launch the Camera app, and you can press it to capture a photo or start recording a video. A light tap and swipe can move through different camera lenses or modes, but I found this annoying. (You can configure it by heading to Settings > Camera > Camera Control.) Press and hold this button, and you'll trigger Apple's Visual Intelligence. It'll use the camera to identify subjects in front of you, very much like Google Lens, so you can ask questions via Google or ChatGPT about what you're looking at.

People Are Pissed Off and Ready to Own Their Shit

Wired September 17, 2026

The train blasts through right as Louis Rossmann starts to speak. This has happened several times already at the event he’s hosting on a Friday night in San Jose, California. All the speakers before him patiently paused when the train on the nearby tracks roared by, its loud horn blaring, then resumed talking. But Rossmann is mid-sentence in his rapid-fire delivery about the topic he’s fiercely passionate about, and he doesn’t stop. He shouts over the train.

This is the penultimate stop of the Own Your Shit tour, a US-wide odyssey of events this summer put on by ownership advocate and YouTuber Louis Rossmann and his advocacy nonprofit Fulu. Around 80 people have crammed into the narrow side porch of a brewery. The final event will be in Silver Springs, Maryland, on October 1.

Before Rossmann spoke, panels featured an advocate from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, students from San Jose State University’s Fixit workshop, and a leader of the Fisker Owners Association, a group of vehicle owners who refuse to let their cars die. The main call to action is to kill a very specific piece of legislation: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Enacted in 1998, this section of the DMCA prohibits bypassing digital restrictions and locks enabled by a product manufacturer.

Ostensibly, the legislation was meant to ensure device security. Ownership and repair advocates have long criticized it for helping companies put software locks on devices and then charge owners for access to their own hardware. Rossmann, along with fellow advocate Kevin O’Reilly, started Fulu to pay out bounties for people who can disable digital locks on a device, even if there are legal consequences.

“How many people here enjoy it when they get threats of lawsuits?” Rossmann asks during the San Jose event. “Raise your hand.” Maybe four or five hands go up, including a grinning Rohit Chopra, the former director of the federal Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. “I enjoy when people try to sue me,” Rossmann says. “When they send me threats, I literally frame them.”

His presentation bounces through his various ownership- and repair-oriented fights. He calls out companies like Amazon, which removed books from people’s Kindles, and home pipe leak detector company Roost, which discontinued stand-alone Wi-Fi products to the dismay of its users. He criticized Apple, Sony, wheelchair companies, and BMW, which recently ran ads for the new Spider-Man movie on their customers’ dashboard screens. He accuses companies of adding paid subscriptions to their products after customers buy them as a form of “ransomware.”

It’s a righteous screed that feels infectious in the crowd. People cheer and call out their own ownership issues. Rossmann is a preacher at the pulpit of people pissed off by subscription services, the steady decline of physical media, and the inability to fix their stuff.

The Own Your Shit tour comes as people grow increasingly angry with companies like Sony ending physical disc support and deleting digital items in customers’ libraries. (Google has recently done something similar and deleted a user’s copy of The Lord of the Rings.) Amazon just ended support for its perfectly fine older Kindles. People feel squeezed by economic pressures as devices get more expensive and want to hang onto their devices longer.

Katharine Trendacosta, a director of policy and advocacy at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, spoke at the event to call out the way companies have turned just about everything into subscription services users have to pay for. “They get the subscription and our data,” Trendacosta says. “It's a win-win for them and a lose-lose for us.”

The tour may be coming to an end, but right-to-repair legislation has been growing worldwide. This year in the European Union, new regulations require companies to help extend the life of consumer products by making them more repairable and giving them more easily replaceable batteries. John Deere, long criticized for its repair-adverse policies, was hit with a $99 million lawsuit and a US Federal Trade Commission ruling requiring it to make its products more fixable. Repair advocates in the US have shot down anti-repair bills and are calling for federal regulation to ensure better automotive repairs and product longevity.

Chopra, the former director of the CFPB, now heads the newly established California Business and Consumer Services Agency, created in July by California governor Gavin Newsom. In a conversation after the event, he shared a vision for what the BCSA will focus on.

“New technology should not just help out people in the boardroom or in the C-suite,” Chopra says. “It's actually supposed to help all of us, but we are seeing how it can sometimes be designed to scam people, to rip people off, or sometimes create some real harm for them. People who are just trying to get by really feel totally hosed by some of these practices.”

Chopra says his goal in coming to this event was to help spread the word about the new agency and encourage people to reach out to their representatives about unfair consumer practices.

“We are going to be looking hard to make sure that we're cracking down on illegal practices,” Chopra says. “That there's actually some real enforcement, but also when it comes to new technology, that it's really actually helping everybody.”

After the event, I ask Rossmann how he’s feeling about the tour. He says he was initially worried that people were coming for the free pizza but was pleasantly surprised at how engaged and passionate the audiences have been.

“I’m feeling like there’s finally a turning of the tide,” Rossmann says.

Review: Soundboks Rider

Wired September 17, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

How loud is too loud? That's the question I find myself asking as I turn up the volume dial on the Soundboks Rider portable Bluetooth speaker. By myself, outdoors, a five or six on the dial is plenty loud; anything more starts to get uncomfortable. But this speaker can push out a ridiculous 118-decibel sound pressure level (dB SPL). That's basically a rock concert.

If that's your jam, this may be your perfect speaker. It's distinct, stylish, built to last, and, importantly, sounds great. But it's absolutely overkill for most people, who would be better off with a smaller, more affordable speaker from the likes of Sony, JBL, or Marshall, all of which offer plenty of tamer options below the Rider's $600 price tag.

Soundboks Rider Specs

Soundboks Rider

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Soundboks Rider looks like no other portable speaker I've tested. It resembles something you'd find on stage at a concert rather than at your next barbecue. Its restrained design is almost the antithesis of the flashy, LED-pulsing party speakers you might find from brands like JBL or Samsung.

The build quality is impressive, confidence-inspiring, and clearly made to last. It's built like a tank, with a steel front grille, silicone rubber ball corners, and a thick plastic cabinet. During a drop test, I was frankly more worried about the speaker breaking my stairs than my stairs breaking the speaker. Another win for longevity is the replaceable battery—it charges via USB-C, and you can swap it in and out in seconds. This feels like a speaker you could have for decades.

While smaller than Soundboks' other speakers, it is still much larger than your average Bluetooth unit, and a bit awkward to carry with its single carry-grip on one corner. I would have loved to see two carry handles, one on each side. That would make the Rider easier and more flexible to carry, similar to the Sony ULT Field 7.

Unlike the larger Soundboks Mix and Soundboks 4, this is meant to be a stand-alone speaker—it does not have Soundboks' wireless multi-speaker connectivity (SKAA TeamUp), a speaker stand mount, or additional inputs (read: XLR).

Soundboks speakers can get loud, and despite the Rider being the smallest in the brand's lineup, its audio output is astonishing. I was frankly scared to turn this speaker up to max volume (11 on the dial, IYKYK).

To spare my New York City neighbors, I took this speaker outdoors and cranked it to 11; even then, I could only manage it for a short while before I worried someone would call 311 to file a noise complaint. Which is to say: the Rider is plenty loud for most parties I can think of.

Soundboks Rider

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

But the Rider isn't just loud—it's clear. Across all volume ranges, it sounds great. While it can produce big bass, it isn't overpowering in the mix. The sound profile matches the speaker's understated, PA-style aesthetic—clear, strong, and detailed.

The speaker can output up to 118 dB SPL. That's well within painful levels, and similar to a rock concert. I'm honestly not sure when or where I'd need to push out that much audio, but if you ever do, the Rider is game.

The app is similarly streamlined and unfussy. You can control basically every speaker function remotely, including volume, sound profiles, EQ modes, and even turning it off.

Connecting, however, was a little finicky. I had to pair, unpair, re-pair, power off, and power on a few times before the app and speaker would actually start talking to each other. That was even more irritating because, after a firmware update, the app told me to forget the speaker and re-pair all over again. I've tested hundreds of wireless audio gadgets—Bluetooth connectivity issues with brand-new products are less surprising than you might think and often get sorted out within a month or two of software updates. Still, it made the whole experience feel decidedly less premium than the Rider's $600 price might suggest.

The Soundboks Rider is an excellent speaker. In terms of loudness, durability, and battery life, it runs circles around most of the competition, including larger party-slash-karaoke speakers like the Sony Tower 5 and JBL PartyBox Club 120.

But as a larger, portable Bluetooth speaker meant to stand all on its own, it's a bit niche, especially for $600. I do think it's overkill for a lot of people—I can't think of many folks in my life who need this combination of loud and bombproof in their speaker. You can also get plenty of portable Bluetooth speakers for less (the aforementioned $500 Sony ULT Field 7 and $330 JBL PartyBox Encore Essential 2 come to mind) that might do the job just fine.

Soundboks says this is a portable party speaker built for spontaneity and outdoor adventure. For my spontaneous adventures, the Rider is overkill. But if your adventures include a lot more people (and a lot more space) than mine, it might be the perfect fit—big enough to bring to any party and durable enough that you never have to worry about it.

Fast & Furious Takes a Victory Lap With a Ferociously Fun Roller Coaster

Wired September 17, 2026

Toward the end of my college days, I harbored a not-so-secret crush. She and I carried on a mild flirtation, dancing around the possibility of more, but it wasn’t until she found out I’d never seen The Fast and the Furious that she gave me an opening.

“What?!” she exclaimed. “It’s my favorite movie!” So we made plans to watch it at her dorm the next day. Even if I didn’t like it, I reasoned, the experience would constitute a worthy reversal of the trope about men forcing testosterone-soaked action movies on their girlfriends. I’ll spare you the details of what happened that afternoon, but it may come as no surprise that I gave the film an enthusiastic five-star review.

In the 25 years since the launch of the franchise, F&F has massively capitalized on such runaway infatuations. The big, bald, sleeveless blockbusters serve as monuments to America’s demented car culture, product placement (Corona, anyone?), and the ambiguously defined bonds of “family”—pronounced “fambly.” With their high-octane set pieces that ignore all known physics, leavened by subpar acting and threadbare storylines, the films invite us to submit to some reptilian part of our brain that cares only for power and speed.

Which is why the series was ideal inspiration for Universal Studios Hollywood’s new foray into cutting-edge outdoor roller coasters. On Wednesday, the long-anticipated Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift opened to the public, offering parkgoers the chance to hop into replicas of the movies’ muscle cars—including Dom Toretto’s 1970 Dodge Charger R/T—that spin and soar along more than 4,000 feet of track at speeds of up to 72 miles per hour. (A different version of the ride is slated to debut at Universal’s Florida park next year.)

The day before, select media and content creators had the chance to experience the attraction without the inconvenience of waiting in line, and I’m pleased to report that it didn't disappoint: I rode it three times in a row and could have gone back for more. Its four launch sections and three corkscrew inversions made for a whip-fast adrenaline rush, augmented by revving motor noise from seat-mounted speakers. In Dom’s lead car, you can even detect the braking resistance as you slide into a drift. I hollered with glee throughout each circuit, making sure to occasionally shout “TOLUCA LAKE,” the name of the affluent neighborhood next door; residents have been very upset about all the screaming.

If you want to feel like you’re a Fast & Furious character within the safer confines of a precisely engineered thrill machine, you can hardly ask for anything better. And despite its innovative design, the overall aesthetic of the ride and its environs demonstrates a welcome nostalgia for the more grounded origins of these movies, when the crew was hijacking trucks full of DVD players instead of launching Pontiacs into space. On your way through the queueing path, you’ll pass garage workbenches littered with tools and LA-style street murals that pay homage to racing culture.

Those welcome simple touches might make you wonder if we’ll ever actually see the conclusion of the increasingly bloated and absurd F&F saga in the perpetually delayed 11th film, Fast Forever. Between the ongoing rewrites and budgetary obstacles, it has yet to even enter production. (The previous film, Fast X, was released in 2023.) Rather than being too big to fail, it’s as though the challenge of topping each successive spectacle has made the Furious brand too unwieldy to push forward.

Could it be that, in the absence of a finale, the F&F rides will cap off the series? In their invitation for Tuesday’s press preview event, Universal noted that Vin Diesel himself would be on hand during a ceremony to help executives cut the ribbon (or, as it happened, a fake plastic chain). But the man synonymous with the franchise was nowhere to be found when the time came to declare the ride officially open. The closest we got was a gaggle of fans in costume as Toretto, complete with bald caps.

When I checked out Diesel’s Instagram account for clues as to what he was up to, I found that he had just posted set photos of himself as Kaulder, his character from The Last Witch Hunter, a 2015 dark fantasy film. Lionsgate confirmed last year that a sequel is in the works, and it appears that Diesel was stoking anticipation with this sneak peek. When this guy isn’t acknowledging a major milestone for the burnt-rubber films that made him a household name, you have to wonder if there’s much gas left in the tank.

Not everything lasts—certainly not college flings that start with stunt-driver flicks. That the Fast & Furious series has earned billions of dollars and spanned a quarter century based on an equally thin premise is a testament to how far this juvenile spirit can take you. Maybe bringing it to life with a really fun roller coaster is the best way to let it roar off into the sunset. When you climb aboard, take a look around at your fellow passengers. You’re the family now.

The EU Wants to Break Up Kids and Their Chatbots

Wired September 17, 2026

The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.

The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to 6 percent of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.

Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.

Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.

The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors’ health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only. “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clampdowns on addictive design more widely.

In documents seen by WIRED, the European Commission says it is worried that dependency on chatbots may negatively impact a child’s development and its relationships with other humans. It’s also concerned by chatbots giving minors dangerous advice, including on their mental health and personal development, which it said can shape and encourage risky behavior.

“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with children’s mental health,” President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press conference on Thursday. Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey across France, Germany, Sweden, and Ireland. Australia and the UK are both attempting to restrict minors’ access to chatbots through their social media bans.

It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes generated by chatbots, which von der Leyen nodded at in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech: “We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.” While the EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August, the rules currently only apply to deepfakes generated for commercial use.

The Commission also blames digital distraction for a decline in basic skills in young people. Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don’t, according to research spanning 91 countries by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling “expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools,” researchers from the independent network EU Kids Online wrote in a report.

Hundreds of Election Deniers Will Be on the Ballot This November

Wired September 17, 2026

On November 3, when voters across the US go to the polls, almost 200 election deniers will be on the ballot. Many of them have repeatedly undermined the very process they are participating in, and they will be looking to win some of the most powerful elected positions in the country—positions that would help determine how voting goes in future elections.

Following the primaries, there will be 197 election deniers on the ballot for congressional and statewide races in the midterms across 43 states, according to new data shared exclusively with WIRED by States United Action, a nonpartisan nonprofit that supports state officials in protecting elections.

These numbers include a sitting US congressman who voted against certifying the 2020 election results; a former state representative who integrated QAnon conspiracy theories into election denialism; and local election officials who have actively sought to undermine election results by pushing baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizen voting.

But for election experts and officials, one of the biggest concerns ahead of the midterms is the possibility that these election deniers could obtain oversight of the 2028 presidential election process. The data shows there are already 27 election deniers in 20 states who hold a statewide office with election oversight, like secretary of state or attorney general—positions that allow the holder to set voting rules or prosecute those they believe are cheating at the ballots. In November, 33 election deniers will seek to secure similar positions in states across the country.

“All Americans should be concerned if people who are trying to undermine trust in elections and trying to interfere in the election process are taking positions of responsibility over elections,” Wendy Weiser, vice president for democracy at the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, tells WIRED. “We've seen in recent years an increasing number of election deniers taking some positions of public trust. As the numbers increase, it just increases the risk to our election system. This really is an attempt to corrode the system from within.”

The huge roster of election deniers on the ballot in November has also been emboldened by a groundswell of local groups and individuals who have been working for years to promote baseless claims about mail-in voting, noncitizen voter fraud, and rigged voting machines.

And from the top, President Donald Trump has increasingly pushed election-denial conspiracy theories, according to data gathered by States United Action. The group’s data shows that 60 percent of Trump’s statements referencing elections since the 2024 election include an explicit claim of fraud, rigging, or theft. That percentage has risen to 84 percent in the second quarter of 2026.

"The election-denial movement is more powerful than ever, and it's a direct threat to our freedom to vote,” Joanna Lydgate, CEO of States United Action, tells WIRED. “Election deniers are embedded at every level of government, pushing conspiracy theories from positions of real power.”

WIRED is keeping a close eye on many of these impactful races featuring election deniers. Here are five of the midterm races featuring election deniers that WIRED and States United Action are tracking:

In the wake of the 2020 election, former US representative Mike Rogers slammed Trump’s efforts to persuade Georgia’s secretary of state to change the election results as “more gangster than presidential.” He was also unequivocal in his assessment of Trump’s role in the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021: “You’re damn right you had responsibility for this,” Rogers said at the time.

But now, seeking a return to Congress as the Republican nominee for Senate in Michigan, Rogers appears to see election denialism as a winning campaign strategy. “I am thankful for President Trump’s commitment to transparency. The news coming out of the White House tonight is deeply troubling—especially that of a voter fraud scheme right here in Michigan,” Rogers wrote on X moments after Trump delivered a conspiracy-filled speech about election fraud, including a long-debunked claim about fraud in Michigan.

Polls show Rogers in a dead heat with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

In December 2020, as a member of Congress, Tom Tiffany signed up for a Texas lawsuit seeking to invalidate President Joe Biden’s victory. Tiffany also voted against certifying the results in Pennsylvania and Arizona on January 6, 2021, after the attack on the Capitol and has suggested he would have overturned Wisconsin’s results too. This year, Tiffany has warmly welcomed the FBI’s baseless investigation into the state’s elections.

As governor, Tiffany would have the power to appoint some of the state’s top election officials on the Wisconsin Elections Commission, giving him the ability to install election deniers to oversee voting for the 2028 presidential election.

Initial polls show Tiffany slightly trailing his Democrat opponent, David Crowley.

Billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy has long questioned the 2020 electron results and has baselessly claimed that it was stolen by “big tech.” Ramaswamy has also called the January 6 attack on the Capitol an “inside job” and “entrapment.” He has provided no evidence to back up any of these claims.

As part of his campaign for governor, Ramaswamy has supported voter-suppression measures that enshrine restrictive voter ID law into the state’s constitution. If Ramaswamy becomes Ohio governor, he would be in a position to have much more power over forcing such measures through and could deeply impact the 2028 presidential election.

Polling suggests the race is extremely tight.

Former Nevada state representative Jim Marchant says being called an election denier is a “badge of honor.” Marchant was among the most ardent boosters of election denial in the wake of the 2020 election, going so far as to help arrange a QAnon coalition of candidates for the 2022 midterms.

November’s race will be a rerun of the 2022 race, when Marchant lost to current secretary of state Cisco Aguilar. While he won the GOP primary in June, Marchant lacks support from much of the Republican establishment and has struggled to raise money. (Filings from July show Marchant had just $13.86 in his campaign war chest, compared to over $1 million for his opponent.)

Marchant has radical plans to overhaul Nevada’s voting system if he wins, including deregistering every single voter in the state, moving to paper ballots, and requiring all votes to be counted by hand. As secretary of state, Marchant would be able to change election procedures and advise county election officials, and he would help certify statewide results for the 2028 presidential election.

No public polling is available for the race.

In Colorado, the Republican candidate for secretary of state is avowed election denier James Wiley. Wiley says the 2020 election was stolen and that, if victorious, his first act would be to delete Colorado’s voter lists and force every citizen to reregister. (This is illegal on both a federal and state level.) He also wants to do away with all voting machines but at the same time place all public records on the blockchain, according to his campaign website.

Wiley, who calls himself “the red flame of liberty” due to his red hair, has admitted using the ELLY tool to back up his claims that up to 25 percent of registered voters in Colorado have issues with their voter registration. The ELLY tool was developed by the creators of EagleAI, a tool created by a former doctor which was used ahead of the 2024 election by conservative activists to challenge voter roll registrations, often based on inaccurate data.

His opponent, Amanda Gonzalez, is the current Jefferson County clerk and previously ran Common Cause Colorado, a nonpartisan, good-government advocacy group.

No public polling is available for the race.

The Trump Administration Sends a New Signal to Alien Disclosure Whistleblowers

Wired September 17, 2026

Just over a year ago, Dylan Borland—a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist—told a House Oversight task force that he'd watched a roughly 100-foot triangular craft lift silently off the flight line at Langley Air Force Base in 2012. But there were some questions he couldn’t answer.

Nearly half a dozen times during the hearing, he told members of Congress he could only answer their questions, such as whether a private company he worked for was reverse engineering nonhuman technology, inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF. He said he was concerned whether he was “legally even allowed to answer” some questions and at one point cited a fear of being charged under the Espionage Act.

A year later, on September 14, the Defense Department announced it had lowered that risk, though it falls short of what some in the unidentified anomalous phenomena research community say is needed to achieve broad transparency.

The Pentagon said on Monday that it had issued a "targeted legal waiver" allowing all current and former “service members, civilian personnel, and contractors" holding UAP-related national defense information to disclose it to the White House–directed effort that has been dumping UFO files on war. gov since May.

The waiver, which hasn’t been made public, "supersedes civil and administrative enforcement provisions" of NDAs and special access program agreements, "strictly for communications directed to the PURSUE team," a reference to the White House program. Basically, if you signed a secrecy agreement and know something about UFOs, you can now tell PURSUE without being sued or losing your clearance, though the same protections don’t extend to speaking with Congress, the press, or the public. The release announcing the waiver says nothing about criminal law, and only covers agreements "previously executed within the United States."

President Donald Trump telegraphed the move over the summer when he reportedly directed the Defense Department and the intelligence community to waive UAP-related NDAs. It was reinforced on July 31 when Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas sent a memo to 18 intelligence chiefs declaring that any NDAs “prohibiting disclosure to the President, or designees like PURSUE, are no longer in force.” The memo cited a “Presidential Direction” it never quotes and gave the intelligence community 30 days to set up its own procedures. That deadline passed in August. The White House directed a request for comment to the Defense Department. An agency spokesperson said it had no additional comment outside the press release and referred further questions to the White House.

Borland, the kind of person all of this was written for, is unmoved.

“Bad-faith actors are talking about, ‘Oh, this allows whistleblowers to go and talk to the public.’ No, it doesn't. It changes nothing,” he tells WIRED. “It's one more place to go.

“Those of us who already became whistleblowers, we already were told that our NDAs were waived. We were legally allowed to talk to AARO,” he says, referring to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, created in 2022 to investigate UAP reports and serve as the official channel for whistleblowers. He adds that the new directive essentially “just repeated what we've been told for three, four years.”

A provision Congress passed in December 2022 already states that an authorized UAP disclosure—meaning one made through AARO—"shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement," complies with classification rules, and "is not a violation" of the relevant section of the Espionage Act. The channel was AARO and Borland used it.

But AARO has little credibility with the people it was built to hear from, especially after its former director publicly questioned the credibility of whistleblowers, and its March 2024 historical report found no evidence the government had ever recovered alien technology. Borland told Congress that he met with AARO in March 2023, but that he withheld sources and methods because he considered the agency's public assessments up until then, "a misrepresentation of the truth." That August, after a former intelligence officer testified about an alleged decades-long crash-retrieval program, Borland filed a complaint with the intelligence community's inspector general over what he says he knew and the retaliation he says he’d faced.

Since then, he wrote in his statement to Congress, he has "been prevented from resuming my prior employment" and remains “blacklisted from certain agencies within the Intelligence Community.”

Other UAP whistleblowers have faced similar issues after coming forward, from break-ins at their homes to leaked personal details.

The new waiver also only covers those who have worked with the Pentagon, leaving a CIA-sized hole in it.

“I'm glad that they're waiving NDAs for everybody who was on the [Defense Department] side,” Borland says. “It doesn't change the [Intelligence Community] side.”

He pointed to the need to offer similar protections to the alphabet soup of intelligence agencies beyond just the CIA, including the National Security Agency, FBI, and others, as well as science agencies like NASA.

Marik von Rennenkampff, a former State Department analyst and Obama-era Pentagon appointee now at the Sol Foundation, a UAP research nonprofit, agrees with that sentiment because of where whistleblowers say the secrets about nonhuman technology are kept. He points to a specific unit in the CIA that’s “allegedly—allegedly, allegedly, allegedly, I can't stress that enough—the quarterback for this alleged legacy effort.”

“What has been announced publicly does not cover the core of the alleged legacy program yet,” von Rennenkampff tells WIRED.

There's a second gap that no memo can close. Many of the people alleged to hold this information work for private contractors, and the government can't waive an NDA it isn't party to. Only the 2022 statute addresses those types of agreements, and only for disclosures made through the official AARO channel.

Despite these shortcomings, UAP researchers and whistleblowers point to, von Rennenkampff argues this week’s announcement is still important.

“After 80 years of government denial, obfuscation, and ridicule on this topic, there's now true political capital invested in this,” he says. Unlike AARO, PURSUE is a “presidentially directed initiative” that is reporting ultimately to political appointees in the White House, “versus career bureaucrats.”

“It shows that the Trump administration is taking extraordinary claims about retrievals of a craft of nonhuman origins seriously,” he says. There’s a phrase in the release that von Rennenkampff says is another curious detail, particularly given how “wordsmithed to hell” government statements about UAP generally are. The Pentagon wrote that “individuals with direct knowledge of UAP-related programs” have historically feared legal liability for speaking.

“It doesn't say people with partial knowledge, half knowledge, alleging knowledge,” he says. “It says people with direct knowledge.”

Borland's hope is that PURSUE answers to someone with the power to act on what it hears. He points to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller—who Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed is working on the UAP portfolio—as someone who would signal the White House is doing more than paying lip service to the topic.

Beyond that, Borland has an offer.

“There's enough smoke, and there's enough people behind the scenes,” he says, referring to himself and other whistleblowers. “If Stephen Miller and Trump wanted to actually know some stuff, they could call us into the White House right now, and I can throw down, and so can the rest of them.”
